div.head: PRIMITIVE AND ODD PLACES.
div.p: PRIMITIVE AND ODD PLACES.

'The Albanian inhabitants are a primitive folk, and look as " autochthonous " as their black, mud-caked buffaloes, round whose necks they hang strings of blue beads. We liked the Al- banians, though I should have been sorry to have travelled through their Country without a large escort before the coming of the Servian • Army. We stayed to bait for half an hour in a pure Albanian village, and they insisted on our partaking of pancakes and Devonshire cream, which appear to be the native luxuries, ' dispensed with true Moslem hospitality. Some of them knew Arabic, having served in Arabia in the Turkish Army, and they told the Arab- speaking member of our party that they had fought last winter against the Servians, and were beaten by the cannon, which they regarded as an unfair weapon in war; war, the game of life, should not be played with loaded dice, was clearly their view. Some others, who spoke to us in the same fashion, were now cheerfully 'wearing the Montenegrin uniform as a means of keeping arms in their hands. The Servians were rapidly drawing their troops out of this region to meet the Bulgars, and feared no Albanian rising as a result. They fought the Albanians to a finish last winter, and have since disarmed them in a way the Turks never did. They have established order and safety where murder and robbery used to be the ordinary incidents of life. They have done this both by rough and gentle methods. They have carried off hostages of the Albanian chiefs' families to Uskub and Belgrade, and they have distributed food and seed corn (maize) in the Albanian vil- lages. We travelled a short way with a Ser- vian officer, who was a specialist at managing Albanians, and we saw Albanians leave their

work in the fields and run up to talk to him, asking him to be their member when the con- stitution was established, and kissing him at parting. Apart from the kissing, I should guess that their relations to this man were rather like those of Indian hill tribes to a Sahib of the right sort. Whether these good relations are the rule or the exception, I am utterly un- able to say. But our impression is that the Servians are at least trying to do their duty by "their part of Albania. The compromise arrived at by Europe, dividing autonomous Albania from this district, my have been the most just, and certainly saved us from European war, so lam all in its favour. But one odd result is that the market towns of Prisrend, Djakova and Ipek are for the first time cut off from the mountain districts, to which they act as the sole trade centres. Some of the Servians wish to put no tariff on goods from the mountains, in the hope of using the trade and intercourse of these towns as a means of insinuating Ser- vian influence into autonomous Allopia. The hamlets at the foot of the mountains are the oddest places I have ever seen. They con- sist of isolated houses, each in its own grounds, buried in lush vegetation. Each of these build- ing is a tall tower of war, with no windows below, and small arched loopholes, like Anglo- Saxon windows, just under the roof. In size, character and purpose they resemble the "peel towers" of our Northumbrian border. Until
last winter, the Albanian warrior patriarchs in

these strongholds used to wage each his blood- feud on the men of the rival clan in the tower over the way. The Servian,minority cowered unarmed in one-storey houses below. That regime is now over, and the population is dis- armed. I hope they won't find life too dull. At Detchani, in the middle of this wild region, we were amazed to find a fourteenth-century Italian church that would have done credit as cathedral to any city in Italy. It was in the style of Siena Cathedral, in alternate stripes of white and coloured marble. The marble came from the mountains above, the Italian architect from the Illyrian Coast, then pitrt Of the Seryian Empire. The saintly King Stefan is I'm:led inside it in a fine marble sa,crophagus worthy of St. Praxed's. The whole interior is covered 'with frescoes in Italian and Byzantine styles. The monks showed us gold reliquaries and vessels that would have, made a collector's mouth water, with inscriptions round them,

saying that King Stefan gave them to the mon- astery. All this before KOSSOVO and the Turkish flood, five hundred years ago! Since then these rare treasures and this wonderful church have been left intact in the midst of a population of professional robbers, like Scott's Highlanders, of a religion hostile to the monks. This apparent miracle of preservation has been wrought by the superstitious awe with which the Albanians regarded the memory and shrine of King Stefan; although they are Moslems, they regard him as "their saint," and when ill they like to come and lie under his tomb. So the sanctuary has been respected all these cen- turies; but the Father Superior told us that he and his monks used not to be able to go out even into the pine woods on the hill opposite their door, without great risk of being shot. And when they wanted to go to Prisrend they had to pay blackmail to two Albanian chiefs to ' ride with them and keep off the others. Mon- tenegrin soldiers are now going in and out of the monastery, where no uniform but the Turk- ish has been 'seen for 500 years. And the monks I and everyone else can go safely about their business.—From "A Holiday Among the Ser- vians," by G. M. TREVELYAN.

div.head: COMMON MISTAKE.
div.p: A COMMON MISTAKE.

When called upon to prepare something b.; heart most people make the mistake of learn- ing it in bits. If it be a hundred of lines of Shakespeare they first attack four lines and repeat these continually until they are known, When another four are tacked on and so on. This is a wasteful proceeding as any psychologist will tell you. A better method is the following. A lecturer of the writer's acquaintance who never lectures with notes; and whose eloquence is often a surprise to his friends, has really little eloquence at all. He first writes out his lecture in full. He then reads it right through from beginning to end attending all the while to gesture and ex- pression just as if he were delivering it to an audience. This having been once done, he puts the lecture by for the night. After about six such repetitions he finds that he knows the whole- thing without the help of a single note. Now the method he has adopted from experience, is one which would find the fullest approval from all those who have seri- ouslw studied the subject from a scientific point of view. The principles involved in the method are these:—do not learn things in bits but as complete wholes; do net weary yourself by overmuch struggling at oce time, short sittings are better than long ones: take a reasonable length of time between the attempts to memorise—even when learning quite sisart things wait four or five minutes between each repetition, and finally do not attempt to recite the material you are co'll.- mitting to memory until you are fairly sure of success for every failure is almost as disas- trous in its effects as no attempt stt all.

div.head: BIBLE SOCIETY'S WORK.
div.p: BIBLE SOCIETY'S WORK.
The Modest, Industrious and Helpful Handmaiden of the Churches.
BURMAH AND OPIUM.

• The splendid work accomplished by the British and Foreign Bible Society is well known, and there was a fair attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Auxiliary of the Society in the Patten Hall on Tuesday evening. The. Rev. A. H. Bestall (late of India and translater of the Bible into Burmese) was ,the principal speaker, and dealt in an interesting manner with the society's work in Burmah. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton presided, and there were also present, amongst others, the Rev. and Hon. C. F. Cross, the Revs. B. Percival, E. L. J. Roberts, E. Morgan, W. Reid, H. Williamson, Joseph Howard and J. 0. Haughton (district secretary, Waterloo, Liverpool), Mr. C. E. Parker, Mr. J. Bailey, and Mr. J. C. Holland (one of the honorary, secretaries). After referring to the family bereavement which had prevented the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis) from presiding, and expressing his sincere sympathA, the CHAIRMAN offered all present a cordial welcome into that building, which had been given by the Misses Wilson Patten. They would all be acquainted with the work of the Bible Society, he continued, .which vas the placing of the Bible within the reach of all, both at home and abroad, so as to leave them without excuse for neglecting the perusal and study of the Sacred Book: (Hear, hear.) The society could not do everything. It could circulate and distribute copies of the Scriptures, but it could not make the people read them. Unless the friends of the society adopted the right attitude they would be in danger of falling below the level of the heathen, because their own privileges were so much greater than those of the heathen. They must use their privileges with more earnestness, and prove themselves worthy of the great blessings which God had bestowed upon them.
Wycliffe P.S.A

There was the usual meeting on Sunday, pre- sided over by Mr. Farrar. The speaker was Mr. Woolley, who gave a very eloquent address Upon "The joys by the way in Christian ser- vice, and the bright prospect of the greater joys before us." If all Christians, he said, were in downright earnest, they could soon fill the churches and chapels. Mr. McEachern and Mr. A. Healey also took part in the meeting 4 Mr. R. Wallington pre- sided at the organ. Two new members received a hearty welcome. Mr. James urged upon the captains and the members to do all in their power to get new members. The secretary read a letter from Mr. A. Griffiths. Ontario, Canada. thanking the brethren of Wycliffo P.S.A. for their kind letter of sympathy sent to him and his family on the death of Mrs. Griffiths.

div.head: LOCAL WORKERS.
div.p: LOCAL WORKERS.

In his announcement, Mr. HOLLAND said that the collections on behalf of the society last year and the year previous amounted respectively to about £4O or £5O. At. one time they came to £6O and £BO, and occasionally nearer .2100. The officers of the society were anxious to obtain the last-nana6d sum each year, and he appealed to the ladies of the town to assist them in the work of collection. After giving the names of several of the collectors, and the amounts ob• tamed by them, he specially referred to the work of the late Mrs. Robert Garnett, and said that the work in Penketh was now being den, by the Rev. J. Gunnell and Mrs. C. E. Parker. On behalf of the committee he thanked the ladies who had rendered assistance to the society for so many years.

GREAT AGENCY FOR UNIFICATION. The Rev. A. H. BESTALL said that although he was at home his heart was beyond the waves. They were met that night as disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ. The word "disciple" was one of the sweetest words in our language to him, for it came home to him many 'years ago. After relating a story in which a British officer had come and told him of a young girl who was attending a sick person, and he telling the offi- cer that she was a disciple, Mr. Bestall said that in Burma' to-day they did not call their con- verts " Christians," but "disciples," and from the frontier down to the sea, when a Buddhist became a Christian, he or she became a dis- ciple. He was pleased to say that in the whole course of his missionary deputation work he had found a spiritual atmosphere to pervade all their gatherings; and unless they had that they would do no good. Every body of men working otde•vW ever sent of at home and abroad for the sooiety must possess tho right attitude of mindto their Lord and f world. (Applause.) G Master. They were few in number that even- ing,ent wd oi e and yet they were at the base of a mighty Bi givingof he ord f Goa very great and useful society, and which was fighting the Those present could do as much in their own odvetmo etnhte—a wholelil movement f m the circleabioa d as. Theythe w finester missionaryesupporters fight and winning the world for Jesus. That great agency for the disemination of the Word of God throughout the world performed a very useful work, inasmuch as it 'brought their minds and thoughts back to the Word of God. He had always thought that a meeting of this description resolved itself into a praise meeting. They praised God for the Bible, and when they thought of it they remembered that it was His gift. Did they often praise Him for such a tremendous gift as the Book of God to them? A glorious company of the Apostles had praised God for His work; a noble army of martyrs had laid down their lives for it. God had given them the Word, not only. to live and enjoy their lives by it, but to scatter it. They should re- fresh their minds as to the work being done by that society, 'which, he thought, was the premier society of the world. He had his own Missionary Society, but he bowed before that great missionary institution, the British and Foreign. Bible' Society. (Applause.) It was a splendid unifier out in the mission "field." Indeed it was the' greatest agency for unification on the "field," and he was glad to bear his testimony to that important and interesting fact. To whatever part of the Church they belonged, the society was the handmaiden— modest, industrious and helpful. After illus- trating the unity which the various mission- aries worked under, and the good results accru- ing from united effort, the speaker instanced Burmali, where le said it was now quite safe to travel alone at night without fear of molestation. The people were getting the Word in their hearts and it was making a vast difference. The great land of Upper Burmah was entering into a life of 'peace and happiness. The opium had been kept out of that country, and, as a Govern- ment, we did' all we could for that land. In the early days of the annexation, hungry India and the Viceroy looked to Burmah, and the word went round, " Revenue ! Opium !" but Sir Charles Crossley said: "These people of this new province are not opium makers, and I won't make them. We ill keep the opium out, even if the • revenue suffers." (Applause.) As a Government, continued the speaker, we are doing much to save that great land. They must, if not as a Government, as a Christian nation, give that great land to Jesus, and there was no society which was more potent in that direction than the Bible Society. (Hear, hear.) He had no exact statistics to give to the meet- ing, but he could tell them that hundreds of thousands of copies of the Bible had been trans- lated into the language of the Burmese, and had been sold in the north, south, east and west for a farthing, although the publications cost 100 per cent. more. They put the small charge on' the books, for if they did not the people would not value them as much. The society, as a great company of apostles, was doing what it/could to save the people, and he asked for the support of the people of Warrington in the good work which they all knew the society was doing. (Applause.) ON COMMON GROUND.

- - - Mr. PARSER proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, the Rev. A. fl. Bestall, and to those who had granted the -lige of the hall for the meeting, and said that he had proposed a vote of thanks to most 'people of importance in the town, but he had never had the pleasure of doing so in the case of Mr. Carleton. It was one of the great advantages of the society that its supporters met on common ground 'and that it gave him an opportunity of •thanking ()he of the grand old men of Warrington. (Api-lause.) He felt sure that the speech which had been delivered by the deputation had impressed all present by its simplicity, power and vividness. He had not heard a more perfect, powerful an.? convincing speech at a meeting of the Bible

Society. The Rev. B. PERCIVAL seconded. He said that if they had the speaker in Warrington more frequently they would all become disciples in the purest sense and become missionaries throughout Warrington. In that event they would, require a larger hall than that to hold the people. There was a great danger of the churches forgetting that they were disciples. but they wanted to return to discipleship. They needed to think far more of discipleship than they did. The Rev. a.nd Hon. C. F. CROSS put the reso- lution, which was carried heartily. Miss Weaver presided at the piano: A collection, was made on behalf of the society,

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Harvest Thanksgiving.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Harvest Thanksgiving.

The thanksgiving services for the safe in- gathering of the harvest were tonducted at Bold- street on Sunday, when the preachers chose sub- jects suitable for the occasion. In accordance with the old custom the chapel was decorated with fruit, flowers and other out- ward and visible signs of the plentitude of the harvest; and this decoration, coupled with the special music, gave a real note of rejoicing and thanksgiving to both the morning and the evening meetings. The anthems, especially the one sung at the evening service, were exceed- ingly appropriate; and the choir is to be con- gratulated on the balance and-general rendition of the pieces. In the morning the superintendent minister, the Rev. W. A. Beckett, chose for his text a por- tion of the Lord's Prayer: "Give us this day our daily bread." The prayer, he said, is a recognition of the dependence of man upon his Creator for his daily requirements. In the evening the Rev. IL 'Williamson spoke on the words found in St. John xii. 24, 25, "Except a grain of wheat fall into the ground and die it abideth alone . . . ." We must, he said, leave the motive which impelled these Greeks to see Christ to inference. It would appear that it was the greatness of soul of the Saviour that attracted them. Christ saw in these men the first fruits of his own labour and self-sacrifice. Here was a welcome sign, amidst much that depressed, that all had not been given in vain. This was the beginning of a mighty ingathering. The illustration is commonplace. A grain of wheat alone is without influence. A grain of wheat in the ground loses itself, and out of the loss comes fruitfulness and gain. This is self- sacrifice, and self-sacrifice applied means that self is no longer the prime consideration. Self-abnegation was the fundamental prin- ciple in the life of Christ, and the Saviour shrank from nothing which the loving will of God demanded. The individual desires of the Saviour were crushed again and again to bring about God's plan. Examples from life of self-sacrifice are num- erous. The influential lives in the nation are not to be found among the selfish men. The effective lives are those given entirely to the service of their fellows. Every one can be effective, and the way to efficiency is through submission of self to Christ. It is in reality a choice of sacrifices. "He that loveth his life shall lose it." But he that loseth his life in self-surrender to Christ shall keep it unto life eternal.

Having given some idea, then, that there is within the body a personality, he proceeded to outline death in order to prepare the way for the proper understanding of "Resurrection." Death, whether bodily, spiritual or eternal, means separation only, bodily death being sep- aration of personality from its- tabernacle, as Peter said, "I must put off this my takernacle" (2 Peter i. 14). Peter spoke of putting off his body, which was bodily death. Spiritual death is the separation which exists between sinners, living in sin, and God, they having no fellow- ship nor, communion with God now while in such a state of existence on earth, and eternal death refers to the future eternal state of existence of the unsaved when separated from eternal glory. Thus, step by step, he proceeded, until he came to resurrection proper, and stated that it only related to the body so far as we are con- cerned. It is not the personality which is raised, but the body. Our bodies in life are continuously undergoing a change, but in death the body undergoes a greater change, it going into cor- ruption, and it will be out of that corruption that God will cause the body to be raised and fitted for eternal endurance in joy or in s,orrow ; resurrection, then, is the raising of the body for the personality, comprising the spirit and soul, to take up its eternal residence therein. Jude was quoted, which says that "those who lived in the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah and died in sins are presently suffering the vengeance of eternal fire." There are to be at least two resurrections, the preacher informed the congregation, of those who are just and those who are unjust (John v. 29, and Acts xxiv. 15). These two separate and distinct resurrections will take place at different times, under different circumstances, and at various stages in the period of time, yet the main feature is that those who are just refers to the ones who through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ pass from death (spiritual) to life now in this world, and have their sins forgiven, which is the work of the Holy Spirit through the preaching of the Gospel of the Grace of God. Thus they will be raised to Eternal Glory when the Lord descends to the air for His saints (1 Thess. iv. 16). Those who continue in sin, refusing to have the salvation offered to them in the Lord Jesus Christ, after death will be raised at the resurrection of the unjust to be judged, thereafter to be cast into the lake of fire (Rev. xx. 15), and the continued existence

in such a place was proved in a remarkable way when it was stated that the burning bush which Moses saw burned continually yet was uncon- sumed, and the fire into which throe Hebrew youths were cast in Daniel's day did not touch them, and in the light of this who can deny the power of God to do the same for the un- saved, while they endure punishment for the rejection of the Lord Jesus Christ as Saviour?

div.head: "The Sin of Not Doing' "
div.p: "The Sin of Not Doing' "

"What is sin, and the sin of not doing?" was the subject of the Rev. Dr. Mellor at Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday. There was, he .said, a clear distinctitai beween sin and crime two things which are constantly being confused. A crime, properly speaking, is a transgression of human him, an °hence against some rule klaid down by society for its preservation. But crime does not necessarily involve sin, and to transgress a humanly-made law, a law imposed from the out- side, is not necessarily to fall into a sin. Sin; generally speaking, is any conscious breach of duty, any deliberate infringement of the com- mands of one's own personal ideal. Sin is wilful, conscious, deliberate departure from the path of the ideal; it is to see the good and not do it, to behold the ideal and not pursue it, either by blinding the eye of the soul to it, or by establishing a lower ideal in its place, or by snking into mere indifference and inactivity. Many thought to avoid sin by trying to preserve their innocence unspotted by supposing that there was an easy road to heaven. That was wrong. They must all fling themselves right into the conflict, keeping nothing back.

"The Catholic Faith." What was needed most in England at present was the Catholic Faith. So said the Rev. A. E. Cornibeer at a meeting of the Warrington branch of the English Church on Tuesday. He did not mean by the Catholic Faith the eon. ception of it people sometimes had There was a tremendous amount of religiosity"" about, and it was very often mistaken for religion. What so many people denounced and refused to have anything to do with, was not true reli- gion, but merely "religiosity." The average Englishman was only too ready to sever his faith from his daily life. They should study the Catholic Faith—a faith which met all the needs of everyday life. It did not do to be always talking about that faith—the most im- portant thing was to put it into practice. . Canon Willis said with regard to Catholicity, t ta was,nt as Mr. the Catholicrnibeerh Faith, had said, very impor- il, and what it meant. They must not forget there were three steps in the Catholic Faith. The first, Roly Baptism, the second the necessity of knowing the faith, and the third to live a Christ-like life.

div.p: Legh-street Harvest Festival.

The yen- greg(ttionsi were large and the edifice was taste-. fully decorated by the ladies of the congregati )11. The Rev. A. J. Chessum preached in the morn- ing from the text; "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon." He compared the palm. and the cedar trees, and said both grew in uncongenial soil. The palm flourished amid the "'lnds of the desert, and the cedar in the cold, sterile soil, of Lebanon. Both were fed by hidden re- source, and each grew up into beauty and utility. Everyday life, compared with these trees, was a perplexing problem. While some were born in almost a paradise, a large percen- tage were born amidst struggle and conflict. div.head: When Warringtonians " Mafficked."
div.p: When Warringtonians " Mafficked."

A curious story of how Warringtonians cele- brated the news of a battle 100 years ago was given in the last issue of the London Sunday paper, " The Observer." The paragraph, quoted from an old file, states: "When the re- port of the battle of the Pyrenees arrived at Warrington, Lancashire, some of the mad loyal- ists waited up for the mail, in order to see Lord Wellington's dispatches, and when they found the news confirmed, they resolved to 'kick up a wand providing themselves with a large jorruoni; of punch, they repaired to the house of the rector, to ask permission to have the church bells rung on the occasion. . The reverend gentleman, not wishing the peaceful inhabitants of the town to be disturbed at so very unseason- able an hour, refused to comply with their re- quest, upon which their loyal indignation was raised to such a pitch that they broke his gate and rails, and entirely demolished the poor sex- ton's windows; after which they assembled in the churchyard, round their punch, and drank 'Success to Lord Wellington, and damnation to the rector.' They then got access to the fire-bell, and rang it so lustily that they alarmed all the neighbours, who, at length, obliged them to stagger home, and thus put a stop to their mid- night orgies."

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN,
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN,
FARM RUTTER-MAKING.

A bulletin recently issued by the Washington State Experiment Station gives a number of useful hint i on making butter on the farm. Butter made from a single herd of cows in a small dairy located on Me farm should com- mand the highest price of any butter on the market. Where one man has control of all the Process through which the milk goes from the time it is milked until the time it is printed as butter, the product should be the best obtain- able, if this one man understands the principle and the art of buttermaking. The first essential in making good butter is good cream. To get this simply.means to take ordinary precautions regarding clean cows and barn, clean attendants and clean utensils; and then cooling the cream at once after separating, either by running it over a cooler, or by setting in running cold water and stirring. Cream should not be stored with any substance ilav- ing an aroma. Sweet cream churns hard and gives a butter having a fat taste. To sour, or ripen the cream, first heat it to about 70 degrees F. (use a thermometer) and let it stand until it has a mild but distinctly acid taste; or, second, add some sour milk or buttermilk (starter) to stare the ripening, at the same time holding it at 70 de- grees. The best cream for churning is that which tests about 30 per cent. fat after the starter has been added. The Temperature.

The temperature at which the cream should be churned depends on size of fat globules, hardness of fat globules, age of cream, amount of cream, percentage of fat in cream, kind of feed the cow is getting, and this cannot be determined except by trial. Thirty-five degrees may be proper on one farm and 60 degrees on the one adjoining. A good rule to follow is to have the butter conie about the size of wheat kernels in about 30 to 40 'minutes. If it takes longer the cream is either too sweet or at too low a temperature, or the churn is too full. If it comes sooner than 30 minutes, the tempera- ture is too high. While the granules are about the size of wheat, the buttermilk should be drained, the granules washed and the salt added. Then they are worked togethef only enough to dis- tribute the salt evenly. When the churn is not stopped until the granules become large, some of the buttermilk is encased andit makes butter of poor keeping quality. Mottles in butter are caused by an uneven distribution of Salt in the presence of butter- milk.

TO INCREASE REVENUE OF DAIRY FARM. There may be many ways, but at this time we will only consider one: As quickly as pos- sible increase the producing capacity of the herd. Right there is one of the biggest leaks to be found on the farm in the low average of production of the cows. There are reasons for it, and it is a pity that so many farmers do not clearly understand that it is in the main the fault of the farm owner in the administration of the farm forces for which he alone is respon- sible. For instance, we find a herd of cows that are badly bred and have been for generations. If there is a good profitable cow it is the result of accident, and not of design on the part of the men who have bred that cow and her an- cestors. Now, who is responsible for the low profit, or, maybe, absolute loss this herd gives because these cows did not have good producing blood in their veins? Who, but the men that have bred them? There is where a lot of mis- chief is played with the outcome of profit. It is bad enough to face the percentage of failures that comes with the best of sires, but when we see farmers deliberately set in to breed cows from poor producing blood, is there any won- der they get but little profit? The trouble is, these farmers have no eyesight for the working of right principles, and so they reap according to the seed they have sown. Cause of Law Profit.

Another cause for low profit is poor judg- ment in feeding. There is a big percentage of farmers keeping cows and pretending at least that they are anxious to make good profit from them, who exercise very shallow judgment in feeding. They fail in two ways : (1) In adapting the feed to the purpose of milk production. They are constantly told how im- portant it is to give the cow sufficient protein daily to enable her to build up her own body, maintain the life of the calf she is carrying, and furnish her natural ratio of curd and albumen in her milk. But they feed without any exer- cise of this dear-bought wit. They can get it cheaply, but they prefer to learn it by years of mistakes, and then, maybe, never learn what Is meant by a balanced ration. (2) They refupe to give their cows, first, enough to carry the milk production to the point of profit. Here lies a powerful working prin- ciple that cuts the ground out from under the feet of thousands upon thousands of farmers. It is as though they had to work to build a house and. all the time they burned up as fast as they built. It is a coriunon thing to find farmers who have no knowledge of how to feed for profit, but who do know enough to feed at a loss continually. Talk to them about the "food of support," the amount a cow Must take from her feed to support the body, which alwayS comes first, and they will turn from you in dis- gust; "Oh, that's some book stuff," they will say.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

Continue the earthing of celery on all favour- able occasions. Draw up the soil a little to the stems of spring cabbage's when they are well- rooted, and keep the. hoe going between rows of autumn-sown onions.
The time is now opportune for lifting late potatoes, and these in a general way keep well if buried in clamps on the geound, well pro- tected with straw and soil.
Early London caulttlowers can be sown in a cold frame for spring planting, and a small sowing of cabbage lettuce may be made in the same- way.
Dig up any ground that is vacant and not in- tended for a crop until the spring, in order to bury weeds and expose as much of the surface as possible.

div.head: GROWING BULBS IN MOSS FIBRE.
div.p: GROWING BULBS IN MOSS FIBRE.

- - - Now that the bulb-planting season . is here again, it is. an opportune moment for calling attention to one of the best Methods to adopt in the growing of bulbs for the house, namely, in moss fibre. The fibre is clean to handle, is free from smell, and there is no danger of damage beirig done to furniture by the percolation of water, as in the case with ordinary pots. Water- tight vases and bowls of. neat design are now purchaseable, and these enhance the beauty of the flowers. Roman hyacinths, freesias, nar- cissi, daffodils, tulips, lily of the valley, Dutch hyacinths, and other bulbs, can all be grown In moss fibre to provide a succession of bloom. With a very moderate amount of care and atten- tion all the •spring-flowering bulbs can be brought on early in an ordinary greenhouse, and numbers of them may be grown in a dwell- ing-house or in a frame, and when in flower in early spring, their presence in the windows will always have a very cheerful effect. div.head: SLUMP IN THE MARRIAGE MART.
div.p: SLUMP IN THE MARRIAGE MART.

In the Parish Magazine of the village of Standon (Herts.) the pastor and editor writes: "One feels sure there is something *rong in having to report no marriage in the parish church for the first six months of the current year. No reason can be assigned for this serious falling off in a lottery where everyone expects to try his or her fortune at one time in life, and the bad state of the marriage market raises the question, 'ls marriage a failure?'" In America they are also complaining of the decline in marriages; and one magistrate, who relies for the great part of his income on mar- riage fees, has lowered his, and is starting a new plan. He makes the following offer, his scale of prices varying from a nominal sum to £2O. For the latter amount lie offers to send his motor to meet the train or car, "to whisk you away to the matrimonial parlour, where everything is provided—a boudoir for fixing up, flowers, and a phonographic wegding march." A photograph is also included—sent to your address next day, whilst a wedding breakfast at the hotel follows with all bills paid in advance. "If," as a correspondent adds, " anyone can beat this corky proposition' he would like to see him."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27, 1913.
PHRASE MANIA.
Catchy Lines which Sent Stolid People Half Crazy.
WHERE DO THEY COME FROM?
"EXAMINER' SPECIAL.

AU human beings, expert alienists tell us, are mentally weak in divers respects, and so it is with nations: Britain has from time to time suffered from national manias, as evidenced by the witch-burning crusade, the South Sea bubble, the railway share gambles, and numer- ous passing fads. For catth phrases they are particularly suscePtible, and, each pantomime sdason finds us suflering from an attack of the disease. Comedians have a lot to answer for, as the mediums* of supplying small boys, and equally as childish men and women, with inane
remarks to shout to the. general annoyance. This annualfd of minor madness commenced,

so far as history can say, about a century ago, though it is possible to conceive the prehistoric Britons and the Roman soldiers may have been similarly afflicted. The first public mad fit recorded broke forth during the time of the Peninsula War, when some actor upon the Lon- don boards seriously asked a colleague, "Does your mother keep a mangle?" It is to be pre- sumed that a mangle was nothing uncommon even in those days; but the utterance sent a select London audience into a roar of laughter. Wits of the -day instantly adopted the phrase, and it was for a time the monopolising laugh- ter-maker in the drawing-rooms of Mayfair; thence it gravitated through all the strata of society to the costermonger, who improved upon it so until it became, "'Hi, does yer muv- ver keep ha mangle?" .Sailors brought it North, aided in the mission. by stage coach drivers and guards, until it awoke echoes in the Scottish strebt, and thence filtered as " Dis yer mither keep a' maungle?" into the country. Then it died unsung and unwept. "Bloke and Moke."

Successes followed in quick succession, until came a jaw-twister: " Wellington's the bloke to snap the moke Nap." One can well appreciate it flowing glibly enough from a cockney tongue, but great must have been the struggles of the rural folk of Lancashire to give the phrase its proper pronunciation. Unfortunately asylum statistics were not kept, in those days, and we have no means of learning the disastrous effect of the absurdity upon the mental equilibrium of our folks, but an old London paper says that many patients resided in Bedlam who could scarce utter anything else, and it is to be believed.

Since the Seventies the annual crop has been prolific. For thi the speedy means of travel- ling has had something to do, and what Lon- don laughed at last night would set the people of Warrington into a roar to-night. It is not uncommon for a new phrase coined in the Lon- don music halls to be wired to Lancashire by operators in London during an idle moment on the instrument, for the people are to-day as fond of bon mots, although not so fine as those of a Hook or Jerrold, as they were a century ago.
The Jingo Rhyme.

The late comedian, MacDermott, was respon- sible for introducing the first Jingo jingle, which alas, has led to a large number of disciples, who are now spoken and written of as Jingo- ists. During a threatened war with Russia over the partition of Turkey he sang:
We don't want to fight, But by Jingo, if we do, We've got the men, we've got the ships, And we've got the money too.

And over that refrain the stolid British race went mad. It promises to last as popular as "Rule, Britannia," or the National Anthem, and even Mr. Joseph Chamberlain has made use of it, whilst a lesser light in Unionist politics worked audiences into a high pitch of enthu- siasm by singing the verse. It came to life again during the Boer War, and will again, when tumours of war re-visit our country, be- come a national cry. Another Absurdity.

Many of us remember the absurdity, "Does your mother know you are out?" It was of provincial origin, and again came to life in pantomime, and soon captured London, as well as the whole country. The cry became a pub- lic nuisance. One young• lady, a forerunner of the woman suffrage movement, coined a neat reply. She was addressing a rural gathering, when a yokel in the audience yelled out the tiresome catch phrase. "Yes I" promptly an- swered the smiling maiden, "and she gave me a penny to buy a donkey. Are you for sale?" The retort. gained her a fair hearing. The late Lord Randolph Churchill, father of Mr. Win- ston Churchill, met with a similar interruption whilst contesting 'a political seat. "Does yer mother know yer out?" cried -" the voice," always heard at political meetings. Yes 1" re- plied Lord Churchill, "and to-morrow she'll know I'm in." Thunders of applause greeted the sally, and his prophecy came true. The " Help " Nuisance.

"Help 1" was surely the most stupid of all popular cries, and it likewise spread forth from the pantomime.- For months it was heard everywhere, and caused amusement and trouble. One still October night the few people' on the promenade at a seaside resort were startled to hear the cry of " Help ! help 1" frOrn the water alongside the pier. Th-ey acted promptly. A couple of boats, which had not been removed at the close of the season, were hastily manned and rowed out in the direction whence came the cry for assistance, whilst (W 9 well-known swimmers, throwing off their boots and coats, ran along the pier and plunged into the water. Search as they did, no one in dis- tress was to be found until an outburst of
youthful laughter from the pier overhead told how they had been hoaxed. Had the perpetra- tors been caught the probability is 'they would have got a cold bath.

"Get Your Hair Cut" Some years ago folk went mad in more ways than one over "Get your hair cut." It was of London origin, and part of a song, but it was to Dan Leno it chiefly owed its popularisation. He had done many ,turns on the stage of a theatre, and still the audience wanted more. Dan leaned over the footlights, whispered some- thing to the conductor of the orchestra, who passed it along to the other bandsmen. The comedian disappeared into the wings, only to return in response to the thunderous demands of "encore." "Ladies and gentlemen," said Dan, coining to the footlights, with a mock solemnity in his voice, "we, as true Britishers, love our beloved King, so let us sing the first verse of the National Anthem." The band struck up the opening bars and all rose to their feet, the male section uncovering their heads, as is customary. Then Dan signalled the or- chestra to stop, which they suddenly did, and his jerky voice sounded forth, "My word, there's 'air. Get yer 'air cut." He fled into the shelter of the wings, leaving the audience momentarily dumbfounded. Someone laughed and the rest caught the infecrion, until a roar of merriment spread throughout the motley throng at the clever way they had been hoaxed by their idol.
W. D. D.

div.head: Progressive Labour League's Splendid Record.
div.p: Progressive Labour League's Splendid Record.

There was a continual downpour of rain on Monday evening, but despite this there was another large attendance at the last of the weekly meetings held under the auspices of the Progressive Labour League at Bridge Foot.
The meetlng3 have become so popular on account of the interesting nature of the speeches that nothing seems to deter the men in their en- thusiasm to support the Progressive cause.
Mr. T. H. Garside, of Manchester, is always at home with a Bridge Foot audience, and had a great deal to say on Home Rule and the land question.
Mr. E. Wynne Jones presided, and gave an in- teresting and lucid retrospect of the work done by the League during the summer.
by the National Service League 'or any other, we must wage incessant war against it.
RELIGIOUS EGUALITY IN WALES.

By bringing into practice the great measure of religious equality, we are going to break down all the tendencies to hatred and bitterness which have existed in the past. I have a postcard, which has been sent by post throughout the country, which shows you the kind of thing upon which our opponents depend. The post- card points out that Sir Alfred Mond is one of the foremost men in advocating religious equal- ity for Wales. They also say that 'Sir Alfred is a Jew. We in Warrington will have the pleas- ure of hearing Sir Alfred Mond in November. ,The Tory party themselves owe more to a Jew than they doto all. the men who have served the Tory party in this country. Disraeli did more for. the Tory party than any other man. What- ever the Tories say, that great measure of re- ligious equality is going to be passed. (Hear, hear.) I am glad that a great (al has been said on that question during the summer. IWe are not going to shirk any part, point or

find any sense in it. The rtatement itself is one of pure bluster; if reduced comes to bluff; and the man who plays bluff is always blind to the hand held by his opponent. They are bluster- ing, bluffing, and blind in that statement.

div.head: FREE TRADE AND FREED LAND.
div.p: FREE TRADE AND FREED LAND.
Mr. JONES expressed his thanks for the way the men had turned up at the meetings through- out the summer. Continuing, he said: We have had a splendid series of 18 meetings, which, in
THE TRANSPORT STRIKER:
I wonder what he and his party would say if I adopted mil:tant methods?"
From Reynolds's Newspaper.

attendance, interest, and certainly in the stan- dard of the speaking, have been pp to anything which has taken place from this pitch before. (Hear, hear.) I don't know whit our opponents would think—perhaps they would imagine they were in heaven if they could get the numbers we have had every week. I understand that the average attendance has been about 1.000 per week, which is really a splendid record. We have discussed various questions. Free Trade we have brought well to the front, and I don't think we must relax our efforts in our defence of the cause of Free Trade. As a result of the work of Free Traders, the Tariff Reformers are being driven 'away. The Free. Traders have made out such a strong case against the taxa- tion of the people's food that the Tariff Re- formers are prepared to drop the question en- tirely. If we have done that, we can make out an equally strong case on the question of un- employment and Tariff Reform. Personally, I don't believe that the Tariff Reformer has the courage of his own opinion, nor the courage of a mouse, because the Tariff Reformers are not prepared to put their opinions into practice. They tell us that so much of the misery and wretchedness in the country has been due to the importation of foreign goods. If I believed that that was the case, I would not be satisfied with taxing these things; I would go in for pro- hibition altogether. (Hear, hear.) I believe that as strong a case could be made against Tariff Reform on these grounds, as against tax- ing the people's food. (A Voice: "Keep them out of it.") .We are going to keep them out of it, I can assure you. We have also discussed at these meetings the great question of land re- form, on which my friend, Mr. Garside, has had a great deal to say on the occasion of his visits to Warrington. (Hear, hear.) There is no question for which a plea of urgency can be ad- vanced with greater force than this question of the land. The monopoly in land must be brokk down, and we are glad to find the Liberal party setting their hands to this great task. They are going to free the land, as well as perpetuate Free Trade. (Applause.) By dealing drastically with the land problem they are going to do much to solve the industrial problem, for land Is the most important factor in the iiroduction and distribution of wealth.

div.head: WAR AGAINST CONSCRIPTION.
div.p: WAR AGAINST CONSCRIPTION.
We are a progressive organisation, and as such our voice must always be lifted against con- scription. I don't care whether it be advanced
question in he full programme of the Liberal party at the present time.

div.head: AN OX-POWER RAILWAY.
div.p: AN OX-POWER RAILWAY.

In various parts of the world there are many peculiar railways, and it is doubtful whether any line is really unique in any characteristic. But an American contemporary tells of a steer- operated railway—State owned, too—which, with its bovine motive power, must nearly merit this designation. The line, owned by the State of Texas, connects the town of Brazoria with a prison plantation at Clemens Farm, six miles away. There are two locomotives, but by a combination of circumstances both were for a considerable period "laid up" at the same time. For the cane harvest two engines were hired, but to save expense these were then returned. The line has, however, considerable traffic, the prison farms accounting for a fair volume of freight throughout the year. Accordingly it was determined to use oxen instead of locomotives, and to employ corn and blackstrap molasses as

fuel instead of coal. The beasts draw strings Qf cars between Brazoria and Clemens,' and in Oonsequence many facetious suggestions have been made. The writer from whom we quote gives some of these. Here is a proposed advertisement :

div.head: QUESTION.
div.p: A QUESTION.

After dealing with the hardships which the Irish have endured, Mr. Garside was interrupted by a query: "Who gave Ireland the liberty she has to-day?" " Where is the liberty she has?" asked the speaker. ." Aye, where is it?" queried a member of the audience.
A Voice: "They have more liberty than Eng- lishmen."
"Nonsense," exclaimed Mr. Garside, indig- nantly; "go to school again. To say that Irish- men have more liberty than Englishmen is a travesty of fact."

div.head: THERE'S A GOOD TIME COMING:
div.p: THERE'S A GOOD TIME COMING:

In conclusion, Mr. Garside put the land ques- tion into a nutshell. He said that as a result of Liberal legislation in the direction of land reform, the people will be able to live a happier, brighter and purer life. Lord Rosebery had said, "This is the end of everything." Not quite, said Mr. Garside, we are not fin- ished yet. I believe the end is coming, of that condition of things which overshadows a baby before it is born, which makes the wife of the working man dread motherhood. The dread of poverty will be lessened, the power of the pub- lic-house will decrease, and the cursed slums driven away. The dry drab grind of everyday life will be past, and the day will dawn when the sun will shine, and we have an England of happiness and freedom. (Applause.) A hearty vote of thanks closed the meeting.

div.head: ULSTER'S NEW GENERAL.
div.p: ULSTER'S NEW GENERAL.

A lot has also been said about Home Rule. I see they have got a new general in Ulster, General Sir George Richardson. I never heard of the name before. Sir Edward Carson men- tioned it, but I don't know how they have come to overlook Mr. Harold Smith as a general. Perhaps he is going to look after the eoncen- tration camp. Perhaps he will like that better than being in the fighting line. Sir Edward Carson has said, "It is time we gave over talk- ing," and still he goes on speaking. (Laughter.) Each time Sir Edward speaks he is making con- verts in favour of Home Rule, and not against it. (Hear, hear.) The time has now come for the reaping of the harvest for all the servi.v rendered in the interests of Ireland in the past. (Applause.)

div.head: SLEEPLESS PROPERTY.
div.p: SLEEPLESS PROPERTY.

We have also touched on Liberal and social reform. Speaking to John Morley on Edmund Burke's great characteristics as a statesman, Mr. Gladstone had said, "There is one remark of Burke's with which' I utterly disagree and that is, Property is sluggish and inert.'" Mr. Gladstone said, "Quite to the contrary; pro- perty is vigilant, active, sleepless. If it seems to slumber' you may depend on it that it has one eye open." We want to support the Liberal programme at the present time, and break down the monopoly over property. (Applause.) We appreciate the way in which you men have attended these meetings, and we hope you will not let your interest in Liberalism and the ' Progressive cause wane;, but do all you can for the cause we all have at heart. (Applause.)

div.head: BLUSTER AND BLUFF.
div.p: BLUSTER AND BLUFF.

Mr. GARSIDE, who had a great reception, said: We are fighting the forces of vested interest. Our Tory friends don't like that phrase; perhaps they don't understand what it means. If there is a Tory here let me explain. Vested interest means holding fast to whatever you have got, no matter how you have got it, and using all the means at your disposal—good, bad and indiffer- ent—to assist you in holding fast to it. , I have been asked to speak upon the general outlook. It is somewhat, difficult as a text, but I man- aged to capture a text as I passed a Conserva- tive van-(laughter)-and that was that "Asquith said to Redmond, You help me to break up the Constitution, and I will help you to break ' up the Empire.' " It is a remarkable text, but the 'Most remarkable thing about it is the truth there is. not in it. (Laughter.) You would have to take a microscope to find a grain of truth in it, and when you had found that you would need another microscope to help you to

began. We have never conquered Ireland, for it is still a natiOn, and still remains a separate people. The Tories tell you that when the flag goes up in Ireland, the cows go on their knees, and the beetles turn and go into their holes. Flags are not worth a penny a gross so long as they cover unrighteousness, injustice and in- equality. The Tories would take advantage of a weaker people. Their policy is blind, bluster, and bluffing. _ _
RATS!

They would have you to believe that the Irish- man living next door to you, because his brogue is so thick, is a Jesuit in disguise, trying to cap- ture the whole of Warrington. In the words of the prophet "Rats." (Laughter.) Sir Edward Carson wants to be put in gaol. lie is anxious that his Privy Councillorship shall be taken from him. He wants to be made a martyr, so that he can say to the Irish people all over, "See what I have suffered for your sake !" (A Voice: "It's a lie.") This is what he is anxious to get, and he won't get it—(bear, hear) —because the attitude of the Government will be "Let him alone." (Laughter.) As Mr. Jones has said, if he made seven speeches per week, instead of five, we should have seven more , Liberals, because the people are getting sick and tired of that repetition of falsehood, calumny, and slander of an Irishman against Irishmen. (Hear, hear, and applause.) •

div.head: TEXAS STATE RAILROAD "The Longhorn Route." • SLOW BUT SURE. No Smoke No Dust! No Cinders!
div.p: TEXAS STATE RAILROAD "The Longhorn Route." • SLOW BUT SURE. No Smoke No Dust! No Cinders!

There are other advantages, as the following remarks indicate :—The road has a Casualty record fax below the 'normal. Indeed, it can truthfully be asserted that it has "never killed a passenger." The locomotive never exceeds the speed law, nor does it prematurely disturb the slumbers of citizens, as steam locomotive are wont to do, whistling merrily as they go cheerfully to work in the early morning. It is not necessary on this railroad to provide water

tanks between the terminals, for the oxen can go six miles without water. Obviously a full crew is not necessary. A driver is, of course, essential, but it is unnecessary to'employ a fireman. If " guards " are needed, they have plenty of them on Clemens Farm. Neither is it necessary to employ train dispatchers, tele- graph operators, towermen or crossing watch- man, although it has, been suggested that the State ought to mark the highway crossings with signboards, reading : RAILROAD CROSSING LOOK OUT FOR THE STEERS!

This arrangement was, hoWever, only a tem- porary one, and presumably by this time at least one of the steam locomotives is again at work. Ox-power was used on another three- mile railway between a State farm and Harlem station, on the Southern Pacific Railway, but a locomotive is now employed.—" The Railway Magazine,"

div.head: ULSTER.
div.p: ULSTER.

I have had more downright fun in reading the Press during the last two weeks than I should have had if I had been to a circus. For instance, I wonder if Sir Edward Carson believes that the Country is taking him seriously? I wonder if the brother of your redoubtable Member imagines for one moment that anyone believes half of what he says? It was F. E. Smith who said the time for talking is past. Is it true? Why are they talking? Because they know that they have failed. Who are the generals besides this General Richardson? It would be interesting to know one name. I - should like to know some of these half-pay captains who. are going to die in the ditches between LeMdonderry and Cork. I should like personal acquaintance with some of these r!en who are organising the tremendous army which is going to die for the flag. Sir Edward Carson and Mr. F. E. Smith know well enough that they have to keep on with their talking; they have got to go on making speeches. They have got to go on with their bluster and bluff, because they have been blind to the fact up to now that the people have not responded. If they were to drop out now their whole c4use would be given . away. Are, you any wiser With regard to the 500 families than you were a month ago? The fact is that Harold Smith, Fred Smith, Carson, Craig and the rest, know well that what they are saying is only to hide that which they dare ot say. (Hear, bear.) If you will go into de- tails you will find how true it is. THE TORY IRISH "POLICY."

What is the policy of the Tory party with regard to Ireland. They say the Irish are good people, but if they were in power the first and last steps they would take would be coercion, and throughout the whole history of the Irish struggle the policy of the Tory party has been whips, whipping and still whipping, winding up in gaol. Their policy represents eviction, death on the high road, starvation in the hedges, the depopulation of Ireland, the bringing into Ireland of an alien military system, and the introduction of a brutal police force, destroying the native language, and at- tempting the annihilation of the national spirit. They have blustered and bluffed, and they are as blind to-day as they were when they

div.head: CAN PATRIOTISM REPLACE RELIGION?
div.p: CAN PATRIOTISM REPLACE RELIGION?

The growth of the British Empire has been marked by a succession of incidents, a thread- ing of a. necklace, bead by bead, with little ci policy or of purpose in each act. Patriotism in the Imperial sense has scarcely passed be! yowd the range of sentiment. The blending of races in these islands has not been com- pletely accomplished. Scotch and English, Welsh and Irish still naaintiain their individu- al traditions, and the sinculdering fires of nationality are only just beginning to feed the flame of the common altar. From the Briton beyond the seas we may have to take our first lesson in Imperial tliought. So that hitherto patriotisra has been simply a back- ground to the national life_ a source of con- tentment rather than of emotion. A good din- ner or a public demonstration provides it with an exceptional "night out;" but the ex- altation, the religion of patriotism, requires conditions very different from those of a great commercial nation at peace within its own borders. We have loved our country with the same measured affection with which, we regard our nearest relatives, with little show of feeling. because the affection is taken, for granted. 'To find patriotism at its highest, we must reurn to the heroic Boman period, to ancient Greece, or to the Jew of the post- exilic years. With them it was difficnit to distinguish between a faith in the gods and a faith in one's country, and where the gods were many the unity of the race gave the cult of country an advantage over any one of the faiths of polytheism. In the Roman Em- pire, an act of worship offered to the Ctesars became the link for many differing peoples; and, in modern Japan, the absence of one do-, rainant religion has given intensity to the Bushito, or the faith of the fatherland. For every practical purpose, this religion is as ef- ficient as any other; tested by the creed cf sacrifice it stands higher than some. The de- liberate subordination of the individual to the nation—his life, his all, at the disposal of the State—is a living example of the ancient heroism. Nothing could be more significant or touching than the Official recognition of tho dead soldiers at the siege of Port Arthur. /laving accomplished victory, the generals set up the altar on the field of battle, invok- ing the spirits of the departed, attributing to them the triumph, and seeking from them en- couragement and impulse to further service. "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."

THE SOLDIER'S PATRIOTISM. In all ages the soldier has shown a patriot- ism restricted to his legion, or to his regi- ment, but there is something more than a caste loyalty in the fetish devotion to the flag. The highest honour is paid to it; an in- sult is resented in blood; and life itself is freely given to save the regimental col- ours. This spirit is developing more dis- tinctly in the consciousness of the British nation. Patriotism is beginning to be taught to the young as a form of religion. It may be that a sense of approaching danger is,inaldng itself felt, but more probably the decline of enthusiasm for the Christian faith is respone- ble for the change. Every great nation lives by its ideals. "Where there is no vision the people perish." For the ,moment, Christian- ity has lost its hold of the national ima- gination, -whereas the Imperial symbol quick- ens the pulses. There is no beat of drum or march of triumph before the symbols of the Faith. Although in its beginnings the friend of the down-trodden and the slave, Christian- ity has never identified itself with a single nation; and the experiment of a civic Chris- tendom, attempted by Papal Rome, practical- ly exlikusted itself in the Crusades. The early. Christians themeselves were "strangers and foreigners," aliens in this world, seek- ing their city of habitation elsewhere.

A RE-BORN CHINA. There are, however, circumstances which might prove sufficiently powerful to indisso- lubly unite Christianity and Patriotism. Let us suppose, for example, a re-born China, of which we have heard much, a living fact in fifty or a hundred years time. Let her take into her hands the leadership of Asia, clear the Orient of the intruding European, and whilst threatening Europe on its land fron- tiers, by command of the sea, reduce Great Britain to vassalage. The wealth and re- sources of the older continent, aided by the

latest science, would give full effect to the weight of her larger population. Asia is not so sharply divided as Europe into competing states. The portentous success of Japan has recently thrilled all Asia. The restless- ness of India speaks of it; and the whole con- tinent is moving, from a defiant Arabia to a lethargic Korea. China, single-handed, the rival -of Europe, is stirring with discontent, conscious of vast powers which her preeent rulers are impotent to direct. The day must come when she will find herself. In asserting her natural right of leadership she will ne- cessarily come into conflict with a Europe which affronts her by its very presence. The' swarming East will regard her as the di- vinely appointed deliverer, not only to re- store their independence but also to give them back that mastery which has only been 'seriously challenged in comparatively late history. The impetus necessary to clear Asia of the foreigner will carry the Asiatic hordes, no longer barbarian as yesterday, but disciplined and equipped, far beyond the li- mits of their continent. Whether Europe or Europeanized America will unite, or, if unit- ed, will prove capable of staying the flood, may become the problem of the century. One thing is probable: autocracy will be main- tained in Asia long after it has been discard- ed in Europe, replaced by smaller political entities, federally associated. In a brutal struggle for power, a homogeneous organisa- Con has an advantage over a variety of states for the purposes of defence.

div.head: VALUE OF A. COMMON FAITH
div.p: THE VALUE OF A. COMMON FAITH

It is, therefore, possible that fighting ships of the future, flying the black 4ragon on the yellow ground, may become fami- liar to our esteiaries ; and, following dis- armament, a few military garrisons would compel these_ islands to accept the suzerain power. In the streets of our industrial towns, we should see the Mandarins, in control of ouf, different Provinces, carried in Oriental state, a silence falling upon the crowds, the traffic held up, a visible triumph of the Pagan. This sight would fill our Christian churches with worshippers; for they would identify Christ with their former liberties. Litanies of intercession would rise to heaven for the coming of the Son of Man. Perhaps the Christian worship would become so in- intensely patriotic as to threaten the secur- ity of the conqueror. In that case, we should see renewed the old Pagan attempt to extir- pate the teaching of the Galilean. Buddhism in a philosophic form to suit European thought might be established as the re- ligion of the Empire, and the penalties for the proscribed worship‘ like the winnow- ing fan of the Master himself, would separate the faithful and the courageous from the indifferent and the fearful. Nation- al abasement, followed by persecution, would do more for Christianity than all the sloth- ful centuries have accomplished since its. first triumph. Can tMre be found any com- bining force so potent as a common faith? Mohammedanism has shewn us nations ok different blood and temperament fused into; an irresistible military power. Nothing but a great religion, suffering defeat, even death, at the hands of its conquerors, and rising on e the third day, can redeem a continent en.'

TOM BROWN'S CONTEMPORARY. A well-known figure in ecclesiastical circles in the person of Canon Francis Codlman Royds passed away on Saturday, at his residence, Bryn Golen, Penmaenmawr. - Eighty-seven years of age, 'Canon Royds was the son of the late Rev. Edward Royds, rector of Brereton, Cheshire, his mother being the daugh- ter of Mr, Thomas Molyneux, of the famous Newshain House, Liverpool, which is now the property of the Corporation of Liverpool. He was educated at Rugby in the days of the late Judge T. Hughes (Tom Brown), under Arnold and Tait, and at Brasenose College, Oxford, of which he was a Hulmean exhibitioner. During his college days he was a noted athlete, and on four occasions had a place in the University boat. In 1855 he was appointed rector of Coddington, Cheshire, where he resided for nearly 50 years. He became rural dean of Malpas in 1892, and honorary canon of Chester Cathedral in 1894, in which year he resigned the living of Codding- ton, and retired to Penmaenrnawr. He married Camelia Frances, daughter of the Rev. George B. Blomfield, brother of Bishop Blomfield, of London, in 1852. His eldest ,son, Lieutenant Frank Massie Royds, R.N.' was mortally wounded at the battle of El Tela in March, 1884. His younger and only surviving son, Mr. Edmund Royds,, is M.P. for the Sleaford Divi- sion,

div.head: Impressive Sermon by the Rev. T. T. James at Wycliffe Church. THEORIES OF THE SCIENTISTS.
div.p: Impressive Sermon by the Rev. T. T. James at Wycliffe Church. THEORIES OF THE SCIENTISTS.

"Do we live after death?" Such was the theme of a deeply impressive sermon preached by the Rev. T. T. James at the Wycliffe Congre- gational Church, at the Sunday morning ser- vice. The preacher took his text from Job xiv.: "If a man die, shall he live again?" He said: A remarkable`address has beentiven this week to the members of the British Association assembled in Birmingham by the President for the year, Sir Oliver Lodge. Doubtless many of us here have read some, part, or some summary, or some of the many comments which have been made upon it. It may be very truly said that the first part of this delivery, dealing as it, does with complex and intricate questions of scien- tific study and research, however comprehensible or easily followed by the trained audience to which it was spoken, forms very difficult ground for the average man to tread. When it, is claimed that the mark of the world of science in our own day is rapid progress, combined with fundamental scepticism, we probably have more knowledge for estimating the progress than for appreciating the difficulties which, science is finding in her own camp. It probably came as fresh news to many people, for instance, that the continuity ,which many years of reading and thinking about evolution had led them to regard as practically established, the uninterrupted and gradual development running through the processes of Nature, stood in need of defence, and that to many modern scientific thinkers "so far from Nature not making jumps, it has become doubtful whether she ever does anything else, so that her hitherto placid course, more closely examined, seems to look like a kind of steeple- Chase." '

div.head: REALM OF REASON.
div.p: THE REALM OF REASON.

With all this I do not attempt to deal this morning, both because if is foreign to the sub- ject on which we are to dwell, and because it needs far more competent hands than mine to touch it. To the ordinary men and women the second part of the address given must have been much more intelligible, and probably more interesting. For it exhibited a sudden descent from a region where any but trained minds must have been more or less at a loss to follow the reasoning, to a realm where the heart of common humanity feels itself to be at home. In the closing passages are to be found a discussion of that problem which has agitated the human mind through the ages "It a man die, shall he live again?" Is the great principle of continuity for which the eminent scientist had been arguing to be regarded as operating in the case of personality beyond the bounds of death? Does personal consciousness persist after the dissolution of the physical frame? The utterance which has inter- ested all thinking people during this week con- tained the personal confession, not made by the speaker for the first time by any means, but made in this case under circumstances which commanded a more general attention than ever before, " that after thirty years' experience ,of psychical research, begun without predilection— indeed, with the usual hostile prejudice—the examined facts had convinced him that memory and affection were not limited to that associa- tion with matter by which alone they could manifest themselves here and now, and mat personality persists beyond bodily death."

div.head: BELIEF IN IMMORTALITY.
div.p: THE BELIEF IN IMMORTALITY.

I said at the beginning that this was a remark- able utterance, and to me it is particularly so in one direction. I suppose that it hardly needs arguing that in our own day the belief in im- mortality is not held as firmly or tenaciously as has been tilt) case in many centuries that are past. Our graveyards are witness to the fact that through many centuries survival of death has been accepted as an unquestionable cer- tainty. "There is life beyond" has been the belief and faith in which men of all conditions and persuasions have been laid away. Ido not think that we shall claim that the human mind on the whole believes to-day with the same strength and tenacity in this fact of im- mortality. The light that has cheered a myriad blank and empty places has become dim, or too often gone out altogether in the night. Nor is ,this without certain reasons that have been at work silently and slowly moving in the mind of the race. There has been a kind of general idea that science has somehow or other disproved, or at least shaken, the reasonable nature of the belief. I have pointed out more than once from this pulpit how we have come into a new con- ception of the universe, how instead of the earth being ,the very centre of the created worlds, it isia mere speck of one of a multitude of systems, and holds a. comparatively unim- portant place in the realm of physical organisa- tions. More than that, we; have learned how man himself is related to the animal creation, how he is sprung by evolution from the animal world, and is the highest point of animal devel- opment. It is not surprising that such an out- look should face us with the question of whether the idea of immortality is not far too tremen- dous an expectation for the human race to hold. If the earth is so comparatively insignificant a place, if man is related to the beasts which perish, what expectation can we have either that our planet is the .home of immortal beings, or that man will not perish with the animal creation? Such has been something of the bur- den which scientific knowledge has laid upon us. There is no need to imagine that the scien- tifits, mind has found invariable rejoicing in the difficulties which its discoveries have offered to religious faith. It was Darwin who said: "Be- lieving as I do that man in the distant future will be a far more perfect creature than he now is. it is an intolerable thought that he and all other sentient beings are doomed to complete annihilation after such long-continued slow pro- gress." TENNYSON'S NOBLE BATTLE.

And against the burden of a threatened faith Tennyson, from the side of poetry, fought, too, a noble battle in the last century; accepting, as he did, every finding of science, and yet holding disbelief in immortality a counsel of despair.

"Why should we bear with an hour of torture, a moment Of pain, If every man die for ever, if all his griefs are in vain, And the homeless planet at length will be wheeled through the silence of space, Motherless evermore of an ever vanishing race, When the worm shall have writhed its last, and it last brother worm will have fled From the dead fossil skull that is left in the rocks of an earth that is dead?"

Here, then, is ;fact in the history of the last fifty years or more, which probably few will care to dispute, that almost insensibly in many cases our -nay/ conception of the universe arising from scientific knowledge,, has meant that the human mind has veered largely to the inaterinl- istic interpretation of life, and to a consequent loss of belief in immortality. And 1 ;say lhat the utterance from the chair of the British Association is remarkable for this very obvicus reason, that it is a definite plea for a wider interpretation of life, for a recognition of its spiritual meaning, and indeed for such an in- vestigation of the problem of the continuity of life after death as will place the fact upon a scientific basis.
