among a heterogeneous collection of shabby furniture. The room was dull and stuffy, and it was with an utter disgust that Dr. West- wood turned to the window and gazed into the gloom outside. He remained some time contemplating the unrelieved monotony of closely-planted 'oeech trees when he heard the door open behind him. Turning around he found himself face to face with a stoutly-built, florid-faced man, of about fifty-five years. A glance at the features—steady grey eyes, shaded by almost beetling brows, strong jaws, and a weak mouth—gave him an unpleasant impression of his uncle.

"I expected you earlier. Could you not have come by the midday train ? " "You are Uncle Richard ? " said Frank, slowly advancing to greet him. But Mr. Westwood had already dropped into a chair. "Sit down," he said, stiffly, ignoring the young man's apparent intention. "Yes, I had preferred your coming earlier. I thought you would have done so." "I wired you of my intention."

"Had you come by the midday train you, would have been able to get back to town to-night. No doubt your time is valuable." "I am sorry my visit is inopportune. But you will remember you fixed no time for re- ceiving me." "We shall find you a bed for the night." "I had rather not intrude," and Frank coloured in irritation. "No doubt I can be accommodated in the village." " No, no, you shall have a bed," and • Mr. Westwood moved, giving intimation of his gout. have _some things to say to you.' _ _ _
Dr. Westwood waited 1.43-r his uncle io lead

"You are very like your father," said Mr. Westwood after a minute's careful observa- tion of his nephew. "I trust you have a greater endowment of common sense." "My father was generally regarded aa a sensible man"

"I knew your father." "And therefore the more unjust your dis- paragement." Another awkward pause ensued, during which Mr. Westwood continued steadily to observe the younger man. kt last Frank's irritation broke out, and he stood up and faced his uncle. "Uncle Richard, you wrote me a memor- andum to come down here to see you. I obeyed the message, and regret very much that I have done so. Your neglect of the or- dinary cou6esies which even one stranger extends to another I can afford to disregard. It seems in keeping with your nature. But strictures on my late father, you must under- stand, I resent. You will please indulge no further in that vein."

He spoke quickly and passionately, looking sternly iieto his uncle's face. "Sit down, sir. You are impulsive—a vile quality in a young man." "I shall intrude upon your time as little as possible. I wrote several times to Bur-. mah asking for information as -to my father's death. If you will please tell me what you know about it I shall be obliged." " H-m ! You ask for a long story with a short sequel. British residents in Burmah sometimes drink, .and, in this reepect, en- gineers are not more ascetic than others." The allusion was vexatious, Mit Frank sat down prepared to listen. "Your father travelled a good deal up- country of late years, and I saw little of him. I did not wish to see him.. But what is known Df his death is easily told. Ho shot himself— drink, you understand." "I don't believe it," cried Frank, vehem- ently. "The fact is unaffected; I am telling you what you asked for—all I know about your father's death."
Frank's face flushed and went pale again. "Shot! How do you know that he wasn't murdered?"
"I haven't speculated on that. They didn't think so at Bhamo."
"If I could but know the truth," Frank mused painfully. "Then go to Burmah," sneered his uncle, "and if you can establish your suspicion and discover the murderer-"
"It would go ill with him," added Frank, coldly. "You would take the law ir-to your own hands?"

"Yes, may Heaven help me; I would be= spatter his brains about for birds to feed on." Uncle Richard shifted uneasily, and nursed his gouty foot. "I did not count upon disprays of this sort. Perhaps you will now give me the opportunity of saying why I sent for you." Frank waited, but made no comment.
"The death of your, father is a pecuniary loss to you. It is useless to remember any other feature of the event. I sent for you that I might make you some compensation for this loss."

" Compensation! If you mean that you wish to repay the money lent you by my father I shall be very glad. I need money. But I shall also be glad if you will keep to the proper name for the transaction." "What is your record of the amount lx:dch I owed your father? _l' I understand about six hundred pounds— Lint you surely know." Mr. Westwood drew from his pocket cheque book and fountain pen, and wrote a cheque which he tore out and handed to Frank. "Twelve hundred pounds! Did you owe so much to my father?" "I owe it to you. Cash the cheque." "Uncle Richard, I have no desire to receive a favour at your hands. Did you owe twelve hundred pounds to my father?" "You are tiresome. If I did not owe you twelve hundred pounds do you imagine I should pay you that amount? I am not 'lentil. mental. Money has a charm for most men who hap- pen to be in need of it, and Dr. Westwood was sincerely gratified. Visions of a rising practice and of Ells Farleigh rose to his mind. After all, his uncle had apparently rugged virtues. Now, sir, I wish to go to my den Mrs. Woods, the housekeeper, will get you some- thing to eat, and will afterwards show you a room." Frank did not feel disposed to quarrel fur- ther. He accepted the arrangement and de- cided to remain. An indifferent meal was served to him in a gloomy and sparsely-furnished dining-room. The time hung heavily upon his hands. He smoked a cigar and tried to read, but by ten o'clock he had retired to bed. Two hours later he was still mapping the future by the events of the evening when a Sound of crashing glass downstairs attracted his attention. He listened for perhaps a quar- ter of an hour without hearing any further sound. Then an uncertain noise reached his ear. A burglar, he felt, had entered the house. Hastily slipping on some clothes he took a poker from the grate, and crept down- stairs. He reached the drawing-room door, and cautiously peered in. A small bull's-eye lantern stood upon a chair, throwing out a strong circle of light, which shone full upon the head and shoulders of a young man kneel- ing before a strong cabinet. Dr. Westwood stood uncertain how to act. At this moment the door of the cabinet was forced open. With a swift movement he sprang upon the intruder and seized him by the riglit hand. The man started and jumped to his feet— already holding an ornamental silver shrine of quaint workmarsahip. ' For a moment the men stared at each other 111 if measuring one another'e strength.

"Who are you?" 'demanded the intrude. "Drop that, my friend. I don't think my identity matter's," and Dr. Westwood tightened his grip upon the man's wrist. I will not. It is mine." "I must assume it to be my uncle's—Mr. Weetwood's., Drop it, I say." "Your uncle—Mr. Westwood's! Are you mad? I say this is my property. Let go my wrist!" He endeavoured to wrench his arm free and overthrow Dr. Westwood by a sudden lunge. But the latter was on his guard, and seized the man in a vice-like grip round the body. He was the stronger man. In lees than two minutes he bad the other pinned upon the floor, his hand upon his throat. "That will do—let me speak!" Frank relaxed his grip, but without allow- ing the man to rise. You think me a burglar. I tell you I am not. I came here to recover what is my own —or rather my mother's property—having failed to recover it otherwisc.:. But before I explain further will you tell me who you are?" - To satisfy you. Dr. Frank Westwood

div.head: MAN FROM BURNAM
div.p: THE MAN FROM BURNAM
By JOHN BYRNE
Author of "The Dark Days," "A Fateful Quar- rel," "The Old Fiddler," "Liquidating the I' Debt," "A Case for the Lawyers," &c.

." You, Frank—and so early! Nothing wrong, I hope?" "No, no, Ella. But I have much to talk to you about, and have paid you a morning call." They shook hands with the easy unre- straint of comradeship, and took seats by one of the drawing-room windows. In .the street they might have passed un- noticed for lack of distinctiveness, but with lighted countenances in each other's pre- sence they invited study—he a medium-sized, clean - shaven, alert-looking „young fellow of twenty-four; she an oval-faced, fair-featured, soft-voiced girl two years his junior. From childhood circumstances had thrown them much together, and a temperamental affinity had kept them fast friends; but that was all. To Dr. Frank Westwood there was no coun- sel more valued than that of Ella Farleigh. "To be brief, Ella, I must leave London— for a time, at least. You know the extent of nay present practice. It is farcical, and not likely to improve; six patients in as many months! My name-plate upon the door of my lodgings is an idle ladvertisement. I have still ninety pounds left, so, my dear Ella, after duly revolving schemes, I have decided to employ my resources ip another direction." "You mean—"

"To emigrate. Half a dozen years in one of the Colonies will add to my experience and capital. With a clear five hundred in my pocket I shall return and buy a small prac- tice. And then I shall begin to give my am- bition play. A few years plough-hqrse plod- ding, Ella, and afterwards life with an in- spiriting purpose ! " He spoke with an enthusiasm that seemed to brace him up physically and morally. Ella's lip quivered, and there was a sus- picion of gathering dew in her eyes. "Do let me urge you again, Frank, to raise five hundred on the security of mother's annuity. Why waste time in scraping to- gether what we can lend you now? Please raise the money, and buy the practice. We shall both be so happy to have you in town." "My dear girl, a thousand thanks! But the scheme is impossible. Gamble with, and perhaps lose, your money, without even a Possibility of repaying it. No, no, Ella. But I have something further to tell you." He handed her a letter received by the morning's past, and she read in surprise its three bald sentences:

"Briefly Lodge, Stamport, —shire. "Dr. Westwood,—Please ' come ' down at once to see me. I wish to do something for YOU. My gout compels me to leave here im- mediately.—Your Uncle, "RICHARD WESTWOOD."

"Your Uncle Richard,. Frank! And you have been writing to him to Burmah. But what a stiff and unaffectionate sort of letter." "Quite a touch-me-not sort of old cus- tomer, I should say, from his style of corre- spondeilee."

"Still, you see what he says, Frank," and Ella 's eyes sparkled, 'I wish to do something for you.' Why, that may mean immense things." "I am not so sanguine." "But he is rich, isn't he, and generosity may bef his great virtue." "A virtue SO evidently aggressive is hardly likely to have much merit in it." "Remember your uncle says he is suffer- ing from gout. Poor gentleman, that may affect his temper." "Welli I shall retain an open mind. If he pays rue the money lent him by my father some years ago I shall be satisfied. A train, I find, reaches Stamport at seven o'clock. I shall go down this afternoon, and wire the old gentleman to that effect." Frank could remain no longer. He had in- formation to look up regarding life and prospects_ in the Colonies. _ _

- "1 shill come to see you immediately I get back, Ella," he said. "I do not expect a long stay nor any great ebullition of friendship on my uncle's part. I have a preconceived idea of his character."

"Which I trust you will find does him an injustice, Frank." She accompanied him to the door. Every- thing he had intended to say had already been said, and yet impulsively something rose t-o his lips which he knew not exactly how to frame in words—something for which he had been altogether unprepared, but which exi- gency _compelled him to utter.

:Wish Le luck, Ella." "From my heart I do, Frank. Good luck and happiness." "And when I return to England, how shall I find you, Ella?" For a moment she looked him straight in the face, thoughtfully. Then the spirit of girl- hood showed itself in miith.

"What a funny question, Frank!" she laughed. "I trust you will find me well and happy, as I shall hope to find you." I question -clumsily. I mean, shall I find you—married ? " "No, not married," she returned, slowly. "Good-bye, Ella, God bless you. lie raced down the steps with the glow of a new feeling, burning in his, heart. At the gate, as he turned to raise his hat, a thought occurred to him, and he came reluctantly back.

"Forgive me, Ella. I did not mean to ask you such a question. It was wrong. You must mix with the world, and—and act as if you did not know me. If I were never to see you again ? " "But you shall! Good-bye again, Frank. I have answered you." A hundred yards down the street he, ven- tured to look back, and a thrill of pleasure passed through him. Ella still stood on the doorstep looking wistfully after him. She waved a farewell, and tlie,n he saw her step inside.

As the train steamed that evening on its way to_Stamport, Frank Westwood could not help wondering at the strange epistle of his gouty uncle, the stranger for the circum- stances which had preceded it. For years Richard- Westwood and his brother William, Frank's father, had carried on successful operations as mining engineers in Burmah. To his son William Westwood had been almost a stranger; while regarding his Uncle Richard the young man knew nothing. Twelve months before a nerspaper cutting and an anonymous note arrived from Burmah announcing the death of William Westwood, and though Frank wrote several letters asking his uncle for particu- lars, he was never favoured with a reply. The brief note in his pocket was the first communication he had ever received from hie uncle. .
Arrived in Stamport Dr. Westwood was annoyed to find that he .was entirely neglected. Nobody awaited him. • Can you tell me where Brierly Lodge is?" he asked a porter.
"Yes, sir, rummish-looking 'ouse in a beech grove 'all a mile beyond the village." "Do you, know the present tenant, Mr. Westwood?"

"Don't know the ge'man, sir." "And, eaket tell, I suppose, how long he has been living there?" "Must be a newcomer, sir. 'ouse was to let lately." Through the porter's aid Dr. Westwood hired a conveyance. From the outside the house could not have been more fittingly described than in the words of the railway. porter. It was a de- pressing, peculiar-looking, low-roofed struc- ture, with a gloomy, weeping appearance that in itself might affect any man's spirits. Smothered in trees, the place seemed conse- crated to melancholy. "Rather an odd taste this," he mused, Wonderingly. The driver jumped-off and opened a clumsy, rusty gate, and then drove up the neglected avenue. Dr. Westwood knocked loudly, and the door was presently opened by a timid- looking woman past middle age. "Dr. Westwood! Yes, sir. Mr. Westwood is in hi-c room, but I shall inform him of your arrival."
I believe the
He was shown into a lumber apartment which evidently did duty as a drawing-room. Here and there, without taste or apparent de- sign. were all sorts of extravagances thrown

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27, 1913.
" Wastwood I Not a son of William West- wood, who was murdered at Bhamo "
"Murdered, you say! William Westwood wee my father.. Tell me what you know, man!" and he allowed him to rise.

"You, William Westwood's son, and in this house! Under the same roof with—! But let me ask, are you under any delusion? I think you said something about your uncle?" "This is my uncle Richard's house— Richard Westwood." _

"Absurd ! Richard Westwood is in China; he went there more than three years ago. If you are here as a guest, I tell you you are enjoying the hospitality of Mr. Angus Brampton, my father—and—your father's murderer." "Good Heavens, man, is this true? Say it —swear it!" "I do not say it—l swear it. 179 is my father—l deplore it—a scoundrel, a liar, thief, and a murderer!" "Then Heaven strengthen my vengeance! His fate is sealed ! " He turned to the door, his face white and set. But there in the doorway stood Angus Brampton, alias Richard Westwood. "You heard, coward—villain! Is this true?" " Did I not give you twelve hundred pounds?" " Death ! Quick ! Answer me, is this true?"

" Yes ! And now?" Frink Westwood's hands clenched; and he made a spring at the murderer of his father. Then followed the crack of a revolver, a flash in his face, and a stinging, searing pain upon the side of his neck, Passion blinded him, and he scarcely knew what followed. He was conscious of a fall, a second revolver report, and then the relaxing grip of his antagonist. Dazedly the two men looked down at the figure at their feet. Heavens! He is dead! That accidental shot has killed him." "I must remain here now and see you clear of this," said the ,stranrr. " Your father is avenged—by Providence. Dr. Westwood made a hasty examination of the body. "Yes, he is dead—l must 6ummon the authorities."

It was a fortnight afterwards before Dr. Westwood was free to return to London. Ella Farleigh oat anxiously awaiting his arrival. "Oh, Frank, what a terrible experi- ence! How near you were to death." Her voice was tremulous, and her eyes spoke thirio which she had not entrusted to her tongue. 'lt is past now, darling" (her face flushed pleasantly at the endearment), "but, do you know, I had a queer sort of presentiment from the moment I was leaving you that something unpleasant overhung me." '"And, curiously, GO had I. But I prayed very earnestly +hat God would protect you." "-He has, darling—perhaps due to your pleading We none of us • know how much Providence may not alter its design of events for the prayers of a good heart. You are the ideal woman, Ella, God designed, for maws betterment." His voice wr.s intense. Ella's gaze sought the floor, avoiding the light which she felt was in his eyes. "Ella, that man, I have ascertained, owed -my father more than fifteen hundred pounds (my father, indeed, appears to have been careless of money matters). I shall have at least twelve hundred out of that sum— enough to start a practice with. Will you be' my wife, darling, my guiding star?" She placed her hand unreservedly in his. " Frank, did I not give you an answer to that question the day you went to Stamport?" "And I had been hoping yem did not under- stand." "A woman not understand when she is be- ing asked in marriage by the man she- ioves!" They sat undisturbed, blissfully regardless of ftiinned "A you will forgive that wretched man, Frank, for the murder of yon, father?" Ella pleaded afterwards'. "I shall try to forget him, darling.. We should entertain no bitterness for one -beyond the grave." Then I am truly happy. The man could not have been wholly bad—else why should he have wished to pay you some of the money which he owed your father?"' "A qualm, his redeeming feature What puzzles rue is that he should have resorted to such subterfuges partly to relieve his con- science. I will charitably hope he had no other reason for settling in Stamport in the name of Richard Westwood." "Yes, let us think of him charitably,"lla said ,IT END.I

div.head: SHUN THE TEAPOT.
div.p: SHUN THE TEAPOT.

For the last ten years or so a number of Irish doctorsiinterstedin mental diseases have been trying lb locate the causes of the widespread, lunacy among the people of County Kerry. It has remained for an eminent ecclesiastic actu- ally to fix it. The Most Rev. Dr. Maugan, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Kerry, nsw attributes this sad mental- state to a far too free indul- gence in the use, and consumption of lea among the young people. As a consequepee he has issued a whrning to mothers to be more spar- ing in the supply of tliat beverage to, their children. "Before. the teapot," says his Grace, "became such a common domestic utensil,

Kerry homes produced a race of men and women that was the admiration of Europe. Instead of beautiful muscular development we now have a population of stunted growths ex- hibit!ng syrnntorns of mental degeneracy. .1 beg of you all, therefore, to shun the teapot."

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
Feminine Foibles, a Principal Subject for Discussion before Church Congress.
THE FEATHER DIFFICULTY.

Women will not only play an important part in this year's Church Congress, held at South- ampton, from September 30 to October 3, but the change that has come over womanhood in the Anglo-Saxon world during the last 25 years is likely to come in for a good deal of criticism. Woman's dress, her amusements, her vagaries, and purpose in life, her love of ostentation and display, her overbearing desire to be fashion- able, and what she will become, are all sub- jects of contention, and sometimes of fierce denunciation from pulpit and platform. These matters, together with the sex problem, social morals, and the evils of the day, will meet with a good deal of attention. Mrs. Creighton, widow of the late Bishop of London, will ad- dress a special meeting for women, and on the Wednesday Bishop Welldon, Dean of Man- chester, will open a discussion on "The King- dom of God and the Sexes." It will thus be seen that the interminable woman question will be one of the principal suTljects before the church Congress. No one can doubt that there is a tendency in these days to put aside what were regarded as womanly qualities in the Victorian period, but that was inevitable, and after all, the revolution in the manners and ideas of women is not such a terrible thing as many moralists would have us believe. THE DUTCH EXHIBITION.

As this year's celebrations of Dutch independ- ence took no official note of the progress made by women in Holland during the last century, two ladies of Amsterdam organised and suc- cessfully carried out a most interesting exhibi- tion of woman's work. An old house was taken, and a suitable building erected in the yard, in which were gathered together evidences of woman's influence in the arts and industries, in the medical and nursing professions, and in the various agencies for social reform. Special demonstrations of the far-reaching effects of women's work for the good of the State were given on certain days, and stirring speeches made by advocates of women's rights, who demanded equal political and economic privileges for both sexes. HONOURS FOR WOMEN.

In addition to the honour bestowed on Madame Curie during the Medical Congress, held this year in London, another French- woman has had the distinction of being the first woman in France elected President of the Conseil de Prud 'homme. The Municipal. Coun- cil of the City of Paris has recently passed a resolution approving of the claim of French- women to the municipal vote. This concession coming from such a quarter fs regarded of the first importance, and expected to lead to im- portant results in the near future. The first woman judge has also been appointed quite recently in Norway, during the temporary ab- sence of the town judge. Ttie lady is an attor- ney, daughter of a clergyman, educated at a university, and passed her juridicial examina- tion in 1900.

WOMEN IN MASCULINE ATTIRE. There are probably many more women pass- ing through life disguised as men than is com- monly suspected, and it is said that the present. period of exceptional activity in the industrial world has considerably increased the number. Such a Clisguise presents few difficulties to the masculine type of woman, who finds she can earn twice the wages as when hampered by skirts. Every now and then an instance comes to light of a woman who has been living for years working and dressed like a man, but for every one of these disclosures, a dozen cases remain undiscovered. It is no use in this coun- try to apply to the police for permission to wear masculine garments, but such applications are common enough in France, • and are usually granted if a satisfactory reasOnis forthcoming. Rosa Bonheur always _wore masculine attire, and the celebrated explorer, Madame Dieubafoy, found male dress so comfortable when on Her travels that she wears it on all occasions. The little lady may often be seen in Paris in well- creased trousers and frock coat, with tie, \tiat and boots, all in the latest masculine fashions. COLOURED FUR NECKLETS. Parisiennes have seized with avidity upon the idea of furs dyed in the most brilliant and startling hues, when employed in the confec- tion of the most fascinating of necklets. The shape is comfortable and becoming, fitting quite close to the throat. A tig choux of handsome ribbon finishes these pretty accessories, and •.iey are fastened at the back or side, according to the taste of the wearer. One of the prettiest • of these novelties has the coloured fur in the middle and a band of some black pelt on either Side. 'A touch of the same 'fur is used on the hat worn with the necklet, either as a border on the brim, or a finish to the crown. In green, mauve, and blue, these coloured furs have a most bizarre appearance, but as neck- lets they are quite appropriate.

A NEW ARTIFICIAL FEATHER. Feathers have by no means lost their popu- larity, but the price of a really good plume fre- quently places this graceful dedoration of a hat beyond the reach of the woman of small means. An artificial feather, which' so closely resem- bles the ostrich, that it is difficult at a glance to distinguish it from the real thing, Will be ex- tensively used this season. The inventor claims for it that it is not affected by wind, rain or sun. It is certainly very effective, and' the Price is less than half that of the ostrich plume. Very excellent imitations of ospreys are shown also, hnd as so much controvprsy has raged round this particular adornment of headgear and coiffures, it is bltter to buy the artificial article. TRIMMINGS FOR HATS.

In the matter of trimmings, there is a very wide choice ; simplicity, however, seems to be the rule. Chin straps in great variety are an Important feature of the new millinery. An Innovation in trimming is supplied by patent leather and suede red, both of which are used for the making of bows, mounts and wings. In addition, .highly-glazed leather, fur, feathers, quills, buckles, ribbon, flowers, and the quaint- est of mounts are used in a multitude of differ- ent ways, and instead of being placed at the back, as during the spring and summer, the majority of plumes and bows stand high and upright, just in front. Where flowers are used as decorations for hats, they are frequently mixed with fruit, such as lemons, musca- tels, and other equally unlikely kinds. Won- derful blue and brown roses, as far removed In colouring from the real flowers as it is pos- sible to make them, are evidences of post-im- pressionist Ideas. Little bouquets of small metal flowers, especially in gold, are favoured at present. Berries are much in evidence, also tiny silk and velvet blossoms. Velvet hats of larger dimensions have often one or two huge silk and velvet roses in a rich tone, for Sole decoration. BUTTONS FOR ME AUTUMN.

Buttons quaint and original in shape ate of an importance this season, second only to the fabrics dn which they fro employed. More prominent than any othei• is the engraved pearl and galalith button in the oddest of shapes. Pearl is shown in combination with gun metal, pearl and jet is another favourite, and for the decoration of tweed coafN an skirts, buttons with a leather effect are in great request.

div.head: WOMAN SUFFRAGE
div.p: WOMAN SUFFRAGE
The Irish Example of Faithfulness to
One Supreme Idea.
APPEAL TO WOMEN LIBERALS.
BY A LADY CONTRIBUTOR'.

The expressions of discontent and grave warnings which have gone forth to the Liberal party from the Council meetings of the Women's Liberal Federation on the present position of the suffrage question, thave been noted with satisfaction by those who, for the sake of the women's cause, stand out Side the party organisations. Whilst the resolutions fall short of what might be desired and hoped for, they are a distinct advance on any previous .utterances of the Council. If they do not de- clam a,n immediate revolt, they foreshadow one, and they reveal the important effects which the events. of last year have had on the minds of women Liberals.

The recent wholesale desertion of the women's cause by the Irish party has naturally aroused bitter resentment, and yet, dispassionately con- sidered, it holds for women a lesson of valuable significance. Above everything else, it means faithfulness to one supreme idea, to which, until fit is realised, every other claim and con- sideration must be Subordinated. There may conceivably be political reforms of even greater importance to humanity at large than Home Rule for Ireland, b'ut the Nationalist parry are of one mind with St. Paul when he said, " I determined to know nothing among you, save the mission to which I was dedicated." In a like spirit, hundreds of women have deliberately severed the ties and fealties of a lifetime and withdrawn their support from comrades and reforms, dear to and desired, by them, in Order to achieve one purpose, which seems to them to transcend all others in immediate import- ance. It is in this spirit and by these methods only that successful revolutions and reforma- tions are accomplished.:

'Women had a right to say to the Irish 'mem- bers, who wrecked the Conciliation Bill, "Are not we Women struggling for the same liberty, the same rights as you yourselves? Have we not stood by you in your struggle and proved ourselves your champions and advocates in the great campaign of 1885?" ,L,yrnpitthy, honour, gratitude called to the Nationalists to stand firm for the women' cause; yet all availed nothing against the fear of possible disaster to their supreme aim. If this desertion is capable of a not wholly ignoble interpretation for us, still more may we commend this interpretation to the further consideration of the Women's Liberal Federation.

div.head: POWER OF WOMEN LIBERALS.
div.p: THE POWER OF WOMEN LIBERALS.

There- can be little doubt that, the suffrage question has been in the power of the organised Liberal women to settle. A quarter of a cen- tury ago they were in sufficient accord to split their great organisation over it, and to place it in the forefront of their raison d'etre. Since ' that time they have steadily increased in strength and influence, they have continued year by year to pass, with practic:l7 unanimity, declarations, manifestoes, remonstrances, and appeals, addressed to the men of their party on behalf of political recognition for women. The prospect of the passing of. a Manhood Suffrage Bill, for which there is so little demand ami:lig Liberals themselves, that they recently refused to include it in a list of immediate reforms,wel- corned by them, has elicited from the Women's Liberal Federation a warning, which, froin so persistently loyal a body, is very significant, nrid which we trust will be made still more effective by a personal pledge by all Liberal suffragists to refrain from party work at the next. General Election, in the event of the Re- form Bill •passing without the inclusion of women.

The highest party loyalty must ever be. sub- ordinated to the root principles on which it is based. As Lord Acton (a great Liberal) said, In the life of every great man, there is a, point where fidelity to ideas which are the justifying cause of party, diverges from fidelity to arrange- ments and understandings which are its machinery." The root principle of the Liberal party is self- government, and when that party shows itself faithless or apathetic towards this root prin- ciple, a higher servive may be rendered to it by rebellion than by subservience. 'Women's co-operation, if needed in the political life of the nation, is needed on the side of the ideal, and the ideal is never easy to serve. A secondary consideration is this: In these days'of congested legislation, it is usually neces- sary to concentrate all available power on any reform considered of primary importance to the temporary exclusion of all others. The jack of this determination among women has dragged on the agitation for women's suffrage over half a century.
The vision to comprehend and the courage to act is what we need.

div.head: QUAINT GERMAN FORECAST.
div.p: QUAINT GERMAN FORECAST.

France is Co be wiped off the mall of Europe, and the, French people are to perish utterly, according to a sensational prophecy !Lade in "The Partition of France," by Adolf. Somm.r- feld, which has caused perturbation in two countries.

_ It is the Germans who are to do the wiping, of course. The French militarists got hold of the book and skilfully turned it to their own uses. The French translation, "La Partage de la France," has become a powerful argument in support of an invincible French army and the benefits of three years' service for conscripts. The trouble begins over Morocco. Spain and France were quarelling, and Germany sent a cruiser to Moroccan waters to watch events. This cruiser was blown up one night in exactly the same way as the Maine in Havana Harbour 15 years ago. It was discovered that a French torpedo had done the mischief.

Austria and Italy, the other partners in the Triple Amanda, decided to help Germany against France. On the other hand England and Russia refused to stand by the Triple Eqtente and help France—Russia, for reasons of her own, and England because (as our diplomats said) France had wantonly provoked war, and had to get herself out of the mess.

From the very first everything went in favour of the Germans and their allies. One Wong frontier town after another fell almost without the firing of a shot! The Italian troops overran the South of France almost as easily as the Germans -had conquered the cast. At the same time Italy an- nexed Tunis and Algeria, the French colonies in Northern Africa.

Then, while the Italians were left in posses- sion of the South of France, two German armies converged on the French headquarters at Orleans. By superior strategy and invincible dash the Germans compelled them to surrendd ; 200,000 men gave up arms, and the conquest of France was practically complete.

"Then came the division of the spoils. Italy retained -Tunis and Algeria, and was given the whole of the South of France across to the Bay of Biscay. England (as the price of her neutrality during the war) got Artois and Picardy, as well as French Indo-China.
Russia collared Persia and Afghanistan; and Morocco was given to Spain on condition that the other countries had free trade there.
Austria was given Madagascar and,/ some other islands in the Indian Ocean.
England joined the Triple Alliance, which then formed an invincible combination of Powers guaranteeing Iv ever the peace of Europe.
Those Dear Girls.

div.head: SHUNTER'S DEATH.
div.p: A SHUNTER'S DEATH.
Saturday Morning Fatality at Froghall
AN ERROR OF JUDGMENT.

A shunting fatality, which took place at Froghall Siding early on Saturday morning last, formed the subject of an inquest before Mr. S. Brighouse at the Coroner's Court on Tuesday morning. Deceased was Henry Savage (46), of 6, Bluecoat-street, a foreman shunter, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway, who succumbed to his injuries shortly after his admission into the Infirmary. Mr. Bland appeared for the company and Mr. T. S. Steel for the relatives. Mi. Brassington represented the National Union of Railwaymen. The widow, Margaret Ann Savage, deposed that her husband had no trouble of any kind, and there was nothing to cause him to take away his life. AN UNEXPLAINED DELAY.

John William Brown, railway shunter, 81, Wash-lane, stated that on Friday night he went on duty about ten o'clock, and was engaged, in company with the deceased, in shunting wag- gons at Froghall Siding. About ten minutes past two on Saturday morning Savage told him to go down to the Liverpool Siding and hook on about 30 waggons, whilst he (Savage) got away the Preston goods train, which was already in the siding.

in reply to Mr. Steel, witness said it was usual, when a train had left the siding, to watch it out of the section: After the departure of a train it Was Savage's custom to call at the signal box. At the place where Savage was standing he would have to cross the line to get to the signal box. Witness could not explain the delay in bringing the ambulance after the accident. The accident happened shortly after two o'clock, but the man was not removed to the Infirmary until three o'clock. ENGINE DRIVER'S STORY

William Owen, engine driver, 23, ,Forshaw- street, said that on the night in question he was engaged in shunting operations, under Savage's direction. At 2.15 Savage sent the Preston goods train on its journey. Witness's engine was then standing in the siding, await- ing Savage's instructions. As soon as the presten goods train was clear Savage signalled to witness with his lamp, and also blew a whistle. The train came forward at a slow pace towards Savage, who could plainly be seen standing in the six-foot, almost opposite No. 4 signal box. When the engine was about two yards from Savage witness saw him step right in front of it. The engine was reversed, and immediately he heard a scream, lie pulled up the engine in its own length, and on getting off found the deceased lying in, the four-foot. The wheels did not pass over him, but deceased appeared to have received an injury to his back. Witness could give no reason . why deceased stepped in front of the engine, except that he forgot its approach' and crossed in front to deliver a message at the signal box. In reply to the Coroner, witness thought that the man did not step wilfully in front of the engine. The Coroner: Cap you imagine what he was doing? Witness: In my opinion he was going across to the signal box to wire the Preston train out. The Coroner: An error of judgment in step- ping in too near to the engine.

div.head: FAMILIARITY BREEDS CONTEMPT.
div.p: FAMILIARITY BREEDS CONTEMPT.

The Coroner remarked that it would be no use hearing any more evidence. He was quite satisfied that it was an accident. The police had made inquiries to see if there was any sus- picion that the man intended to do away with his life. Those inquiries had entirely dissipated that suspicion. On the contrary, he was a good husband, and there was nothing to suggest that he had ever had such an intention. Deceased knew the sidings very well, and it was another illustration of the saying that "familiarity !'breeds contempt." Men engaged in that occu- pation walked in and out of waggons and over lines where other people would be frightened out of their lives. It, was their every-day em- ployment and they thought nothing about it. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
Mr. Bland expressed the company's regret at the loss of such an excelent, servant. Deceased was very much respected and they could not wish for a better workman.

div.head: SIMPLE REMINDERS.
div.p: SIMPLE REMINDERS.

In order to remember thin„o•s that have lit- tle logical 'connection with each other, mnemonics are useful. TheEe are devices by means of which a set of related letters or words calls up son re other set with which they are associated in the mind of the learner. For instance, take the fact that when an electric current pass,?s along a wire which is stretched above a magnetic needle, the needle turns to the east. The student often feels it difficult to remember whether it turns to the east /or the west. There is nothing in the wire or the nee-le to (rive to on. tion over the other. But let the bewildered one carry in his mind, the word "nose," and he will never make a mistake again, for the word is a simple reminder of the fact that it is desired to recall, and may be read as if the current flows from N, over the needle to the S. then the needle turns to the E. A. student friend had great difficulty in remem- bering the horrible names of the joints of the claw of the crayfish so as to indicate the order of those joints from base to apex. The examiner at the time he was studying for his examination was the distinguished laiolowist Beddard, and he got out of His difficulty, by coining the sentence. Can Beddard Inject Many Crayfish Per Day?• The initial let- ters of the words in this sentence give the clue to the order of the troublesome joints of the appendage. One other little matter. Is there any con- nection between memory and intelligence? Do clever people remember better or worse than people less intellectually endowed? Opinions differ, but the evidence goes to show that the greater intelligence is usually ac- companied by the better memory. On the other hand there are many instances of abso- lutely stupid people having quite an abnorm- al power of memorising lists of words.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
NO EXCUSE.
Laziness Only Cause for Neglect.
A SAD CASE.

"It is nothing but downright, abominable, personal idleness and dirtiness." Such were the words of the Chairman (Councillor H. Roberts) at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, when James and Hannah Mather, 11, Rodney- street, were summoned for neglecting their six children. Mr. A. Browne prdsecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. The Clerk (to defendants) : Will you have-the case tried here or at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions? Mather: You can please yourself what you do with it. • The Clerk: Are you guilty or not guilty? Mather: Not guilty. Mrs. Mather: I have to plead guilty.

Mr. Browne said the case was one of wilful laziness on .the part of the wife in not keeping the children clean. They had been under the observation of Inspector Wainwright for over 12 months, and the school attendance officers, as well as Sunday school officials, had tried to get the woman to keep the children clean. The heads of the children were verminous and they were in such a filthy condition that they were objectionable at school. The man had been warned several times, and matters had come to such a pitch that the society felt bound to prosecute. One of the children had been absent from school 50 times in five weeks through hav- ing a verminous head. Defendants were under an order to send one girl to school, but the Education Committee were unable as yet to apply for committal to du industrial school. The husband was a labourer at Dallam Forge, and his average earnings for five weeks was ..t1 13s. 4d. per week. He 'had only given his wife an average bf 18s. 10d. per week. On one occasion Mather had bought some bedding, which the wife had pawned. It was pure lazi- ness on the woman's part. There was no drink in the case, so far as they had been able to ascertain. Their principal object in summon- ing the husband was to show him that he could not treat warnings of the officers of the society with contempt and to make him aware of his responsibilities. The society wanted to get the children clean, and there was no one better able to look after the children than the mother. He asked that the case should be adjourned for a month, and also that the defendant should give an undertaking to give his wife more wages, and that the wife lova( after the house and keep the children clean. They had lost a large amount to the Education Committee for fines for the absence of children at school. A most remarkable thing about the case was that the food in the house was of the very best, and yet the children were in such a filthy condition. The Chairman said they would adjourn the case for four weeks, and he thought the unani- mous, opinion of the Bench was that unless there was a substdntial improvement the penalty would be severe, because there was no excuse for the neglect. It was nothing but downright, abominable, personal idleness and dirtiness.

div.head: BA TUFF ASSAULTED.
div.p: BA TUFF ASSAULTED.
Warrington Woman Heavily Fined.

/ UNTRUTHFUL WITNESSES. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. J. Rymer Young (in the chair) and other magistrates, Annie Craughton, 9, Vere- street, was summoned for assaulting a bailiff named Gallop, 34, Dial-street.

Mr. J. Longland, who prosecuted, said that the defendant's husband had been the tenant of a house in James-street, under Mr. Gittens. He had got in arrears of rent and they left to go to Vere-street. Mr. Gittens 'discovered this. He issued a distress warrant and put • Gallop in

possession on Tuesday morning. • Whilst Mr. Gittens was away some men came into the house to see a lodger. Mrs. Craughton told Gallop that they were not going to pay the rent, and even- tually she got hold of the man and pushed him out 'of the house. Gallop tried to prevent her, without using violence. It was not so Much for the injury that the summons was taken out, ,lytit for the fact that it was extremely difficult to get bailiffs to do that kind of thing unless they were protected. It was not an uncommon occurrent.!e and the bailiffs felt they could not carry on their duties of rent collecting unless, they wete protected. With the other men being in tl.e house, Gallop thought discretion the better part of valour and did not defend himself as strongly as he might have done when defendant laid her hands on him. Defendant denied laying her hands on Gaihop. Mr. Gittens said that defendant had said to him: "I have put him out." Defendant: You would not take the rent I offered you on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Gittens : They made a fraudulent removal. Defendant :‘ No; I gave you notice on the Wednesday as I left on the Thursday. -Gallop went out on his own accord. A soldier named Flanaghan, who Was in the house, said his opinion was that Gallop got restive and went out on his own. Mrs. Craugh- ton never touched Gallop. A brother-in-law and a lodger said that the woman did not touch Gallop, and the lodger added that she asked Gallop to go and he did. Mr. Longhand: An obliging sort of bailiff. (Laughter.) Gallop said that he had been in possession of a place for font weeks and two days, and it was a caution if lie were going to go out after two hours. It was not his place to go out. She did push him out. . The Chairman: We are of the unanimous opinion that the case has been proved, and it has been very much aggravated by what we regard' as the absolute untruthfulness of the witnesses. Defendant will be fined 20s. and costs, or, in default, a naontles imprisonment.

div.head: FRIDAY.
div.p: FRIDAY.
Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton and Pierpoint, Messrs. T. Locket, A. J. Jolley, S. Wright and W. Furness.

A STARTLING CONFESSION.—Thomas Richardson, 59, King-street, West Bromwich, was charged with having been drunk the previous day.—The Chief Constable said that prisoner went up to P.C. Faulkner and said he gave himself up for the murder of his child, Enid Richardson, at Stockton-on-Tees, three years ago. He said she was then nine months old. He repeated that 'statement to the Superintendent and him (the Chief Constable) at the Police Station, but hay; ing regard to his condition, a charge of drunken- ness was preferred against him. They bad written to the Stockton-on-Tees police and other places. After prisoner had sobered down he said it was all bluff and that he merely made that statement for the purpose of getting back to Stockton-on-Tees. He (the Chief Constable) asked for an adjournment for seven days, in order that inquiries might be made. He would have time for reflection, and would learn that he should not put the authorities to such trouble in' future. He was saturated in drink and the adjournment would do him good.—Prisoner said he Was sorry. He had never been to Stockton in his life.—He was remanded for a week.

div.head: BAND OF HOPE JUBILEE. Great Gathering Takes Place To-day
div.p: BAND OF HOPE JUBILEE. Great Gathering Takes Place To-day
at Manchester. WARRINGTON REPRESENTED.

Two Bishops, several M.P.'s, and many other influential people, including the Mayors and Mayoresses of several boroughs, have, inti- mated their intention to take part in the jubilee of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of f-lere Union at the Exhibition Buildings, flu.l.l6lme. Manchester, to-day. • The celebration has 'aroused the' liveliest in- terest among the friends of temperance work among the young. Between four and five thou- sand specially .appointed delegates from every town and district of Lancashire, Cheshire and North-West Derbyshire, for whom all the Rail- way Companies have offered special facilities, will, in the afternoon, attend a great workers' rally. The arrangements for the rally prdvide that these workers shall be grouped according to districts to facilitate a " Roll Gull" of local- ities. Congratulatory messages .will be pre- sented by all the great national temperance and allied organisations, and an effort to raise a Jubilee:of Hundreds for Temperance Teaching in Schools and other purposes will be inaugu- rated.
At the close of the rally the huge company, which Will include some of the original founders of the institution, will take tea together.

The day's proceedings will be wound up with a great demonstration open to the public, at which special music will be contributed by a massed choir and orchestra of over 600, brought together from Oldham, Wigan, Warrington, Rochdale, Todmorden and other centres.

The union, which is the largest provincial temperance organisation, has carried through striking events, but, as an interesting booklet issued in connection with-the jubilee sags, there is every reason to' believe that this celebration will surpass them all and constitute a record in the history of the Band of Hope movement.

About 13Q delegates will 'attend from War- rington Band of Hope Societies. A choir, con- ducted by Mr. Alfred Spruce, will also take part. in the celebrations and will form part 01. tie great choir which will indlude 600 singers, drawn from all parts of Lancashire and Cheshire. •
Arrangements have been made with the Tram- ways COmmittee of Manchester for running special cars for conveying delegates.

div.head: NATURALIST RAMBLES IN EASTERN
div.p: NATURALIST RAMBLES IN EASTERN
TIBET.

"The 'Land of the Blue Poppy: Travels of a Naturalist in Eastern Tibet" (by F. Kingdon Ward) gives a description of his travels in Eastern Tibet. He adds: "My one hope is that by the time these lines appear I shall be back again in the Land of the Blue Poppy." The land which he thus designates lies north of Burma, east of the land of the elusive Abors at the eastern end of the Himalayas. It is a country of uplifted ridges and river gorges. It was from Shanghai that Mr. Ward set out, but not by way of the most wonderful of Chinese rivers, for he sailed round to Rangoon and went up through Mandalay, past the Burman frontier, reaching the upper waters of the Yangtze ten weeks after he had left its estuary. It was by the side of this and the other rivers, or across the divides between them, that his routes lay; and the fascination of their strangeness and beauty was not lessened by the hardships and the risks of travel, but in retrospect, at any rate, was heightened. This picture of the Ambassa- dors' lioad to Talifa is good reading : "As for me I have an eye for plants, and to my mind the high plateaux between the deeply. scoured trench-like valleys, now blazing with scarlet rhododendrons and pink camellias, that I was .almost oblivious of anything else.. . . _ _

_ After the mid-day halt I would leave the men to load the animals, and, taking my gun, wan- der alone among the park-like, undulating hills, finding here sheets of mauve primulas blooming on emerald, grassy slopes, dog-roses yellow and white, pale blue irises, and other delightful flowers."

This was but at the gateway to the land which he was searching for flowers, and which, while rewarding the search • with individual rarities, presented commoner flowers, blue sal- vias, as well as the blue poppy, mpnkshood, lovely asphodel in extravagant profusion, so that we receive the impression of a land whose heights are exposed to the bleakness of a sub- arctic winter, but whose valleys are clothed with the flowers of an eternal spring. Not less vivid than this impression, of the flowered carpet of the valleys is that of the gorges of the rivers, notably that of the Mekong. The Mekong has neither the tremendous current of the Salineen nor the breadth of the Yangtze, but as at night the traveller heard it thundering through its gorges he thought, he says, the grandest river of them all. The road by "this amazing gutter" was high above it, but ti-T valley walls tower high above the road. "Sonlc- times we must have been 3,000 ft, above .the water, so that we could look down on great rapids and yet hear no sound." The rivers are crossed here and there by swaying rope and plank bridges.

Mr. Ward is interested in the people he meets, their habits and their characteristics; he is always ready to make inferences concerning the geological and georaphical history of the localities he passes through. He appends a list of plants collected and of mammals identified, and his volume is a valuable addition to the scanty knowledge of a little-known region. But one of its chief attractions is that the know- ledge is so imparted and the travels so well written that they must prove of the greatest interest to that intelligent and growing body of the public which can recognise in some books of travel a higher and more satisfying form of entertainment than any fiction.

One of the tribes Mr. Ward encountered, the Lutzu. use the cross-bow as a universal wennon, and even the boys in the river vnlleys have small cross-bows which serve the purpose of catanults. There are, accordingly, scarcely any birds in these valleys.
Don't meet trouble half-way—make it race after you. Some fellows marry poor girls and settle down, while others marry rich girls to settle up.

HISS AINSIIIE'S PEARLS.
BY CHARLES D. LESLIE
Author of "A Change of Relations," The Confidence of Dr. Smart," "Juliet of Straker's Farm," "A Fair Deceiver," &c.

Among the things which Miss Ainslie did not know—and the ignorance of a carefully- brought-up girl of nineteen concerning the things that matter is only equalled by the extent of her useless knowledge—was whether her father was rich or merely well-to-do. He was a solicitor, with an office in Lincoln's Inn Fields, arid an old-established clientele of solid, well-to-do families, and lived com- fortably yet unostentatiously in Hampstead with his daughter and his daughter's com- panion, Miss Canister, who also filled the position of housekeeper. The pearl necklace was his gift to his daughter on her twentieth birthday, and Miss Ainslie, possessing the appreciation of "pretty things" common to her sex, went into a girlish ecstasy over it. She declared it " lovely ' about twenty times as she pea- cocked before the mirror with the circlet of pear-shaped, silvery-white globules round her neck, and she hugged her dour-looking father till he stopped her. "There, there, what a child you are. I think, Prudence, you had better keep them in the safe., Though I've no doubt our ser- vants are perfectly honest, it will be better not to put temptation in their way." " Yes, papa," said Miss Ainslie, submis- sively, and in the study safe, when not worn, the necklace reposed accordingly. It was just as get-at-able there by its fair owner as in her bedroom. The safe worked by a combination of letters, and the word which unlocked it was know n to her. She was very proud of the fact that her father made her 'his under- study in this matter, and that no one in the house save he and she knew how to open it. Miss Ainslie wore the 'pearls at two dances to which she went that week, and at a small dinner-party at home, and the necklace was much admired, especially by her particular friend, Minnie Collard, who, calling a few weeks later, confessed: "I've come to ask a great favour. I'm go- ing to the ball at the German Embassy /next week. Lady O'Brian is to take me. And I've no jewellery fit to wear for such, a swell function. I shall look so much the poor rela- tion. Prue, darling, would you be sweet enough to lend me your pearl necklace?" " Yes," said Miss Ainslie; but, being a I conscientious young woman, wondered I guiltily, even as her friend hugged her, if she woUld have granted the favour had Minnie not been Jack's brother. Minnie and Jack, lived in a flat in Crickle- wood, and between Jack Collard and Miss Ainslie there existed a sentimental attach- ment. Jack had a billet in a bill broker's office at a salary of two hundred and fifty a year, and vague expectations of a partner- ship. So he remained an undeclared lover, and Minnie found Prudence a very useful friend; and Misr Ainslie dreamt vain dreams,, and fondly imagined the state of her affections was unknown to Miss Collard.

Minnie duly wore the necklace at the Em- bassy ball, and then petitioned to keep it four days longer. She wanted to wear it at a dance in Kensington. Miss Ainslie retrieved it after an absence of five days, just in time, for twenty-four ‘hours later Mr. Mane said, "Wear your !necklace to-night, Prudence. I want to show it to a friend who's coming to dinner."

When she entered the drawing-room that evening her father and the visitor were stand- ing talking on the hearthrug; the latter, a thin, elderly man with shaggy eyebrows and very dark eyes' gazed approvingly at the slender, white-robed figure that approached. "My little girl," said Mr. Ainslie. "Pru- dence, Mr. Grindrod. By the way, Grindrod, you are an authority on pearls. Give me your opinion on my daughter's necklace? Mr. Grindrod has lived in the East and dealt in pearls," he added to Miss Ainslie. The authority on pearls bowed and ex- pressed his pleasure on making the young lady's acquaintance; then he smiled at the fair-haired girl with the speedwell blue eyes before him, and said .drily: "Apparently, Ainslie, your s daughter d - •:4- urnrth while to wear her fogey like myself is the in answer to his host's • ie added, quietly : "Miss artificial.'

does this mean, Pru- dence? Have you had a copy of the necklace made without consulting me?" "No, papa, it's—it's the necklace you gave me," stammered Miss Ainslie. She raised her hands to her neck and stripped it of its adornment. "Oh, Mr. Grindrod, it can't be artificial ! "

The expert took the, necklace and glanced at it as it lay in his palm. "Not even good imitation pearls," he pronounced. "Can you explain this, child?" demanded her father, with hardly suppressed wrath. "When you've not been wearing it, has the necklace been. anywhere except in the safe? Has it ever been out of your possession?" Under the fierce glance of his eyes Miss Ainslie trembled and lied. "No, papa." Then, to her relief, came a knock at the door. "If you please, sir,- dinner is served," an- nounced the butler.

Mr. Ainslie bottled his anger. "Miss Canister is not down, Hemmings, go and tell her we are waiting," and as the man with- drew; "Let us drop \ the subject, please, Grindrod. i must investigate this mystery later."

With the advent of an apologetic Miss Canister the quartette went in to dinner. "How and when could the metamorphosis have taken place?" Miss Ainslie asked her- self. /t was impossible the substitution had taken place while the necklace was in her possession. But for five days it had been out of her possession. What had Minnie, its tem- porary owner, been about? Had she been lending it to somebody else? That might ex- plain the mystery. But even as she tried to argue herself into this interpretation of it, another came, fantastically impossible on the face of it. But the ugly suggestion, onze formulated in her brain, declined to depart. It rose from recollection of a recent talk with Jack—some bitter remarks he had dropped as to his poverty. "Riches are not everything." The platitude had come to her lips uncon- sciously. "Far from it, but money is the chief in- gredient in almost every recipe for it. Lack of money means lack of ability to catch for- tune by the skirts, when she cornea in one's way. Here's an instance: I was given a splen- did tip the other day about a moribund pri- vate railway in Argentina. It's going to be taken up by the Argentine Government. If I only had a little •apital to plunge with, I might make a few thousands. But I'm too poor to speculate. Too poor even to marry." Had Jack Collard taken her pearls and pledged them, substituting the sham neck- lace? Impossible, surely, for he waS a man of honour—and yet, was it impossible? The temptation had come in his 'way, and he had vielded to it. But if he had sinned, his love .for her had been the motive. So she argued with herself.

But though he felt suspicion pointed ta Jack, the lie told her father must be con- fessed, and at the ewliest possible moment. It soon came. . The ladies had not returned to the drawing-room many minutes befold Mr. Grindrod entered. only to take leave. Mr. Ainslie parted from his guest on tiJ doorstep, and encountered his daughter in the hall.

"Papa, I've something to tell you." "Do you know that necklace cost two thou- sand pounds?" vociferated Mr. Ainslie, when be had heard her confession. "I was a fool to allow you to take charge of so valuable an ornament."

" But, papa, it's absurd to suspect Minnie." "Well, at any rate I mean to hear this very night what she has to say about it. Put a cloak on, child" ; and five minutes later they we 1? in a cab bound for Cricklewood. Minnie greeted her unexpected visitors cor- dially, and bade the maid whe admitted them fetch Mr. Collard, who was sitting with a bachelor friend on the floor above. Then, vecosznising from her friend's face that some- thing untownrd had brought them, she asked, when the servant had closed the door, what was wrong. Mr. Ainslie answered: "I learnt this evening for the first time, Minnie, that Prudence lent you her pearl necklace a week ago, and you only returned it yesterday." Miss Collard opened her eyes. "Is that such a serious matter?" she inquired. " No, a trivial matter, though I consider I wught to have, bee;Ltold. But what is serious
tnat tne•pearis are gone, ana an imitation necklace has been substituted. A friend, an expert, dining with us to-night detected the fraud."

"Good gracious ! " "Where did you keep the necklace while in your posseesion? " "I gave it to Jack," replied Minnie, "Oh ! :here he is. Jack, an awful thing has happened. Prue's pearl necklace hese-been stolen and a sham one substituted."

Jack came forward and shook hands in silence. "When was this discovery made?" he asked. Mr. Ainslie briefly put him in possession of the facts, as far as they were known, point- ing out how impossible it was any substitu- tion could have taken place in his house. "It was only to-night I learnt Pruilence had lent the necklace to Minnie, who has had it here for 'nearly a week, Only returning it twenty- four hours ago. So I naturally come to ask if Minnie or you can throw any light on this mystery?" "May I see the imitation necklace?" Jack examined it carefully before he spoke again. "Whether this is or is not, the necklace I had charge of day and night, except on the two occasions when Minnie was wearing it, I'm not sufficiently an expert to say. At least it's marvellously like it. But the necklace was not changed while in my possession. That I will swear. I carried the case containing it in an inside pocket all day, and slept at night with my door locked and the case under my pillow." "Then you can offer no explanation how the substitution was effected?" "None, sir, I regret to say." "And you, Minnie?" Miss Collard shook her head hopelessly. "I shall have to take the matter to Scot- land Yard." _ _ _

"That is the only course to take, air. I'm sorry Minnie's vanity has' involved us in the mystery of the loss. Personally I knew nothing of the loan till Miss Prudence brought the necklace here the day of the Em- bassy Ball. But I will answer for my sister's innocence and my own." He spoke proudly, looking the elder man straight in the face as he did so, and Miss Ainslie uttered a sigh of relief. How absurd of her to have snspectecl Jack even for a moment! Mr. Ainslie winced. The young man's father had been a friend of many years' standing. He blew his nose, and answered, warmly: "My dear Jack, of course you and Minnie are above suspicion. Scotland Yard will be bound to suspect everybody, including Pra- dence and myself. But I assure you that I ab- solve you both from any knowledge of how the substitution was effected."

"Thank you, sir, perhaps I had better in- form you at once that any detective put on the task of discovering the thief will be bound to suspect me." "Why so?" "For a reason which I acknowledge throws suspicion upon me." "And that is ? "
" Three days ago I handed Abbott and Co., the stockbrokers, banknotes for eighteen hun- dred pounds as cover, buying, speculatively, a block of Castilardo Railway shares." "You did ! "

"I've already on paper made four thousand pounds by the deal, but I anticipate they will go higher, and the account is still open." "And where did you get the money?" "Unfortunately, sir, I'm not at liberty to mention the name of my financial backer." _ .

i "Jack," sail the solicitor n another tone, "better be frank, my boy, if you wish to keep the good opinion of your friends." "At present, sir, 1 can say no more." The young man turned to Miss Ainslie. "Pru- dence, you at least will absolve me of being concerned in this mysterious theft?" "Oh, yes, Jack, oh, yee," she cried, eagerly putting her hand in his; "if you say so I know you're innocent." He bent and kissed her, hands. " klumph !" grunted Mr. Ainslie, staring at the young couple with sckewed-up eyelids, making a discovery of even more importance than the theft of the necklace. He took Miss Ainslie away, and sat in grim silence as they drove home. So Jack Collard loved his daughter. That was a small matter. But the girl loved the young man. That made it serious. Nor was it possible to ignore the fact, for next day Jack took advantage of his luncheon hour to call on the solicitor and formally beg periais- sion to ask Miss Ainslie to marry him. "It won't do, Jack," said Mr. Ainslie, "even setting aside the necklace business; it won't do. I have other ,views for the child's future." _ . _

"What are your objections to me, sir?" Thus challenged, the solicitor hesitated, and had finally to confess that if Jack had a little more money, and if the necklace mys- tery was satisfactorily cleared up, and if Pru- dence was willing, he could advance no reason why the young man should not become his son-in-law. At present he pointed out the three " ifs " „held the field. But the suitor withdrew so cheerfully that the father feared they were fences he anticipated no difficulty in clearing. Meantime, Scotland Yard hid been in- formed of the loss of the ,pearls, and three days later a voice -Which introduced itself over the telephone as Inspector Bungay rang up the solicitor and expressed a desire to visit in his company his Hampstead home. To this Mr. Ainslie replied that if Inspector Bungay would call at Lincoln's Inn Fields at five o'clock he was quite at the detective's disposal. Inspector Bungay proved to be a cheerful- looking man of thirty or so, with an alert manner and twinkling black eyes. He ex- plained that the case having been turned over to him he had been working on it for the lasi two days. Well, the results had been nega- tive so far, but he hoped in examination of the safe that had guarded the necklace might yield some clue. Mr. Ainslie shook his head. "I fear not. I'm firmly convinced the substitution took place while the necklace was in the possession of the Collards—not that I suspect either of them," he added, ." they are both incapable of the theft."

"I'm convinced so too, sir. Though I naturally began by suspecting the gentleman owing to the information you gave on firm re- porting the loss. I called on Mr. Collard. He very foolishly declined to enlighten me as to the source of the banknotes he had handed over to stockbrokers earlier in the week. But it was not a difficult matter to trace them. They were paid over the counter of the London and Edinburgh bank to old General Macintosh, who has an account there, and is a shareholder into the bargain." "Jack's godfather ! " exclaimed Mr. Ainslie. "I don't know why Mr. Collard made such a mystery of the matter." "But I can guess," said the solicitor. "The poor General is a hen-pecked warrior, and probably feared his wife knowing he was speculating on the Stock Exchange. Jack had a first - class tin about a South American rail- way, and wanted a little- capital for cover; he probably went to the General who lent him the money on the strict proviso not to men- tion his name in the matter.
"Well, sir, I have, at least temporarily, crossed both Mr. and Miss Collard off my list of suspects. The evidence at present points to Miss Ainslie."

"Are you serious?" asked Mr. Ainslie, angrily. "Quite, sir," replied the detective, coolly, "though I have no doubt the young lady will be able to clear herself. Shall we start for Hampstead?" On the way the Inspector chatted cheerfully on the benefits of Tube Railways and the salubrity of Hampstead, but Mr. Ainslie was haughtily distant. Five minutes' walk frost the station brought them to their destination, and by aid of his latch-key the solicitor ad- mitted himself and his visitor into the house. The study, a. roomy, handsome apartment, was on the ground floor, the windows looking into the garden, but exit was barred by a deep WM. for the old-fashioned house con- tained a basement storey. As they entered the room Mr. Ainslie called to Hemmings, who appeared at the kitchen end of thc hall, "Tell Miss Prudence I desire her presence hem."
The detective cast a keen, roving eye about the room, and let it settle on the safe; he was still dwelling on it when Miss Ainslie entered.
"Here is my daughter, Inspector. Now kindly inform me what evidence .you have pointing to her IA the purloiner of her own necklace ! "
Mr. Bungay, totally unabashed, bowed to the amazed Miss Ainslie, and taking a letter from his pocket-book silently handed it to the solicitor.
" Good Heavens!" ejaculated the latter, "Prudence, here is a letter from you to Had- don's ordering a replica of the necklace! " The girl stared at the letter in netrified (Continued in next eolumn.)

div.head: NEV! ZEALAND'S DEMAND FOR DOMESTIC SERVANTS.
div.p: NEV! ZEALAND'S DEMAND FOR DOMESTIC SERVANTS.
Comfortable Homes offered to Girls.

The social unrest which has disturbed so many elements of Society has not escaped the servant . class, who, rightly or wrongly, are largely dissatis- fied with their present lot. Infected with the spirit of adventure and romance which has been Id abroad by the great colonial, nigration movements now on , root, thousands of servant girls are brooding over their grievances, real or imagined i —the smallness of their wages, the length of their hours, the scantiness of their leisure—wistfully considering the greater opportunities offered in impire.
;pret er
BEAUTIFUL LAND.

Surely no Colony or Dominion of the British Crown has greater attractions to offer to these young women than New Zealand, described by travellers as "The Wonderland of the World." This beautiful land has a delightful climate, warmer and more equable than that of Great Britain, and without extremes either of heat or cold. The loveliest scenery', lies at hand within easy reach of the towns—majestic mountains, rushing waterfalls, magnificent canons, and mar- vellous lakes. _
The towns themselves are well planned and well lighted, and social attractions, such as theatres, cinematograph halls, skating rinks, &c., are numerous. '
GOOD WAGES AND EXCELLENT LIVESrG. There is no lack of opportunity for domestic servants in this w.alderful land.

Thousands of competent and reliable girls could get immediate engloyment in New Zealand. The wages pale range from 20s. to 30s. per week for. cooks, 15s. to 20s. for general house servants, 10s. to 20s. for household farm servants, and 12s. to 15s. for housemaids, board in each case included. The cost of living is, generally speaking lower, as compared with earnings, than it is in Great Britain.

Young women who are approved by the. High Commissioner for New Zealand are granted passages at reduced rates. Those girls who desire to go to New Zealand should write to the High Commissioner for New Zealicud (Emigration Department), 13, Victoria Street, London, S.W., a post card would do, and. he :would at once supply the fullest information in regard to New Zealand and the voyage. The fare is only £2. 165., as compared with the- ordinary fare of £lO. Those to whom teduced ride passages are granted walk off the steamers free agents and may work where they like and for 'whom they may desire in New Zealand, / the Government making • r no restriction in this j UrrCi .222_ matter provided the girls t take up domestic service. No part ion of the fare conceded has to be riyanded. 460

tinction is made between ordinary pas- sengers and those having re— cinced rate passages. , In cases where approved' domestic servants have not sufficient money to pay their IN SERVICE IN fare, the High Commissioner NEW ZEALAND. would advance the amount to them.

The girls are accompanied by an experienced matron and doctor. The voyage lasts about six weeks, and as excellent food is provided and the steamers are large, of the highest class, and fitted. with modern improvements, the trip out is in itself quite a, holiday. Most of the steamers call at Teneriffe, the beautiful island of the sugar-loaf mountain, Cape Town, with its magnificent table mountain, and. Hobart. At t'lese ports parties of girls are made up for the shoe and visit the more interesting " sights " of the cities during the stay of the steamer. Thus the voyager sees for the first time something of the great and beautiful world that lies beyond the seas.

div.head: PRINTER AND HIS STONE.
div.p: THE PRINTER AND HIS STONE.
A remarkable gravestone has been placed in the cemetery at Jefferson, Ohio. . _ _ _

It stands at the head of the grave of J. A. Howells, the veteran editor of the "Ashtabula Sentinel," who died there recently. It consists of the " make-up " stone tzsed by Mr. Howells for fifty years during his successive evolutions as printer's devil, printer and editor. It is Inscribed with these lines, written by William Dean liovv'ells, a brother of the editor: Stone, upon which with hands of boy and man, He framed the history of his time until. Week after week, the varying record ran, To its half-centured tale of well and ill.
Remember now how true through all -those days, Re was—friend, brother, husband, son— Fill the whole limit of your space with praise, There needs no room for blame—blame there was none.
MISS AINSLIE'S PEARLS—continued.
horree ere she found her tongue: "Papa, 1 never wrote it ! "
"It's your handwriting ! " thundered her father.

"Or a clever forgery," put in the detective, quietly. He turned to the girl with a smile, Miss Ainslie, not for one moment did I sus- pect you. Had you really desired to deceive your father in this matter you would not have wriitten openly. from this house ordering a re- plica of the Jewellers who sold Mr. Ainslie the necklace. You see this letter is dated ten days ago. Mr. Haddon accepted it as genuine, and a week later sent the replica here by registered post. It was posted only three days ago." "Then Jack is cleared beyond a shadow of dcubt," cried Miss Ainslie, triumphantly. She looked at her father. "Papa!" she added, reproachfully. The solicitor was embarrassed. "I beg your pardon, Prudence; but what a clever forgery this is! Who could have written it?" "Someone in the house," said the detec- tive—" someone who intercepted the case from the jeweller." He paused, for Hemmings, the butler, en- tered at that moment with some letters on a. salver. The detective's twinkling black eyes raked the staid, middle-aged serving-man. " Buckley! " he exclaimed, with a sudden. shout. "Mr. Ainslie, we need'nt look further for the thief. With a ticket-of-leave man whose speciality is word combination safes in the house—" The butler, panic-stricken, sprang at the open window and essayed to jump forth. But Bungay, lithe as a cat, leaped and caught him by the ankle. With a sudden wrench the other freed himself, overbalanced, and van- ished into the area below. There came to those in the room above the sound of a faint thud, then silence. "Silly fool," growled the detective, peer- ing down; "he couldn't escape." But he was wrong. The fugitive had broken his neck.

The pearl necklace VMS found concealed in the butler's room. Jack Collard called on Mr. Ainslie next day, and with the air of a millionaire stated he could settle five thousand pounds on hie future wife.

'Thanks to the old General'e loan," com- mented the solicitor. He smiled at the young man, and smothered a sigh. He had never known how fond he was of his daughter till he knew he was shortly to lose her.

"I want no settlement from you, Jack. I'll do all that. Go and talk to Prudence, you'll And her in the drawing-room, and if she-" He stopped perforce. Jack Collard had hastily quitted the room; Mr. Ainslie heard him pelting upstairs. He eighed again. "Hang the pearl necklace ! " he muttered. "I see now this forthcoming marriage Wag inevitable, but my birthday gift . baa ad- vanced 4t. at least a tuelvemonth.".
