div.head: MONEY-LENDING VAMPIRES
div.p: MONEY-LENDING VAMPIRES
How Warrington Working-
men are Fleeced.

div.head: 1,300 PER CENT. INTEREST.
div.p: 1,300 PER CENT. INTEREST.
A Sure Way of Keeping Poor M.in Poor.
COMMUNITY'S RESPONSIBILITY.

It is said, and it is true, that our great com- mercial system is largely based on credit, money lent. There are those who have money and do not care to use it, or do not know pro- fitably how to use it, and there are those whb can use profitably more money than they pos- sess. Hence A large part of the capital in use does not belong to those who employ it; it is borrewell on interest. - In most cases borrower and lender are independent of each other, the obligation is mutual, or rather there is no obligation on either side. Where this independence exists the lender cannot extort an exorbitant interest, and the borrower cannel make his own terms. This is not always ,the case. There are those in all grades of society who are on the look-out for those in great need, or with little sense, from whom exorbitant inierest can be got'.

div.head: HOW Is. MAY BECOME £409 10s.
div.p: HOW Is. MAY BECOME £409 10s.

We find local representatives of this class in Warrington,' and the money lent is more than many in our town know anything about. It IS satisfactory to be able to state that this evil IS not as prevalent as it was two or three years ago, when it was conducted inside several of the Warrington works. The masters and the workmen have practically stamped this out. if it continues at all, it is done very secretly. There is a system of short loans at large in- terest, which, is 'very Profitable to the lender and 'very unprofitable to the wage-earning Ifbr- rower. Money is lent by professional money- lenders, who, under law, are compelled to regis- ter their names and places of business. This Obligation is frequently not complied with. Persons systematically lending ,without regis- trations are liable to a heavy penalty. che • sums lent are on the security of the promise to repay when the weekly wage is. re- ceived. It may be lent any time during the week, even on the Friday night, but must be repaid with, interest on pay day. The interest charged is worked upon the shilling, and is generally Ltireepence, or at the rate of 25 per cent. weekly.

We understand that through competition the money-lending rate, has in some instances, come down to twopence in the shilling. A shilling, if lent week after week, will earn in the Year, apart from compound interest, 1,300 per cent. per annum, on the threepenny }oasis. It will have grown from one shilling to fifty- three. But with compound interest it will amount to more than £4OO. Let us see how. A money-lender starts with a capital of one shilling. lie meets a thirsty worker at the gates of one of our Warrington works, and lends him this shilling, say, on a Monday, the worker engages to pay back is. 3d. when be gets his wages on Saturday. The process is repeated, say, for four weeks. The money- lender has then two shillings to lend on the fifth week. In another four weeks this two shillings has, as before, doubled itseq, and become four; at the end of the third four weeks it will have become eight, and s 6 on. Now there are thir- teen four weeks in the year, and if the lender is able to continue lending as he accumulates, .it the end of the year his capital would be £409 10s., all made out of one shilling. But not ex- actly made out of the one shilling; rather out of the foolishness of the borrowers who parted with other shillings. Shillings do not multiply like rabbits. But what does this 'foolishness mean? It means that the tiorkers have parted with £409 of their wages and got nothing for it. "But," say some, "surely the borrower has managed to quench his thirst, has got his beer —for it is beer upon which this borrowed money Is generally spent?" Not at all. The money increase has nothing to do with the value of the beer. The borrower has paid for that in addi- tion. The £409 is composed entirely of the in- terest that he has paid on his loan, and is apart from the money borrowed. The man has got he beer, the publican a shilling, and the lender another shilling in repayment and threepence as well. And it is of these threepences that the £409 is made up.

div.head: LENDERS NOT SOLELY TO BLAME.
div.p: LENDERS NOT SOLELY TO BLAME.

Of course, it would te very easy to throw the whole blame upon the money-lender, to speak of him as oa. moral vampire, who waits at the works gate and takes advantage of the thirsty condition of the worker, something in the same way as the cunning Jacob jockeyed Elie hungry Esau out of his birthright. Certainly, these in- dividuals are not of the class who ought to command the respect of any decent citizen. .Leir trade, if it can be ,called such, is an un- worthy one, their usury is exorbitant. They •,)hit by the weakness of their fellows, they 'do nothing to enrich the world, they make noth- ing, they improve nothing. Their work is en- tirely unproductive, they are drones in the hive or industry, parasites who live upon others. And all the time they think themselves as worthy of respect as the man who plants pota- toes or hoistS a sail.

But they are not the only Ones to blame. We have, no doubt the money-lender has reasons which seem good to himself .for following this form of gain. He may say that the borroWer is a free agent, respousible for his own actions, and if he thinks well to spend one and three- pence for a shilling's worth of beer, what busi- ness is it of the lender. If he did not lend it, someone else would. He finds the original shilling, runs some risk of not ge:tiiig it back ; and has to stand at the yard gateq, of the works in rain and shine to give facilities to the bor- rower. If a goose comes asking to be plucked, or a sheep to be shorn, why should he be blamed for plucking or shearing him straight away, and making the most he can out of feathers and wool? He may tell us that at times he forgives the loan, or at any rate the interest. He may claim Mat by facilitating the consumption of liquor he is encouraging an important local industry, and the like. Prob- ably with such a profitable method of getting other people's money, he has no desire to con- sider the reasons against it, and therefore any- thing said to the money-lender is like water spilt on the ground—he will not gather a drop.
THE FOOLISH MAN AND TIIE COMMUNITY.

The blame is not all with him. Why are the borrowers so eager to prove themselves foolish? But why should anyone object, if they like to waste their money? Have they not earned it? Why shoUld Anyone interfere? There are limits to the right of possession, and this irre- spective of class, which are becoming more and more recognised. The man who, on being re- proved by the magistrate for kicking his wife, replied by asking the question, "Well, is she not my own; cannot I do what I like with my own?" This man is dead! It is not true that a man has a right to do what he likes with his own. First, he has his family obligations. No. man can rear a family properly and at the same time indulge in the foolishness of paying 25 per cent. for a week's loan. But the community have something to say to this man. It is in connection with foolish workers of this sort, men without forethOught or grit, with which most of the Serious social difficulties arise. It is this man's children Who need to be schosol fed, this man's child who requires clogs, this man's house that becomes a slum, this man's family that has to be publicly fed, when any difficulty arises, the result of temporary stoppage of

div.head: "TiE EXAMINER" OFFICE.
div.p: "TiE EXAMINER" OFFICE.
THE EXAMINER,
SEPTEMBER 27, 1913
"THE VOICE OF REASON."

'There can be heard once- more the "Voice Of Reason," which was raised by. so many Tory organs during the Constitutional Conference in 1910 to priklann that the .consideration which had in the past committed the Tory party to an anti-Home Rule policy no longer had any force. The "Daily Telegraph" asserts that there must be some change in the government of Ireland. The "Times" reminds those who assume the Unionist. party to be indissolubly wedded to the existing system of government in Ireland that, if such an assumption once accurately reflected Unionist policy, then Unionist policy has changed. • Mr. J. L. GARVIN recalls, after a long peri6d of discreet oblivion, the vigour with which he once trumpeted the "Voice of Reason." All of these voices, it is true, are still prepared to denounce the Goverriment's solution of the Irish problem. But they avow that there is a problem, and that a solution is imperative.

From the time when the Liberal Government was returned to office by the General Election of 1910, the Tory party has pursued a certain line of tactics in regard to the Home Rule ques- tion. This line was not diverted by the, intro- duction of the Home Rule Bill. The Tory tactics have accepted what in Tory parlance is stigmatised as a " lethargy " on the part of the British elector where the Orangeman's indigna- tion against a Home Rye Bill is concerned. It would be imprudent, Tory tacticians decided, to make Home Rule and the Ulster Orangemen's intransigent attitude a leading issue at by- elections. The prudent course was to set the party's sails to catch the transient gales of the Insurance Act's unpopularity, and let the Home Rule question wait until the Orange LodgA of Ulster had given the Government, and perhaps the British-,public, a good fright. Trouble in Ulster was to be the same godsend for the Tory party in the Home Rule issue as "two black winters" would be for the Tory party on the Tariff Reform issue. But ,politicians who can- not control the seasons can at least work upon human prejudices and pafsions. And Mr. BONAR .LAW'S historic 'hand-clasp with Sir EDWARD CARSON at Craigavon was an unmis- takable indication of the " spade-wgrk " which the Tory leader wanted done. The Tory leader had quite a different object in view from the man whom he delegated to this job of spade- work. Mr. BONAR LAW wanted a storm raised which would give his party the opportunity to try their luck at 'yet another General Election before it was, due. Sir EDWARD CARSON wanted to ensure, by•any means, however reckless, the riumph of a Unionist policy, which the" Times," pronounces to be out of date., Now some of the shrewdest Tory politicians are beginning to see that their Leader enlisted at Craigavon lan embarrassing ally—an ally who would be, per- haps, even more embarrassing 'to the Tory party in power than to the Tory party in opposition.
Will the Voice of Reason" be listened to— especially as it is now admitted that there is an Irish problem that will have to be solved?

div.head: TANNERS' WAGE QUESTION.
div.p: THE TANNERS' WAGE QUESTION.

Matters have taken a more serious turn in regard to the wage question at the Warrington tanneries. Several conferendes have been held without result, and a full meeting of the employers was held on Tuesday, and it is understood that a definite course. of action has been decided upon, but wnat form this will take has not been disclosed. The employers of Iluncorn and Warrington are acting in con- huiction. Humours are prevailing that a lock- out contemplated, and the fact that some of the limes in a few yards are being run empty has been accepted as an indication that the masters contemplate, such a step. Whether a lock-out is in view cannot be ascertained, but those most in touch with • the trade are in- clined to place no credence in the story. 'Trade is too busy and profits too good for a lock-out," said one employe. However, some develop- ments may be reached within the next week'.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEVrEMBER 27, 1913. THE PASSING WEEK.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEVrEMBER 27, 1913. THE PASSING WEEK.

this remarkable lead, the silence is oppressive. Has anyone heard a whisper of any Tariff Re- form League wishing to follow the eNample. which it has been set? We are glad to think the Women Tariff Reformers, whether in War- rington or elsewhere, are hesitating before they make themselves into the laughing-stock upon the scale they were invited to do at Walton.

div.head: "P. AND K."-AND A GROWL.
div.p: "P. AND K."-AND A GROWL.

As we announced some weeks ago, and as the annual.report•now,issued confirms, the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Ltd., had a very good time during the twelve months which ended June 30th last. The Balkan War adversely affected the iron and steel trades— yet "all departments of the company's business show satisfactory results for the year." The report contains the usual political growl. The National Insurance Act has added .largely to the cost of production, we are told, "without resulting in benefit to the company's workmen proportionate to the expense." Surely we have a confusion of ideas here. The employers, not the employes, are concerned with the cost of production, and the employers seem to have made ends Meet in spite of this most terrible of "serious burdens imposed by recent legislation upon the iron and coal trades." Messrs. Pear- son and Knowles have done so well, in fact, that they have advanced their rate of interest to 10 per cent. on the half-year, making the divi- dend for the year through 8 per cent., an in- terim dividend of 6 per cent having been already declared in respect of the first half-year. Curious as it may seem in a commercial document, there is •a suggestion—whether to the Government or not does not appear—that it would be better to have an insurance scheme administered in con- junction with the Old Age Pensions, and deriv- ing "its revenue from the 'same source." • Old- agp pensions are paid for out of the public purse, and if insurance charges came from "the same source/ it would no 'doubt be a relief to manu- facturers. But this plunging for alternative methods, under which, may be, somebody else may pay, leads to endless confusion. It is not so long ago that Mr. Harold Smith, who, we assume, belongs to the same political party as the Board responsible for Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' report, appeared to suggest to a Corn- hill audience that the Insurance Act was all right except that it should be voluntary and not coMpulsory. I,Vhen old-age pensions were established the great cry of this same party was , that old-age pensions should be Contributory; 17, but should be that is, those who received them should have paid for them beforehand. Now they say insur- anceb.ehocloenetroimbumtounity . It is some paid fsohro UhT, notthe v‘ satisfaction to know that the Insurance Act has , not ruined Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, and it seems a pity that the bright year's record should be partially blighted by croaking—for political effect—about the future. On the face lof the report everything is as it should be, even stamp-licking though has been in operation for over a year—but the future! "In normal times," says the report, in its most sepulchral passages, "the contributions will be a serious tax Upon wages, as well as profits." "In ' normal times." What does that mean? •Do Pearson and Knowles look upon .worse times as " normal " ? If they are enjilying abnormal times now they are doing so under what they would call, in derisive tones, Lloyd George finance. Would they like lo return to the normal under, say, a Tariff Reform regime, with Austen Chamberlain and Bonar Law and the Colonies directing our affairs? We think the worker, in Lancashire at all events, will prefer these abnormal times, when dividends reach 10 per cent. on the half-year at Pearson and Knowles', and when they themselves are in full emplOyment. "In non;ual times!" It is a curious world in which we live. f

div.head: WHAT OF THE DOCTORS?
div.p: WHAT OF THE DOCTORS?

It will be remembered that prior to the pass- ing. of the Insurance Act, and as long as there was any chance of political capital being made out of an untried piec'e Of legislation, a section Of the Warrington doctors joined the fractious members of their prOfession elsewhere, in de- manding the scalp' of Mr. Lloyd George, and opposing the measure which they pretended was to do so mkt' injury to them ns medical men. Where are, those doctors now? We asked the question ~of a gentleman, .l a position to know as well as any- o‘r\en.cl Yeeci.nitsl n His reply was brief and to .the point. "The doctors in Warrington who were loudeSt in their denunciation of the Act," he said, "are better off than they ever were in their lives. It has been the making of them. Most, if not all, have set. up motor cars." But if the doctors- ane making more than 10 per cent. under the Act, they have the decency to remain quiet, and they are not looking for- ward to bad times, when they can re-enter upon their political campaign. They, at all .events, prefer these "abnormal" prosperous times, and are not sighing for the future to come to their relief.

div.head: AND THE WORKING CLASSES?
div.p: AND THE WORKING CLASSES?

As we have pointed out on previous Ova- Lions, the Insurance Act is intended to put the working classes in the same position on a smaller scale, as the employing classes. That is to say, when they are feeling ill, 0r " uff_ colour," as they put it, they can now consult a doctor and take a rest without the fear of con- tracting a doctor's bill and running into debt that may cripple them for years, perhaps for life. Hitherto, a poor Working man has had to stick it until he broke down ; now he can go in for his rest cure; a rest in a truer sense of the -word than when used by those in better finan- cial circumstances. We know that actual ex- perience is very, rapidly proving in Warring- ton, as in other part j of the country, that this care Of the worker, this prevention of his going on to the last gasp and final disaster, is effecting a marvellous change in the stamina of the worliing people. That is the side of the question that affects "the company's work- men." Cost of productiA has its relation to the 8 per cent. dividend. There may be, it is true, a way in which, the effect of the Act may be felt on the cost of production, but it is scarcely in the ,way that the Pearson and Knowles directors would be anxious to put prominently forward; it would be too favour- able to the.._Act and the framers of the Act. Workmen in -good health and kept' in perfect condition by timely aid, will- be much more likely to reduce the cost of production than anything we know. There is nothing so expen- sive as labour performed by men out of con- dition.

div.head: NEWS FROM THE SEAT OF WAR-THAT-IS-
div.p: NEWS FROM THE SEAT OF WAR-THAT-IS-

_ _ TO-BE—PERHAPS. They are getting on in Ulster. They have enrolled their vdlunteers, inspected their nurses and even appointed their general. Sir Edward Carson says they have other' generals on hand, some of the greatest in the British, Army. But the General-in-Command happens to be a gentleman rof whom we never heard at the "Examiner" Office. Perhaps that is accounted for by our ignorance of military matters. But we have heard of Lord Roberts, Lord Kitchener and one or two others, who have survived the dangers of the field' in many parts of the world. They, we think, are among the great- est we have, but they can scarcely be going to serve on the staff of the gentleman of whom we had never heard till Sir Edward Carson mentioned his name. It has been almost forgotten that we *e to have a concentration Camp in Warrington for the women and children of the Orangemen who may—perhaps--elect to take the field against the King's Government. Mr. Harold Smith called for volunteers who would have no fewer than 1,000 Orange women and dhildren dumped into their homes, so that Warrington. might "lead. the way." That is to say, the Warrington Women Tariff Reformers were, by their bad example, to induce the Women Tariff Reformers of ,other towns to go • on lines laid down for themselves by. the Member for Warrington. Weeks have passed and we have !not heard that the thousand homes in War- rington will be forthcoming. We should have been " astounded " livid it been discovered that .there were so many foolish people in the town, the good name of which we all hold in such reverence. And. as to other towns following'

div.head: MR. BEAMONT'S HISTORIC OFFICE.
div.p: MR. BEAMONT'S HISTORIC OFFICE.

It seems to have been overlooked by those gentlemen wh6 combined last week to honour and perpetuate the memory of the late Mr. William' Beamont, who was elected first Mayor of the borough on its incorporation, that the office in which he laboured for fifty eventful years, has other claims to our regard. In 1910,. when the centenary of the Infirmary was being celebrated, the writer having occa- sion to go into the history of the institution, found that the buildings known to have been used as the Dispensary, did not account for the whole hundred years under review. At the Infirmary land the Museum there are docu- ments recording the fact that it was decided in January, 1810, that a dispensary should be established, arid ,that a building should be pro- cured and converted into a dispensary; and such a dispensary was undoubtedly opened on April 12, 1810, but none of the documents say where this temporary resting-place was. The dispensary seems to have become such an im- portant place all at once that all its letters and notices, printed and written, were dated. from "The Dispensary "—this, and nothing. more. Even a bill, a .copy of which is still preserved, announcing that ,a certain learned gentleman intended to give an exhibition of solar micro- scope, as a tribute,of respect from the lecturer to Warrington and the institution; set' forth that the treat would take place in "a room at the Dispensary "—and so the tantalising records go on. All the records conspire to remain silent on the question of the locality of the Dispensary. It occurred to the writer, in the course of his investigations, that the century-old balance- sheet might reveal the interesting secret of the first hone of the Infirmary, and a careful search showed that the rent was paid to 'Mrs. Beamont—though that fact is mentioned on only one occasion. The name suggested a visit to the office of Messrs. Robert Davies end Co., in the Market-place, and here he found that not only was the location of the Dispensary known, but that that well-known solicitor's office Was itself .the original Dispensary. He was most courteously shown over the place, and saw the old-fashioned cupboards, which the imagina- tion could easily stock with medicine bottles and the like.

The tablet to Mr., Beamont is on one side of the entrapre to Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.'s office. May we suggest that a record of the fact that the Infirmary was born on these same premises might with mucli fitness Ze placed between this tablet and the door?

div.head: MONEY-LENDER VICTIMS.
div.p: MONEY-LENDER VICTIMS.

In a special article oil "Money-lending Vam- pires," which appears in "The Examiner" to- day, we have drawn attention to .a practice that is eating like a canker into the lives and homes of many of our working men. The victims of the pernicious system are drawn so completely into the net of the money-lender, that they are reduced' to 'a chronic state of poverty and brought permanently into the clutches of the men who haunt the gates of the works with their tempting money bags. We have heard of cases in which men, working at the same job, earning the Same pay, are in vastly different circumstances. ' One will have saved enough to be practically independ- ent; he has abstained from lierrowing. -His neighbour has pot a. shirt to his _back ; he has parted with his • sithstance at the expense of the comfort of his whole household. The money is borrowed/for drink or betting, but the result is the same—that in many cases a man's whole week's wages are mortgaged before he draws them, and every 'succeeding week his home expenses have to be run upon borrowings, which can only be made at an unconscion- able rate 'of -interest. We publish our article in the hope that the foolishness of the bor- Fowers may be made apparent to them, and that they may see the wisdom of shaking them- selves free from a custom that has found them poor, and will undoubtedly keep thdm poor.

div.head: LOST CHAMPIONSHIP.
div.p: A LOST CHAMPIONSHIP.

The team of anglers who represented the Northern Anglers' Association, and included several members of the Warrington Working Men's Association', will claim the sympathy of all sportsmen. Competing, for the English championship last Monday in the _Dee above Chester., they had the laurels well within their grasp, Via had to release their hold in conse- quence of a breath of rules. Most competi- tions allow the use of two hooks, but in this cOmpetition Only one hook is permitted. One of the Northern team thoughtlessly overlooked this difference, and paid dearly for his negli- gence. Fish were " off " last Monday, but luck came the way of the angler in question, and early on he caught a bream weighing over 21b., 'which .would not only have placed him iniTi- vidually at the head of affairs, but was suffi- cient to carry his team to victory. But dis- qualification followed upon the use of two hooks, and although our men totalled 31b. 50z. Idr. on the day, they had the mortification- of seeing Nottingham carry off the championship and the substantial trophies that .go with it, with the smaller total of 21b. 150 z. lldr.

div.head: OLD WELL.
div.p: THE OLD WELL.

_ Voe are informed by an old inhabitant that the oldikwell discovered in the rear of the Fox Inn, Buttermarket-street, and described, in last week's "Examiner," Was' the source from which the water was obtained for the use of the brew- :louse attached to the Old Crow of former days. ke adjacent cellars also belonged to that once famous inn. Several shops—about three—situ- ate near Market-gate had the right to use this well, which supplied water of such quality that no better could be ,found. The Old Crow was nicely retired up- a pas- sage. "In the 'early days of my father," said our info/ilia/tit, "this was one of the houses where the better class of tradesmen met every morning at noon. They started at the George at eleven with a glass of beer, and then went on to the Old Crow."

, "Sympathetic." . "Only a month !" called a Warrington pris- oner over the dock rail, as he "went down" for drunkenness. A woman, who, it was stated, was the prisoner's mother, called back, "It will do ~y9u .good. If you let me try you, I would give/you two."
Pair of Twins.

A correspondent brings up the question of twins -again by asking how many children a pair of twins represent—Answer : Four. Twins mean two of a kind, and a pair of twos make foui. Two children of the same age are twirls, but not a pair of twins.

Getting in Trouble. "The little son of the hostess is mighty ugly, Isn't he?" "Do you think so?" "He certainly doesn't take after his mother. Must look like his father." "His mother says he does. I'm his father."
Funny "Fun."

We never saw the beauty in discoloured optics, yet a witness at the Police Court on Tuesday said that a, woman had a pair of " bonny " black eyes. He added: "She is ashamed to come down. It was only drunken fun." This sort of " fun " does not appeal to us. Back to the Road.

"People have actually been held up in Liver- pool-road, and money has been demanded from them," Said the Chief Constable at Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, in regard; to two beggars. -He added, "The town is infeSted with these cadgers."
We shall be having the mail held up at San- lie-) some night, perhaps.

The Spider in the Newspaper. When Mark Twain in his early days was editor of a Missouri paper a superstitious sub- scriber wrote to him saying that he had found a spider in his paper and asking him whether that was a sign of good luck or bad. The humorist wrote him this answer and printed it: "Old Subscriber: Finding a spider in your paper was neither good luck nor bad luck for you. The spider was merely looking over our papet to see which merchant is not advertising, so that he can go to that store, spin his web across the door, and lead a life of undisturbed peace ever afterwards."
Why Fish !lave Scales. "The late Prof. Corson, of Cornell," said a. Cornell instructor, "had little sympathy with the freakish philologists of the modern school.

"1 once quoted to Prof. Corson an extremely interesting and old analogy that had just been suggested for a Celtic word. He smiled, and said tha the analogy was about as probable as that which linked fish scales to shingles. "A little girl, he explained, once asked ,her mother
"'Are scales fastened on fish like shingles on a roof?' "'Yes, dear,' the mother answered.
"They're put on that way, of course.' said the little girl, to keep the fish from leaking.'"
in His Own Hands.

"Look here, young fellow," said a father to a young man whose chief occupation was writ- ing verse. "I think it's about time that the date of your marriage with my daughter was fixed." "Yes, perhaps," the young man agreed, "but I am leaving that entirely to Ermyn- trude." "Ah ! Is it to be a quiet or a stylish wedding?" "I think, sir, answered the young man, "I can leave that safely in the hands of Mrs. Bell." "Yes. Quite so 1" Mr. Bell agreed. "But a young fellow generally has some idea with regard to expense—bridesmaids' gifts, you know. And, by the way, what is your income?" "Well, that, Sir," said the young man, modestly, "I am leaving entirely to you I"

The Servant Problem. "Why are yoit wandering about the country instead of looking after you wife and children at home?" inquired the lady of the tattered tramp. "Well, ma'am, its like this," explained the tramp. "My wife has a very fine servant. A perfect treasure." "I don't believe there ever was/ such a girl." "There's only one, ma'am, and my wife's got her." ' "Good, gracious,! She's a very lucky woman." "She is, ma'am. But the trouble is that girl don't like mc" "Well?" "She didn't like me and she told my wife she must either discharge me or her, so my wife discharged me, ma'am." "Poor fellow! Here's something for you."
Weavers' Talk.

Weavers are given the reputation of being very noisy in conversation, but I did not find them so the other morning (writes a correspon- dent in the "Manchester Guardian ") when I watched a weaver's wedding. Half the congre- gation were women weavers, who kept up a constant comment without a word being uttered. They moved their lips, they worked their features, they talked with their eyes, and made signs with their Sands and fingers. The bride's dress was discussed, the behaviour of the bridegroom remarked upon, but there was no audible speech. The fact is that weavers are wonderfully skilful in the art of lip reading, which is taught to them by the mother of in- -vention. Working in a clatter of machinery, where it is imilossible to "hear my own ears," they are driv6n to the practice of speech which, although dumb, is perfectly intelligible. "Weavers' talk" is a well-understood term in the loom districts of Lancashire. To the non- weaver it is as mysterious as Freemasonry, but to the weavers it is part Of their craft.

div.head: Harvest Festival at Latchford.
div.p: Harvest Festival at Latchford.

The Harvest Festival was celebrated at Christ 'Church, Latchford, on Sunday. The Rev. G. C. Briggs, the vicar, preached in the morning, and the Rev. F. A. Screeton, Seacombe, occupied the pulpit in the evening. The choir tastefully :rendered appropriate music.

div.head: Burned in the Face.
div.p: Burned in the Face.

While employed at the Firth Iron Company's Works on Thursday, Annie Green, 5, Gilbert- street, was injured by burning, and sustained severe injuries to the face, head and neck. She was reported last evening at the Infirmary to be Out of. immediate danger.

div.p: Serious Accident at Daliam' Forge.

Yesterday afternoon another bad accident ,occurred at Dallam Forge. George Mannion, 49, Folly-lane, had his left arm badly mutilated -and sustained a severe injury. He was con- veyed to the Infirmary, where. it was found necessary to amputate the arm. His condition last night was described As very serious.

CJive and Co. wilt offer for sale, in the Blue Bell Inn, 10 houses and one shop in Winwick-road, with a rental of £ll9 125.; six dwelling-houses in Marsh House-lane and Godfrey-street, rental ,tB5 10s., and a dwelling-house at 240, Manches- ter-road.

div.head: Struck AVith An Iron Bar.
div.p: Struck AVith An Iron Bar.

A serious aCcident pecurred at the Dallam Forge, Warrington, on Wednesday. George Miller, 8: Charles-street, while engaged at his Work, was accidentally struck on the body with heated bar of iron and received such injuries that he had to be detained in the Infirmary. It Was reported that last night his condition was extremely serious.

div.head: Car Drh ers Protected.
div.p: Car Drh ers Protected.

Passengers on the Latchford route of thelVar- rington tram service on Tuesday night com- mented upon the protection afforded the driver on the special car which ran for the first time that wet and muddy night. A glass screen is Practically all round the front of the car, and the rain, instead of pouring mercilessly on the exposed driver, strikes on the glass and streams down, the driver being kept dry. This is an idea which is giving great satisfaction to the drivers, and the car will now run regularly. It an for two hours on Tuesday evening.

div.head: Liberal Women at Belle Vue.
div.p: Liberal Women at Belle Vue.

There will be a most interesting gathering at Belle Vue, Manchester, on Monday, when the Warrington Women's Liberal Association, as already announced in these columns, are to hold a demonstration. Two special trains leave the Central Station, Warrington, at -1 o'clock and 1.10 in the afternoon, and tlise will go direct to the station near Belle Vue. There will be many attractions provided for the Warrington com- pany. Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield and Miss Truda Crosfield are to be present, and will speak.

div.head: David Livingstone.
div.p: David Livingstone.

An interesting lecture on David Livingstone was delivered to the members of the Sunday School Union in Gelborne-street Baptist Sunday Schools on Monday evening by the ,Rev. H. Ogden. The lecturer described the early strug- gles of this great missionary pioneer and explorer, and told how, by self-eOucation, he rose to be such a great man. Livingstone's love of learning was illustrated by the fact that ,his first savings were spent, not, in tickets for theatres and picture palaces, as so many boys' and girls' savings were spent to-day, but on a book containing the rudiments of Latin •gram- Mar. • "Livingstone, by his attempt to suppress the slave traffic in Africa, had performed a !great bit of Christian work.

div.head: Tribute to a Railwayman.
div.p: Tribute to a Railwayman.

Amidst many manifestations of sorrow and 'regret the funeral of the late \ Mr. Henry Savage, who' was killed at Frog,hall Siding last Satu'rday. -took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday. The Rev. W. Bracectp conducted a short service in the house, an the Rev. J. Davies, vicar of St. Ann's, officiated at the grave- side. About 50 railwaymen, representing all departments of the London and North-Western Railway, attended, and the coffin was borne by railway workers with whom deceased had worked. The chief mourners were Mrs. Savage (widow), Mr. G. Savage, sen., Mr. Henry Savage, Mr, John Savage (son), Mr. and Mrs. Norbury (son-in-law and daughter), Mr. John Savage (brother) and Mrs. Savage, Mrs. Hazlehurst (aunt), Mr. and Mrs. John Savage, Mr. George 'Savage (cousin). Mr. and Mrs. G. Ormerod, (Rat- cliffe), Miss Wright, Miss Johnson. and Mr. john Stokes. Wreaths Were sent by the raournerq. "Neighbours and friends," Ancient Order of Foresters, Traffic Department. London and North-Western Railway, and the National tnion of Railway Workers, Mr. and 11irs. Dum- bell. Yesterday was the anniversary of the maarriage of Mr. and Mrs, Savage.

div.head: 1,000 Scholars at a Service.
div.p: 1,000 Scholars at a Service.

About 1,000 deeply-interested Sunday gthol ars attended the united service of the local branch! of the National Sunday School Union held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday afternoon. All the local Nonconformist Sunday Schools were represented and the service was of It most inspiring description. The chairman Was the Rev. W. Reid, minister of St. John's Presbyterian Church, and he - expressed his delight that they had secured such a great gathering. It did &Ali scholars and teachers good to attend such a gathering, and it was now More necessary than ever that a close union Should exist between the teacher and the pupils. The training of the teachers was receiving more ftttention, and he outlined the course which was :to be pursued tit the local training centre. . Mr. -tkrthur Mounfield had arranged a series of lec- tures, which would prove of great service to the teachers.—The Rev. J. S. Chedburn gave an in- eresting discourse specially to the children, and Pointed out that every cause had a standard, but 11_O standard was so glorious ai that of Christ, round which all should rally. The prayer was led hY the Rev. E. Morgan, Padgate, and the was read by the Rev. T. T. James.—Miss ' Carton delivered an appropriate recitation.
KITCHEN RANGES, FIRE GRATES, TlLES.—Large !_toek, reasonable prices.—J. S. GARLAND. Iron- ulonger, 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.

div.head: Death-rate of Warrington.
div.p: Death-rate of Warrington.
The deaths in Warrington last week num- bered 28 (13 males, 15 females). The death- rate was 19.6, compared with 9.2 in the same week last year.

div.head: Still More Prizes.
div.p: Still More Prizes.
The horses owned by Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Warrington, are still out for prizes at the closing agricultural shows of the season. At Altrincham on Wednesday several other prizes were annexed.

div.head: Scarlet Fever Outbreak.
div.p: Scarlet Fever Outbreak.

Like most towns, Warrington is now suffering from an outbreak of scarlet fever, but the num- ber of cases reported last week—ten—were not sufficient to cause any alarm of an epidemic. Three cases of diphtheria also occurred.

div.head: Accident at Crosfield's.
div.p: Accident at Crosfield's.

Last evening two men were admitted to 'the Infirmary suffering from injuries received in an accident at Crosfield's Works. One, named Lowe, had a leg badly broken, and the -other, named Blease, was bruised on the back.

div.head: Mites of Humanity.
div.p: Mites of Humanity.
Some 38 mites of humanity arrived in War- rington during last week. The number of births was 38 (17 males, 21 females), as aim- pared with 37 in the same week in 1912. The birth-rate was 27.4. -

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Open Meeting.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Open Meeting.

Those who wish to gain inside knowledge of the splendid work accomplished by the Wycliffe P.S.A. can do so to-morrow. by attending the onen meeting. The speaker will be Councillor Miller, of Widnes, and the Rev. T. T. James will preside.

div.head: Whence Came the sswans?
div.p: Whence Came the sswans?

A_ pair of fine swans have this week been keeping the seagulls .company on the old 'por- tion of the Mersey behind Wilderspool Cause- way. No person seems to know where they came from, but their presence attracted much attention from observers.

Crosfield's Band and the Great Trophy. At the great band contest, to be held at the Crystal Palace, London, to-day, erosfield's Band are making a special effort to again • secure the I,QOO guinea trophy. The band left Warring- tAn yesterday for •London, And were reported in. first-class playing, form.

Liberal Association s Conference. There will be a special conferenhe of delegates from the various Liberal Associations to be held on the 27th of - November at Leeds. On the 28th (Friday evening) 'a mass meeting is to be addressed by Mr. Asquith, the Prime Minister. The Warrington representatives will shortly be selected.

• Workmen Scalded With Steam. • Two employes were injured through an acci- dent at the St. Helens Cable Works on Tues- day afternoon. The lid of a steam pan, used for " curing " rubber, blew off, and a quantity of steam escaped, with the isult that Jack klcock, of Lord Nelson-street, and William Bradbury, of Orford-lane, were scalded. Alcoek was taken to the Infirmary. where be was de- tained, where it , was found his injuries were not serious.

div.head: AVArliers' Education Association.
div.p: AVArliers' Education Association.

Those interested in the Workers' Education Movement will be pleased to know that so much progress has been made locally that a meeting is to be held next. Friday for the purpose of forming a University Tutorial Class for War- rington. , This meeting, to which intending gtudents are • invited, will take place- in the Museum Lecture Room at Vight o'clock. Mr. E. J. Hookway, the organising secretary of the district, will be present.

div.head: Two Shop Fires.
div.p: Two Shop Fires.

Two small fires have occurred during the week. The first took place on Saturday evening, when a fire broke out in one of the storerooms at the shop of Mr. C. Mounfield, hatter, a.. Horsemarket-street. It was at once discovered and attempts made to extinguish it.; However, the Fire Brigade were summoned, and in a few minutes the flames were entirely subdued. The other fire was on Tuesday night in a smallware store off Queen-street. The brigade were sum- moned, and the fire was put out in a short time.

div.head: P.S.A. Social.
div.p: P.S.A. Social.

Under the auspices of the Warrington P.S.A. an enjoyable social was held in the Cairo-street School on Thursday :evening. Mr. R. 'Nelson presided over a large attendance, .and the vari- ous items were thoroughly enjoyed. Mr. Sefton sang a solo and took part in a couple of duets given by his wife and himself. Mrs. Seftqn also delighted with her song . "Within yotir heart." Mr. Trow's musical selections were greatly appreciated, and Mr. G. B. Starkey was a popular humorist. A vote of thanks was heartily accorded at the close-

div.head: "Miss Hook of Holland."
div.p: "Miss Hook of Holland."

This dainty lady will be ready to. welcome thousands of visitors at the Royal Court Theatre. Warrington, from 13th to 18th Octo- ber. "Miss Hook of Holland" is the popular musical comedy, and for six 'nights it will be Presented by the members of the Warrington Musical Society. Rehearsals are going on apace, and this comedy promises to prove one of the greatest successes achieved by this talented society. Those who would like to see what will be a splendid production should book seats early. The plan will be open at the theatre on Wednesday.

div.head: Territorial Band in the Park.
div.p: Territorial Band in the Park.

By the kind permission of Lieut.-Colonel B. Fairclough and the officers of the 4th Battalion (South Lancashire Regiment), the band will play in tbe Bank Park on Sunday, under the-conductorship of Mr. C. ,Wainwright. The concert, commences at 3.15, and the programme will be: Sacred -march, "Onward. Christian soldiers," 'Hartmann: selection, "Gems of ," Ord Hume; Neapolitan seren- .rdeel,Bl`lolllPlSllY-Atio." Canna; sacred song. "Ora Two nobis." Piccolomini : selection "Sonnam- bula." Bellini; gout,. "The .rosary," Nevin; grand march. enilnli.rnllt." Ord Hume: regimental march, and "God Save the Kink."

The Warrington Leather Trade. Trade this week in leather was, according to "The Leather World," more animated. A steady succession of buyers and would-be buyers gave a much livelier tone to matters, and if the figures did not come out at an unusually large total, it was due to the fact that the leather was not there; anything in sight found buyers sooner or later, the only trouble being there was noth- ing like enough to go round. A fair amount of both prompt and forward short date buying was done during the week at prices which are for the moment satisfactory; it was fairly easy to make small advances, and in several cases buy- ers taking up parcels did not hesitate at pay- ing d. more for a further lot to come along. This is only indicative of the feeling all round that prices will gradually go harder until the .middle of Pecember.

div.head: Preachers for To-morrow.
div.p: Preachers for To-morrow.
The following' are the church and chapel ser vices for to-morrow : Bewsey-road „Wesleyan—Morning, Rev. E. Morgan; evening, Bev. W. A. Beckett. Harvest festival services. . _ _ _
Bold-street Wesleyan—Morning, Mr. R. H. Sutton; evening, Rev. H. Williamson.. Cairo-street Chapel—Morning and 'evening, Rev. Dr. Mellor.
Padgate Wesleyan—Morning, Rev. W. A. Beckett; evening, Mr. F. Wright. Afternoon young people's service, Mr. A. Luinb. Harvest festival.

Wycliffe Congregational—Morning and even- ing, Rev. T. T. James. St. John's Presbyterian—Morning and even- ing Rev. W. Reid. even- ing, Baptist—Morning and evening, Rev: H. Ogden. Latchford Baptist—Morning and evening, Rev. J. S. Chedburn. Christadelphians, Assembly Rooms, Bridge- street—Evening, Mr. G. Wilde, Huddersfield. Thursday—St. Ann's Parish Church, harvest thanksgiving, 7.30 p.m., Rev. J. R. Jones, Sankey. Sunday, sth October—Morning, the Vicar; after- noon; Rev. 'J. H. Garnett; evening, Rev. G. C. Briggs.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27,1913. WASTED Bt•AINS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27,1913. WASTED Bt•AINS.
St. John Ambulance Brigade.

As will be seen fromittn advertisement in an- other column, the new season of the Headquar- ters Division of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade begins next Wednes- day. Members are requested to, parade at the Police Station at eight o'clock, in uniform. All the old offieers are available, including Chief Superintendent Waring, Superintendent Baldry and Mr. A. E. Spann, the secutary.

div.head: "Education and Progress."
div.p: "Education and Progress."

Professor Benjamin • Moore, M.A.D.Sc., F.R.S., of Liverpool University, will deliver a lecture this evening at the Adult School, Academy-street, on "Education and Progress." Professor Moore took a great interest in the recent meetings of the British Association, and what he has to say 'on the subject upon which he will speak will be well worth hearing. A special invitation is extended to those who are interested in- the Workers' Educational Asso. ciation.

div.head: Junior Cricket League Concert.
div.p: Junior Cricket League Concert.

The annual concert in connection with the Warrington and District Junior Cricket League took place at the Working Men's Mission. Councillor Henshall, one of the vice-presidents, occupied the chair, and was supported by Mrs. Henshall and the Rev. J. S. Chedburn, chair- man .of the League Committee. After tea an attractive programme of vocal and instru- mental music was rendered by the players and a number of their friends, and at the close Mrs. Henshall presented the medals, which had been awarded to the members of the Working Men's Mission team, who were successful in winning-- the League Championship for the season.

div.head: "The Lapse of a People."
div.p: "The Lapse of a People."

The lapse of a people from attained standards of truth. to depths of decadence formed the sub- ject of the Rev. W. Reid's discourse on Sunday evening at St. John's Church, Wilderspool. This he described as aggravated by the fact of the righteous preceist and example of their fathers and their consequent sin against light and knowledge. He urged the young people present in the pursuit of their literature and recrea- tions to avoid the many altars raised through- out the land, bearing the Image of the beast, upon which they were being continually in- vited to surrender their best, and acknowledge only the one altar of the one God.

div.head: KILLED BY MOTOR 'BUS.
div.p: KILLED BY MOTOR 'BUS.
A Little Girl's Terrible Death in a
Warrington Street.
LAST NIGHT'S FATALITY.

Last evening a terrible motor 'bus fatality occurred in Bewsey-street.. The victim was a little school 'girl, Mabel -Hall, seven years of age, who resided with her grandmother! Mrs. \Wight, at 43, Bewsey-street. This is, the first fatality which has occurred in Warrington since the motor 'buses were introduced by the

Corporation. The motor 'bus was coming on a return journey from Bewsey to town apd was• driven by Harry Mason, of 8, Parr-Street., Warrington. .As the vehicle was approaching the " Examiner ". Office, the girl suddenly stepped off the .footpath and went straight in. front of the 'bus. The left mudguard caught her, and at that moment Driver Mason swerved the vehicle to the right, in an endeavour to miss the child.
Unfortunately he' was not siccessful, as the girl seemed to roll right into the vehicle, and the front wheel passed over her body, inflicting terrible Injuries.

The street was well filled with pedestrians at the time, and the accident occasioned a -sensa- tion. The child was picked up ,and hurriedly conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary. Dr. Charles -Law made. a hasty examinatidn, but could only pronounce life extinct, death having.tal:en 'place en route to the Inflxmary.

div.head: PEARSON AND KNOWLES.
div.p: PEARSON AND KNOWLES.
Annual Report Says Satisfactory Results in all Departments. BUSINESS AND POLITICS.

The annual report, which will be presented next week, at the annual meeting of the share- holders of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and fren Co., Ltd., has some strange and striking passage, the record of a bountiful year being mixed up with opinions on the Insurance Act and " many other serious burdens," which have a distinctly political flavour.

div.head: EIGHT PER CENT.
div.p: EIGHT PER CENT.

The profits for the year ending June 30th, 1913, amount to £118,870 3s. 9d., and the balance brought forward from last year is £13,822 16s. 6d., together £132,693 Os. 3d. An interim dividend at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the first and second preference shares and 6 per cent. per annum \on the ordinary shares was paid in March last' for the half-year ending December 31st, 1912, amounting to £28,250. The directors now recommend that a 'dividend be paid for the past half-year at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the first and second prefer- ence shares, and 10 perU cent, per annum on the ordinary shares, making with the interim divi- dend 8 per cent. for the year, and a total dis- tribution of £67,988 6s. Bd. The directors further recommend that £30,000 be added to the reserve fund, raising it to £82,500; that the sum of £15,156 is. 5d., which represents the expenditure on capital account for the year, be written off, leaving a balance of £19,548 6s. 2d. to be carried forward.

div.head: PA RTINGTON WORKS.
div.p: PA RTINGTON WORKS.

The directors consider it prudent to recom- mend substantial allocations to reserve, in view of the company's investment in the shares of Partington Steel and Iron Company, Ltd., and to the guarantees undertaken on its behalf.

The company holds all the ordinary shares in the Partington Steel and Iron Company, Ltd., amounting to £250,000, which are fully paid up. The works are now rapidly approaching comple- tion, the colie ovens and two blast furnacts are already working satisfactorily, and it is anti- cipated that the remainder of the plant will be In full operation before the end or the year.

div.head: IN NORMAL TIMES.
div.p: IN NORMAL TIMES.

All departments of the company's business' show satisfactory results for the year, although a serious check in demand and a fall in prices occurred in the June quarter mainly due to the effects of the Balkan war, which adversely affected the steel and iron trades. These un- favourable conditions still continue—the coal trade, however, maintains its position. Attention has been directed in previous re- ports to the many serious burdens imposed by recent legislation upon the iron and coal trades, As was anticipated, the National Insurance Act has added largely to the cost of /production without, in the experience of the Board, result- ing in benefit to the company's workmen pro- portionate to the expense. In normal times the contributions will be a serious tax upon wages as well as upon profits. Thl Board are of opinion that a scheme administered in conjunc- tion with • old-age pensions, and deriving its revenue from the same source, would be worked with greater efficiency and economy, would dis- tribute the burden more equitably among the various classes of the community, and do much to remove the present admitted' hardships 'kind discontent.

Mr. R. Brancker has retired from the posi- tion of managing director of the colliery de- partment, which he has held since the year 1893. In compliance with the Articles of Associa- tion, Sir Harmood Banner retires from the Board, and is eligible for re-election.

div.head: Our Plea for University Scholarships Arouses
div.p: Our Plea for University Scholarships Arouses
Great Interest.

div.head: JUSTICE CM! BE DONE AT SMALL COST.
div.p: JUSTICE CM! BE DONE AT SMALL COST.

The letter of a correspondent, " Arduus ad Solem," in "The Examiner," and our article drawing attention to the fact that the Educa- tion Committee do not give a single scholar- ship to the Universities, has interested the town, and particularly the scholastic portion of it, profoundly.

It is recognised on all hands that the Educa- tion Committee, having conducted aspirants to fame as far as the end of the Secondary School ladder, should go one step further and provide facilities for proceeding to the Univer- sity.
1; value £5O. "Platt" scholarship, 1; value, '£so.

Lancashire County Council scholar\ships (very variable), about 15; value, £6O each; donor, Lancashire County Council; persons eligible. residents in county. Cheshire County Council (variable), about 3; value, £5O each; donor, Cheghire County Coun- cil; persons eligible, residents in county.
AIIDUUS AD SOLEM.

div.head: REAL STATE OF AFFAIRS.
div.p: THE REAL STATE OF AFFAIRS.

It is stated that the Education Committee have, in th 6 matter of Univer§ity scholarships, adopted this attitude: 'We 'will take individual cases upon their merits, as they arise, and if a deserving case comes before us, we will con- Sider the advisability of granting a scholarship in that particular case.
This surely is the wrong, principle to work upon. A boy. or girl would have to study for years on the off chance of finding a sympathe- Un-
tic‘ coinmittee in power at a given time . . _ _

certainty of this kind would be worse than The certainty of a dead-stop under present condi- tions. What is needed is a system of Univer- sity scholarships that can be *worked up to, year after year, with the knowledge that ability and perseverance will find its due reward.

At the present time there is only one University . scholarship in Warrington, the Beamont scholarship at the Gram- mar School, and this, being tenable .for three years, once won, leaves us without even one for that length of time. Such privately endowed scholarships would be very acceptable, but it is snot for (hose we now ask. We ask for publicly-provided scholarships, which shall give a natural outlet to the genius that is half discovered and ihree-parts devel- oped in our, public schools. If we might suggest, we would say that two scholarships a year for three years, each of the value of £5O, would give us the nucleus upon which we could make a trial in order to see wilat demand there really is for assistance in higher education.

div.head: LOST CHANCES, IS LIFE.
div.p: LOST CHANCES, IS LIFE.

There can, we think, be little doubt on this point, for great strides have ,been made during the last four or five years at the Sdcondary School, which has had ,many scholars who would have been capable of taking scholarships at the Universities.
At present facilities are offered at the Second- ary School and the Grammar School to take children up to a certain standard, and then,

in the absence of financial assistance, many parents are unable to continue their children's education, and the childro, instead of going on to the higher positions of life, have to be content, with the middle walks. Many of our best scholars lave to be content with second- Mass Civil Service clerkships; although they would have been quite competent for first-class clerkships haq the University training. Y had the advantage of a
Moreover, many boys, well up in science, have had to take subordinate posts in our works, when a University training would have enabled them to take positions of greater re- sponsibility. _
We hope to see the Education Committee tackle, beloi-e long, Efi. is most important pro- blem.

div.head: MANY STJFFERERS THROUGH
div.p: MANY STJFFERERS THROUGH
NON-ACTION.
110 W THE TOWN MIGHT BENEFIT BY TRAINING ITS SONS FULLY AND COMPLETELY.
.Sir,—My last letter was only very short, not anticipating your warm and kind reception of my suggestion ; consequently I beg leave to elaborate.

You were correct in your conjecture that I was a student; old student, perhaps, would have been nearer the mark, but an old student who has realised to a large extent the necessity for a scholarship. And lam not alone. I could name at least _a dozen students who would

have welcomed a `scholarship, and goodness knows how many more may have been induced to try for a University education. This shows that it is not a new topic, aikl the wonder is that there has been no Press coMment until now.

I think I know to whom you refer in "Four well-equipped lads," and I can say that I heartily endorse your statements. All of them are taking up Civil Service , rather than the teaching profession, and this shows their atti- tude to this honourable profession. Probably they regard rnatter in a similar light to Mr. Jarman. Even if the lads are going in for Civil Service, a University education is an enormous aid, giving them a training for the higher exams. By this, I do not intend to siiggest scholarship merely for "Service " men; rather make it into a Science Scholarship, since the school is strongest in science subjects, and the
town would benefit more by it. Thus 'the town would benefit itself by training its sons so as to be more efficiently 'equipped to be9ome true citizens.

I have just read of Sir William Lever's recent donation of £lO,OOO a year to Bolton education, and of the late Mr. Thomasson's scheme of University scholarships (1877) at the same town. Cannot Warrington men emulate these inuni- ticent gifts in some way—great or small? The intention of Sir William Lever is to make Bol- ton an educational centre. But Warrington, as we have seen in the past, and as Professor Dixon told us recently, is Admirably situated for forming an educational centre. Also we ought not to forget Professor Campagnac's address at the prize distribution, and Warring- ton's work in the advance of education. Surely Warrington is not going to be backward in this rapidly progressive age! div.head: HANDICAPPED BY GEOGRAPHY.
div.p: HANDICAPPED BY GEOGRAPHY.
IS IT A MISFORTUIV; TO BE pOIIN THIS
SIDE THE BOUNDARY?

Sir,—To be born a Warrington child, with above the normal ,supply of brain and an am- bition to become something other than an ele- mentary school teacher, is, a sad dmisfortune. Geographical luck might have ordered his or her birth to have been beyond the borough boundary, and then all would have been well. Lancashire and Cheshire certainly do as War- rington does, offer sugared bursarships to tehipt youths and maidens into the crowded ranks of the elementary teacheft:, But they do more than Warrington—they endow by scholarships to the Universities the more brilliant of its scholars. Warrington leads them on, encour- ages them by yearly doles of a XlO note, and finally forsakes them just as visions of a Uni-, versity career and an after profession as com- mercial, chemist, engineer, or doctor begins I to reveal itself to them.

The present policy ,of the committee is to await events—to deal with each case at it pre- sent's itself. They do not see that the really promising youngsters irks at the uncertainty, qualifies at an early age, and enters into less useful and less promising pursuits, than if he knew, if worthy, he would be helped and not scrapped at 17 or 18,years of age. A. B.

div.head: SUFFERER.
div.p: A SUFFERER.

OLD STUDENT WHO PLEADS FOR THE STUDENTS TO FOLLOW. •Sir,—Allow me, through the medium of ,your columns, to support the proposition suggested in the letter which appeared in your last issue upon the subject of University scholarships in connection with the borough of Warrington. It is a .disgrace to a town of • Warrington's industrial standing that there .are no better educational facilities than those afforded at present. And Who must be held responsible for this state of affairs? ,Obviously, it 'is the Education Committee. It -does not reflect ..any credit at all& on the Education Committee, when one recollects that the subject has hardly ever been mentioned. I myself was promised by n certain. person prominent in local educational circles that he Would do all he could to in- augurate scholarships in this town. 'Evidently that- promise was sudden inspiration to quieten me, or else the said person .had a bad lapse of memory.

Again, I can mention a case which has come under my notice of a student, who gained a great honour, which gave much credit to the town. Of course, the Education Committee claimed the credit for this, where they were in no way responsible for it. Now we come* the important point. The student applied to the authorities for help to continue his studies, but had a deaf ear turned to him. Here was an instance where the ability was known to be, and yet no attempt was made .to encourage it, and no attempt will be made until the Education Committee ceases to follow the example of most of the governing bodies of Warrington, and abandon talk for action. The Education Committee certainly does want rousing to action upon this subject, and the sooner the better. Either the wrong men are in charge, or else they do not trouble them. selves about the progress and future of the borough, so long as they themselves are all , right, in which case they are unfit for the im- portant position MOCK 'ley hold. Ido not plead for benefit tO myself, for, as far as I myself am concerned, as mentioned in the : letter last week, it is now too late, but it is the future I ern thinking of, and the possibilities which it always holds. •

div.head: ANOTHER PHASE OF BRAIN WASTAGE.
div.p: ANOTHER PHASE OF BRAIN WASTAGE.
WHAT CAN BE DONE. FOR THE POORER WORKING CLASSES?

Sir,—As an "Old Boy" of the Warrington Secondary School, I rejoice to see your appre- ciation of the worli carried om,in that institu- tion. Many of its past students have done well and many could do well, and, -perhaps, even better had they the scholarship to help them to a University.
But the scholarship must only be given, to ;he needy boy.
There is, however, another aspect of brain wastage, to which I wish to call attention.

I refer to the lack of facilities given to the children of our poorer woi:7ing classes. I know from experience that there are dozens of children in our poorer schools who far out- shine, with all their disadvantages in the home life, any of your better-class children.

But, Mr. Editor, at fourteen these poor un- fortunates become a very necessary source of income. Five or even seven shillings a week is what they represent, with no expense as regards good clothing. It is inipossible for their parents to avail themselves of free tuition and £5 per annum, or even £lO per annum, at our Secondary School. The prospects are, moreover, ,none too bright, even if such a course were taken.

Could not some scheme be devised by which a head teacher could call the attention of our sympathetic Director to such cases, and a special private grant be made, equivalent to the wages which a poor boy earns in a works? The cases wbuld not be over numerous, the committee could easily Supervise them, any abuse could immediately be stopped, and brains that are at present wasted will be given a real chance to develop, bring credit to the town, and prove of value to the nation.

div.head: BRITISH BAND FOR AIiCKLAND EXHIBI-
div.p: BRITISH BAND FOR AIiCKLAND EXHIBI-
TION, NEW ZEALAND.
The Royal Artillery Band, of Woolwich, re- puted to be one of the finest military bands in England, has been engaged to go to Auckland to provide the chief music during the exhibi- tion. _

Seal,••• Negotiations for securing this important and famous band have been in progress for many months, and the authorities of the exhibition have at times felt themselves on the verge of serious disappointment. During the earlier negotiations, six months ago, it seemed as if the arrangement would not be made, hut His Excel- lency the Governor was keenly interested in it, and it is in a great measure due to his efforts that success has been achieved. It is a unique event for a British military band to be allowed to go so far from England.
DICKENSON.
His latest photograph in International jersey, cap and badge.
Photograph by Burrell.

div.head: GEORGE DICKENSON
div.p: GEORGE DICKENSON
Popular Warrington Centre who Takes His Benefit Next Week.
MAY IT BE A BUMPER!

The match, Warrington v. St. Helens, which Lakes place at Wilderspool next Saturday, has been set aside by the Warrington Club as a benefit for George Dickenson, an old 'and con- sistently good player, who has been a favourite for the last thirteen seasons.

div.head: BRILLIANT RECORD.
div.p: A BRILLIANT RECORD.

George Dickenson, ,who lives at 101, Winwick- street, with his wife and .two children, was born in 1882, so that he is now 31 years of age. This is a fair age .for a man who still finds himself fit to take part in Northern Union football, and
)t only fit, but worth his place in such a

_ 'rigorous team as Warrington- First. As a natter of fact, Dickenson .holds the record for ong service in the ranks of the Warrington r7.C., for whom he is now playing for the four- eenth consecutive season.
He is the product of the Works Competition, ;0 which the town team owes so much. In 1899 ic was playing for the White Lead Works, and,

his skill beingApticed by that good judge of talent, Mr. Haify Ashton, the next season, 1900, saw him playing centre for the Warrington "A" team. Promotion came rapidly, for, after four matches with the"A" team, Dickenson was drafted into the first team, so that he has, since 1900, been a first team player. Steadiness, and a desire to keep himself in the best of form, have contributed to these somewhat remarkable results.

div.head: CUP. COUNTY AND INTERNATIONAL
div.p: CUP. COUNTY AND INTERNATIONAL
HONOURS.
Dickenson was soon in the thickest of frays. his first season 'Warrington won their way

into the final of the Northern Union Cup Com- petition, and the subject of our sketch, though only eighteen years of age, was in the team that battled against Batley. Unfortunately on that occasion Warrington were not successful, but that was not the fault of Dickenson. In
the next season, before he was nineteen, he pluyed for Lancashire County, and at twenty

he gained International honours. Altogether Dickenson has played in three Northern Union Cup finals—against Batley, Hali- fax and Hitll Kingston Hovers, when the cup first came to Warrington. He would have played last year against Huddersfield in yet another' final, but he had been on the injured list for some time. As it was, he was placed on the reserve He has played five times for Lancashire and International six times—three times against Wales, twice against the 411 Blacks," and once against the "Kangaroos." He is naturally very proud of his Inter- national and county caps, and also of the fact that he captained the team for two seasons dur- ing which they were very successful, and that he was sub-captain to Ji4cli Hallam in the season that Warrington met *id defeated Hull King- ston Hovers for the cup.

Another point that Dickenson likes to, recall, and \Varrington football enthusiasts delight to remember, is that he played centre to the great Fish, who scored many of his brilliant tries from passes made by Dickenson. Indeed, it is held in authoritative quarters, that Fish scored more points in conjuhction with Dickenson than with any other centre who partnered him.

div.head: AN EXPERT OPINION OF DICKENSON.
div.p: AN EXPERT OPINION OF DICKENSON.
MODEST, CLEVER AND POPULAR.
An " Examiner " representative interviewed Councillor Osborne, chairman of the Warring- ton F.C. Committee, with a view to getting an expert opinion of the object of next Saturday's benefit.

"George Dickenson," said Councillor Osborne, "is one of the most modest-looking footballers I have ever seen, and certainly he is one of the most unassuming, Popular players I. have ever net. His reputation for "playing the game" is not confined to Warrington, but is well known in every town where the Northern Union game is played. On his day—and one regrets that years will creep on such an artist—he was one of the best centres in the Union. Without fear, and always scrupulously fair, he has, on very many occasions, 'delighted the ' crowd ' by his lire and dash, and the happy knack of beating a man and sending his wing over with a tiz4 BY his straight and manly ways he has alwa.y.s been a favourite with the members of the club and players alike."

div.head: MUTUAL REGARD.
div.p: MUTUAL REGARD.

The " Examiner " representative recalled the fact that earlier in the day Dickenson had told him to "give the Warrington Committee a good name. They have always treated their players well," he said, "and I have been particularly well treated." " Dickerison," said Councillor Osborne, "has .deserved the best treatment we could give him. He has been no trouble whatever. He has always looked well after himself, kept himself in condition, and has ,always been reliable to the uttermost degree _
So Ilia!, it is a scase of mutual satisfaction and respect:
"Will he play against St. Helens in his own benefit thatch?"
"I hope," replied Councillor Osborne, "that he will be available and that the committee will be .able to see their way to select him to figure in the great event."

div.head: AN ORNAMENT TO THE GAME.
div.p: AN ORNAMENT TO THE GAME.

div.head: WORKHOUSE BREAD.
div.p: WORKHOUSE BREAD.
The Rev. A. M. Mitchell Makes a Complaint.
VACCINATION QUESTION.

Several interesting points were raised- at the meeting of the Warrington Guardians; held on. Wednesday. Mr. E. L. Bent, the chairman, presided. The subject of the bread supplied to the Workhouse was raised, on the minutes of the House Committee being moved for adoption. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL asked whether the committee had received a complaint as to the bread supplied at the Workhouse on the 18th' September. I am told, he added, it was un- eatable. It was so bad that a fresh supply had to be brought in from outside. If this is the case there ought to have been a report in the minutes, as it is a very serious matter. I think it is not due so much to the baking, as to the quality, of the flour, and the matter should be looked into before we fix tenders for flour.

_ The CLERK (Mr. A. Bottoniley): We are not asking now for tenders for flour, because we have a sufficient supply in hand for the half- year. This has been caused through the oven at the Workhouse not being ready, and there- fore we have had no need to get a fresh stock. Mr. MITCHELL: Might not the fact that you have had the stock so long have something to do with it?
The CLERK: I, cannot answer that question. Mr. FURNESS: The longer you have flour in stock the better it becomes.
" Where Did You Get the Complaint?"

The CHAIRMAN: Where did you get this com- plaint from, Mr. Mitchell? Mr. MITCHELL: 1 do not think you should ask such a question. The CHAIRMAN: There is no reference to the matter in the committee's report. Mr. MITCHELL: It came to my knowledge through an authoritativq source. I was sur- prised and very sorry to hear about. it. I hope an inquiry will be held, and perhaps then the matter will prove to be less serious than it appears on the surface. Mrs. SIMPSON : Before anything else is said, It would be wise to have an inquir;y. The CHAIRMAN: There may have \ been an accident.
Mr. MITCHELL: I do not Want anyone to think was due to the fault of the baking.
The matter dropped on the understanding tat the committee would make inquiries.
Medical Officer.

On the motion of Mr. MATHER, the following was adopted unanimously: "That inasmuch as Dr. Richard Sephton has for many yeare past satisfactorily 'tilled the office of medical officer for the No. 3 district of the Union, and

his present residence and surgery, although situated out of the district, is accessible and convenient to the Union patients, and there being no duly oolitic(' man resident within the district, he be reappointed medical officer of that district for a further period of three years, terminating on the 30th September, 1916, at a salary of £3O per annum."
£13,000 For New Buildings. _ The meeting proceeded to consider tenders :or the erection of a bbilding to-accommodate the male and female imbeci:e and epileptic

patients. Six tenders were receit,ed, and fhe amounts asked were £13,875, £14,749, £15,780, £13,454, £13.550, and £13,275. Mr. KNOWLES strongly objected to thp names being disclosed in the .presence of the Press. He moved that the matter be taken in mittee, and this was agreed to. Later, it was announced that the .tender of £13,275, by Mr. Harry Fairclough, had been accepted.
Sympathy With the Blind.

The Ho'beck Guardians, Leeds, sent a reso- lution, which they asked the Warrington Guardians to adopt, urging the necesgity for the Government to afford facilities for the pass- ing of the Blind Aid Bill. , Mr. MATHER : I move that we take the next business.
Mr. MiTcHELL : This is a matter of grave im- portance, and ought to be taken up by the Board.
The CLERK suggested that the matter shotfr— be referred to the Poor Law Association.
Mr. MITCHELL: Wily should we refer it there. or let it lie on the table, when we can give some support to the Bill? We, as a Board of Guardians, ought to be more in sympathy with the blind. •
The C.LErtx : I do not think any Board is more in sympathy with the blind thali this Board.
Mr. MITCHELL': I am glad to hear it.
The matter was allowed to drop.
