div.head: r.E.COP.DS CF GEOLOGY.
div.p: r.E.COP.DS CF GEOLOGY.

Sir,—l. am in complete agreement with "Old Journalist," when he says that geology, as a science, lacks humorous possibilities.. The fact is, that geology like its sister science, astronomy, is far too sutlime a subject to be dealt with jocosely. Great poets have held it in reverence, and have turned to it for inspira: Lion, as witness this of Tennyson: The hills are shadows, and they flow From form to form, and nothing stands; They melt like mist,,the solid lands, , Like clouds they shape themsAves and go. Among writers, Carlyle was proficient in geology, and constantly derived his metaphors from it; while as for Buskin, that author's "Modern Painters" might serve almost as well as a text-book of geology as for a guide to painting. The fact of the matter is that geology makes a special appeal to the expressional giants of history. The .stupendous events—for example, the uprise of the Alps, the storing of the coal measures, and the descent of the ice sheet on Britain—which 'it records retain an abiding interest for the exalted minds of every nation.
EUREX.

div.head: PRESENT IRISH DIFFICULTY AND THE WAY OUT OF IT.
div.p: THE PRESENT IRISH DIFFICULTY AND THE WAY OUT OF IT.
" Phil Squod's"

Sir,—ln your issue of the -2(Ati I see what pur- ports to be replies to mine of the 13th inst. I much regret that the tirst one should contain so much vulgarity. and . mud throwing. If " FAV•ti." expects me to follow hun through his tirade of abuse no is mistaken. I may tell both your correspondents that I have not got lily inspiration from the Duke of Norfolk, or any of the Other Lords they mention, not , even from. Bonar- Law or Carson, nor do I read the "Morn- ing Nst " or "Globe." On the other nand, I do not recognise any of the Irish agitators, or so-called patriots, us having any. bearing On the present phase of the Irish question. I also decline at present to discuss the merits or de- merits of Romanism and Protestantism in 'rela- tion to Home Rule or the governineint of Ireland, but shall be most willing to take' up the sub- ject at sonic future date. I can afford to wait. My first ground of opposition to Home Rule the methods taken to override all opposition to it by the susvension of the Constitution under the Parliament Act—a Government may amend the powers of .either House of the Legislature, but it has .no right to destroy it, or suspend its, . powers. My opposition also applies to all Bills passed under the same regulation. • Reform the Constitution as much as you like, but you have no right to suspend or destroy it. My second argument is the Unsuitable ele- ments at present existing in Ireland for forming a homogeneous government to ftflfil all require- ments. I appeal for my evidence on this point, on the one hand, to the articles now appearing in your columns from the pen of " F.W.8.," who is unearthing 'all' the .slander he can find against Orangeism, and,-perhaps, on the other hand, you might find a member Of that organ- isation, who would tell you all about the Fenianism of the 'sixties, the Land League of ,the 'eighties, and the Hibernianism of thei pre- sent day. The calm that has reigned over. Ire- land in recent years has been the result of the beneficent efforts to improve the condition of Ireland, and has redounded greatly to her pros- Pority, until the present Government rejuven- ated the Home Rule bogey. My third. argument is, perhaps, one with which Mr'. O'Brien may agree, and is as fol- lows : That it is inimical to the best interests, politically and economically, of the Empire, to want Home Rule to Ireland. I think that Home Rule should be decently interred once for all, and I care not whether they plant shamrocks, primroses, or orange blossoms on its grave, so that it is out of the 'way. The heart of the Empire should not be divided, but should form .one homogeneons whole. Our aim and aspira- tion ought to be .to form a homogeneous nation- ality, and as a first move in that direction I would abolish the Irish Viceroyalty and Chief secretaryship, bringing the whole of the United Kingdom and Ireland under one central. Gov- ., eminent. This would Oahe the British Isles ' one unit in the scheme of. Empire, though, of course, it would be the prir*.dpal unit. Within the British Isles, for the purposes of devolution anti tol relieve the strain on the central Govern- ment, a scheme of provincial assemblies for local affairs might be created. Being an assem- bly for each of the four provinces in Ireland, and in Great Britain, Wales, with Monmouth, might form a province, Scotland another, while the rest of England miglit be divided to corre- spond with the .ecclesiastical provinces of York and Canterbury. These provincial aSsemblies might deal with the local matters of,each, leav- ing the supreme Government free to deal with national 'affairs.'
I see no ground for preferential treatntmt of any section of the British Isles, for no section

is entirely of one race, even our Iloyal House being of mixed blood. . The sooner we abandon the idea of purity of race the better. Ireland has never been inhabited t_iy a single ,race, the North being more or-less of Scotch blood, while the South is largely Hibernian. All over the Brit- Al the various. -races' are 4inextricably mixed up, and while. We may be. proud of the race- to which we may think we belong, we ought all to coalesce for the good of the country and for its honour and glory. Proud of our dear homeland, the land of the brave and the free; what glories we have won in the past! What honours may we gain in the future? Let me, in concluding, remind my critics that in my previous letter no reference was made to Itomanism, but an endeavour was made to show the benefit accruing • to Ireland by its associa- tion with England, and an appeal was made to associate the interests of all in forming a corn- piete homogeneous nationality, in which, while each section prided itself of its individual race, formed one solid heart to the Empire before the world.
PIIIL SQUOD.
Queer Vianias.
Among strange manias, that of the well-to-do
Frenchman, with an "irresistible temptation "
to make off with other people's articles of cloth- ing, which he promptly burns, seems one of the strangest. There are many other peculiar manias, sucli as cutting off locks of hair from
women's heads and stealing their shoes, whose causes are well known .to medical men, but the psychology of the trouser stealer seems hard to understand.

div.head: : . . "i / T .„ Ifr , " t• , ....fit – –
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

" Mum " is the word this week.. Chrysanthemum growers are responsible. Tales of wonderful flowers have been told. Two dead hares were seen in the canal. An inquest has not been held on them. It seemed a palpable ease of double suicide. The dock strike has vexed a Stockton Heath man. - He lives by the side of the Ship Canal. This " Heathen " sags he has not been able to sleep.
The cause is the absence of the 'music of the ships' sirens.
These noisy things act upon him like sleeping araugnts. _ ; _

Of --course, it is very difficult to please every- body. Two swans appeared on the canal this week. The passin'g barges ,annoyed them, however. So they have shifted to the old Mersey, near the Causeway.

Courting couples have a walk which is very popular. It runs from London-road to Hill Cliffe. There are several secluded, nooks en rout,.. At one a notice board used to stand. It was a ,warning against the act of trespass. A wag with a tar brush, however, came along. He tarred out the official notice effectively. Another wag hove upon the scene later. , With chalk he wrote upon the notice board. The cryptic but expressive words, "Kissing allowed." Gourtiers _ are reported now to be availing themselves of the privilege. There •is now a "Kissing Spot" in this "Lovers' Lane."
Bugle and drum now disturb the silence of the More particulorly so in tho vi(•inity of Hill Chile. •
The members of ,the Boys' Brigade have got new instruments.
And ,we good people enjoy the nightly serenades. Harvest festivals have now become the rage. In fact, "everybody's doing it ". just now. The 'largest vegetable marrow will probably now appear.

Quiet on the Canal.—lt is a long time since the Ship Canal has been so slack as it has been this week, owing to the dockers' strike at Manches- ter. The traffic was practically nil. Stockton Heath folk, however,, know what will happen after work is resumed. They will be held up at the Swing Bridge almost continuously.

Wesleyan Growth.—The Wesleyan cause in Stockton Heath is progressing rapidly and a satisfactory state of things exists. The Wes- leyan Church at the corner of Walton-road and Heath-street every Sunday cOntains large con- gregations, and the demand for seating accom- modation is reported to have reached a record. Generally the Wesleyan cause seems to be thriv- ing in the township.

Boys' Brigade.—There was an interesting little gathering at the school of the Hill Cliff° Baptist Church on Wednesday evening, when the mem- bers of the local detachment of the Boys' Bri- gade were presented with a new set of pretty instruments. Members of other corps\were also in attendance and the function proved of an attractive character. The new instruments were presented by Mrs. T. Williams, and several tributes were paid to the useful work the Boys' Brigade were performing in connection with the youth of the district. The proceedings were enlivened with songs and duets.

Burmah.—A lantern lecture on "Burmah" was given in St. Thomas! Church Room on Monday evening by the Rev. E. H. Day, the organising secretary of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, in the Dioceses of Liverpool, Chester and St. ASaph, Wales. The Rev. J. Collins, the vicar, presided. The Rev. E. H. Day furnished some interesting information about the habits and customs of the Burmese and smile hopefully of them all becoming Christians in the future. They were an enlightened Oriental race and were ready to grasp the truths of Christianity. The number embracing the faith was steadily grow- ing, and at one place the native converts were sufficiently numerous as to enable them to erect a church without outside aid. Some excellent views of Burmese life and scenery were shown.

Class Service in a Garden.—On Sunday after- noon, thanks to the kindness of Mr: and Mrs. Lyon, the members of St. Thomas' Men's Class B, together with their leader, Mr.. Hallows, and a number of friends, met at Appleton Hall. After a walk through the beautiful grounds and gar-. dons, the party gathered on the lawn, where seats had kindly been provided. Here the usual class service was held, the lesson being read by the Secretary (Mr. Morris), and a very instruc- tive and interesting address was given by the Rev. C. F. Cross, vicar of Stretton and rural dean; on " Rehoboam." The singing, which was very hearty, was led by Mr. Baguley on the cornet. At the close Mr. Stannard and Mr- C. Hallows, on behalf of the class, thanked Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, the Rural Dean, and Mr. Bagu- ley. Mrs. Lyon, who, with a few other ladies, had been with them during the service, said how pleased she was to meet them once,more at the Hall. A parting hymn was then sung, and the party quietly wended their way home, well pleased 'With the visit.

div.head: MR. PILLING'S ADVICE.
div.p: MR. PILLING'S ADVICE.
Street Improvements.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday, a letter was road from the Local Governrdent Board, giving their formal sanction to the borrowing by tbe Rural District Council of .t 1,924 for the making of Victoria-avenue, Albert-road, and York- drive, Grappenhall, under the Private Streets Works Act.

Mr. Pilling: Get it done as soon as they can manage it. The Clerk: Tenders will be before the next Council meeting. The Local Government Board also intimated that an inquiry into the Parish Council's appli- cation for a £2,520 loan would be held on Octo- ber 2nd, at tho Hall Cafe. ,

div.head: NO SURGERY.
div.p: NO SURGERY.
Guardians Refuse a Request from Stockton Heath.

The application by the Stockton Heath Parish Council to the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday that Dr. Bower, the district medical officer, be required to have a surgery in Stock- ton Heath, with fixed hours:of attendance, was refused.. The Clerk read a letter from the Parish Coun- cil Of Walton Inferior, making a similar re- quest, stating that it would be greatly, appre- ciated by the sick and infirm. Stockton Heath Parish Council wrote Making their application in conjunction with Walton Inferior.

The Clerk said he had prepared Dr. Bower's returns, so that the Guardians might see the number of cases in Walton Inferior and the surrounding 'districts. For the fortnight ended July 29th there were four cases in Stockton Heath, one in Walton Inferior, and two in Grappenhall. Of these, only one appeared to have attended at the surgery at Stretton from Stockton Heath. In the other cases the doctor appeared to have made house visits. House visits were made entirely in Walton Inferior. In Grappenhall one attended at the surgery and the others were house visits. Unless there were cases which had not come to the Medical Officer's books, simply from the. fact that the surgery was so far away, there did not seem much evidence of the necessity of opening a surgery at Stockton Heath.
Mr. be Prez (relieving officer) said he did not think it was necessary to have the surgery. The greater trouble. seemed to be in getting the medicine.
Mr. Hallows: Yes; that is a great difficulty. A Voice: There are very few cases in Stockton
Heath where it is necessary to go to Stretton unless for medicine. ___

Mr. Hallows said the poor had a great diffi- culty in getting the medicine. It meant three- pence or fourpence to go to Stretton, which was a lot out of poor people's pockets. If some arrangement could be made to send the medi- cine into the village it would be a God-send to the people. The Chairman said that it appeared to him that on an average there were only three or four cases in Stockton Heath.

Mr. A. Lister-Kaye: Dr. Bower is very good in carrying it round Grappenhall. Mr: Piling: I know for a fact that Dr. Bower does all in•his power by sending medicine down regularly into Stockton Heath and Walton Inferior. A milk cart calls at the place, and when he knows of the medicine required he sends it down to the •village. Mr. Woodward said the disability did not apply to Stockton Heath any mere than other areas. Norley people had to go nearly five miles. It was not fair to make a distinction in favour of any parish. Mr. Linaker moved that the Board write the Parish Councils, informing them that the Board conld not see their way to grant the application. This was carried.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM ,LYMM.

Is a " Post Impressionist " needed? The query is prompted by a Council remark. One councillor said the danger posts were too modest. His reason was .that he did not think them glaring -enough. There is a class of painter called a "Post Impressionist." . Perhaps the Council might invite One on a visit.

......... . Ile could come to Lymm and make his im- pression on the posts. A little touching up might make them im- modest enough to please the councillor. Burford-lane still remains unlighted with gas. There was a lot more Council talk about the matter. . . And a step forward is to be taken—when? An engine off the line delayed Lynna traffic on Saturday. , ' Employers bound Manchester way were an- noyed; as it made them late. , The ,juniors were delighted, as it meant for them a shortened day. The youngsters, however, changed their tune later on. They were afraid that the reittrn journey would make tKm late for football. Of course, they ought to know they cannot have it both ways.
School Managers.—Councillor Warburton and Councillor Davies have been appointed managers of the Oughtrington School as representatives of the Urban District Council.

Council Accounts.—The accounts of the Lymm District Council have been issued by the Clerk, Mr. W. Mußard, and show that the receipts amounted to £4,586 15s. 11d., having a balance on the year's -working of £l9l Os. 6d. The revenue from gas amounted to 4.19,886 12s. 9d., leaving a balance of ,;.0.16.1 2s. 11.

Members at the Council.—The monthly meet- ing of the Lymm Urban District Council was held in the Council Chamber on Tuesday even- ing, Councillor S. Davies presiding. Dere were also present Councillors R. H. Got4ed (vice- chairman), G. L. Welford, J. H. Holt, W. G. Groves, 0. G. Smith, T. H. Warburton, P. LoAyer, the Rev. G. B. Thurston, with Mr. W. Mullard (clerk), Dr. B. M. De Jong (medical officer), Mr. D. Mort (surveyor), and Mr. W. L. Donaldson (gas manager).

Widening of a Bridge.—The following letter was read at the Lymm Council .on Thursday, from the Manchester liffiip Canal Company : "Re Ditchfield's Bridge Widening—Dear sir,— Your letter, with plan attached, has been laid before the company, and I am instructed tb say that while the company could not contribute towards the cost of widening, they would be pre- pared to provide so lunch of the company's land as was required free of cost, on condition that they be relieved of all responsibility for the repair of the bridge and approaches thereto, sub- ject to the span of the new bridge being 40 feet on the square, with a headway lift. 6in. above water-level, as stipulated in a letter of October 21st, 1911." The Clerk said the measurements would be right.

Salt Works Plan was reported to Lymm Council on Thursday that at a meeting of the Building and Fire Engine Committee a plan of salt works plant for Messrs. Verdin, Cooke and Co. was referred to the, Council meeting to be considered after report of the Surveyor.—The Council approved the plans.

Hospital Reopened.—At a meeting of the Lymm Council on Thursday the Medical Officer reported that he had been obliged to again open the hospital and engage nurses, arid on the motion of Councillor Gotobed, seconded by Coun- cillor Warburton, it was decided that the action of the Medical Officer be confirmed.—At the same meeti4 a letter was read from the Local Gov- ernment Board, asking for further information as to the intended use of land for sewerage dis- posal.—The Clerk was directed to inform the Local Government .Board that some portion of the land was intended for a refuse tip, and that probably a destructor would eventually be erected on the site.

Lively Sunday Night Scene.—The peace of the Sabbath evening in Booth's Hill was rudely dis- turbed on Sunday by the strange behaviour of a 'bus driver. The driver, Percy William Magreth, of Warrington,. after bringing his party up from the village, applied for refresh- ment at the Crown Inn, but was refused. A few minutes later the 'bus, by being driven on to the cobble-stoned footpath near the bottom of Cherry-lane, was almost upset. Considerable excitement ensued, and the man was eventually removed by Sergeants Washington and. Robinson to the Lymm Police Station. Ma4reth was brought before Messrs. S. Coxon andlS.'Davies, at a Special Court on Monday morning, charged with being drunk whilst in charge of two horses. He was fined 10s.

div.head: BURFORD-LANE LIG:AT!NG.
div.p: BURFORD-LANE LIG:AT!NG.
Council Have Another Lively Discussion Over The Question.

Shall Burford-lane be lighted with gas was the chief topic .discussed at the Lymm Council meeting on Thursday, and an interesting debate took place. It was stated that the present plant at the Gas Works was inadequate to supply the lane, and at the end it was decided that a thorough investigation of the Gas Works be made, and if this was found to be satisfactory, the matter would be proceeded •with. Councillor Gotobed proposed the original rem - lion, that the mains be laid at once, and the Rev. G. B. Thurston proposed the amendment, which was carried, that the Gas Works be ex- amined at once. ,
All the metnbers, except one. were agreed that

div.head: "Take In Hand At Once."
div.p: "Take In Hand At Once."

Councillor Gotobed proposed the following resolution: "That the Council take in hand at once the laying of a six-inch gas main from Heatley Station to the top of Burford-lane, at an estimated cost of £952; that the Clerk be instructed to advertise for tenders for the pipes, and to negotiate a loan for the covering of the cost."

He said that time after time the matter had been discussed. He did not think they would be wise, if they were going to do this work, if they put a main in which was smaller than six- inches. A four-inch main would cost about .t3OO less than the proposed sum, but that length was going to serve Mill-lane as well as Burford-lane, but he thought they would be well advised in sticking to the six-inch main. They should get the matter in hand with as little delay as possible, for the sake of public safety, and amenity of the residents in Burford- lane. For all reasons, it was a matter of jus- tice to the people in the district if they passed the resolution, which was on a matter which had so often occupied the attention of the Coun- cil.

div.head: Arguments Quite Irresistible.
div.p: Arguments Quite Irresistible.

Councillor Smith said that the arguments in favour of carrying the gas down Burford-lane were quite irresistible. Some• people looked at the gas concern as purely commercial, and they wanted to serve it purely from that point .of view. It was simply a question of " divi." with them, how much dividend could they make. For himself, and he hoped most of those pre- sent, he took another view, and which was, that the Council were guardians of public safely and' wellbeing. It was their duty to administer the gas concern in the interests of the -ratepayers as a whole. They were sent to the Council Chamber by ratepayers and not by .gas con- sumers, -as such, and their duty was to all. There was a -lot of traffic went dewn Burford- lane, and he could not imagine one of the most important lanes of the district remaining un- lighted. They might be told that now they had the borrowing borrows, there might be a ten- dency to excess and. extravagance, but if they. took 7 the outside figures. £.50 per year interest. and set off against that what they were going to make, he thought, after also considering the public importance of the lighting, that the financial side of the question was not a pressing One.

div.head: An Amendment.
div.p: An Amendment.

- The Rev. G. B. Thurston said they had had so many mere premonitions of the unsatisfac- tory' state of. the Gas Works—they had on at the last meeting of the committee—and to spend L 950, and then, perhaps, fail in ,the source of supply, would be a grievous misfortune to the public, and a misfortune for Which the Coun- cil would deserve censure. They had ap- pointed a committee some months ago to go into the question of the Gas Works thor- oughly, and they had looked forward to the reports. He agreed with the proposer of the resolution that it was time the Gas Works were in proper ordeN, but he thought it would be better if they Accepted his amendment, which was: "That after thorough - investigation of the gas undertaking, to be held at once, the Council—if its findings be satisfactory—take in hand forthwith the laying of 'six-inch gas mains from, Heatley Station," &c., &c. Assurance should be given that the gas could be supplied safely. _ .

Councillor Groves seconded the amendment. He did not think that there was any member of the Council but admitted that Burford-lane ought to be supplied with gas. and he 'did not think the financial aspect would step in at all to stop them from lighting, but the larger ques- tion was, Were they in a. position to supply the lane, in face of the present state of the Gas Works? They ought to find an answer to that question first. If the plant could supply the lane, then he would say "proceed," but until they had had .an examination he could not sup- port the resolution. Rev. G. B. Thurston: We have had the mem- bers appointed to go into the examination.

div.head: Modification.
div.p: A Modification.

Councillor Warburton said there was no one round the table felt the necessity of Burford- lane lighting more than he did, but it did seem that £932 :was a. large amount to spend on the matter. He thought four-inch mains would do the work quite as well as six-inch mains. For practically the whole of Lymm they had only six-inch mains, and to go to the extreme boun- dary of their district, where it was unlikely that the land would never be built upon, and lay six-inch mains, was not wise. The four- inch mains, which • would Serve the purpose, would be £3OO less,- and expenses must be cut down.

Councillor Holt advocated the six-inch mains. He said they did not know what would come about in that district, and the interest on the money would only mean a halfpenny rate. If investigation was necessary, theY should pro- ceed with the whole thing at once, and be satis- fied that their Works were satisfactory. They had made promises about the lighting of Bur- ford-lane for a considerable time. Councillor Groves: If the committee find that the present plant is capable of supplying this lane, it will only delay the matter a month. Councillor Gotobed said that in ally case the pipes would have .to be tendered for, which meant another month, and even when the work was put in hand it would mean two months. Ile was anxious that there Should. be as little delay as possible over the examination. He felt the necessity for thorough investigation, and he agreed with the Rev.Mr.Thurston in that. Re would not be satisfied until such examina- tions had been made. Apart from that he thought the Council might pass the resolution Without the amendment. He would like to accept the amendment, if he did not think ' it Would retard the work.

div.head: AU Wanting To Do It.
div.p: AU Wanting To Do It.

- - Rev. G. B. Thurston: I put in my amend- ment "at once" and "forthwith" Councillor Holt: I propose that the Clerk advertise for 'tenders for six-inch pipes, and that in the meantime the committee meet. Councillor Gotobed : I cannot accept that. Rev. G. B. Thurston: My amendment implies that if the -gas plant is not satisfactory it be made so.

Councillor Smith: Your borrowing powers under the Act are limited to £2,000.\ Councillor Gotobed said that the extension of the gas would not mean more than was consumed at " Beechwood " and Oughtrington Hall, How- ever, he consented to withdraw his motion on condition that investigation be made at once, and the whole matter put in• hand as early as possible.

The Rev. G. B. Thurston: We all want to do it. The amendment was carried, and it was decided that a committee consisting of all the members of the Council meet at the Gas Works at three o'clock on Monday.

'Dogs' Poisoned: Dastardly Act.—Much indig- nation has been aroused. in and around Fearn- head by the poisoning of several dogs. Some of these dogs were not only "pets" with tlx mem- bers of the fax4iilies to whom they belonged, but were high-bred ones and Valuable. Natur- ally there is much, feeling against the perpe- trator of such a cowardly and dastardly action. div.head: GOOD WORK IN NIGERIA.
div.p: A GOOD WORK IN NIGERIA.

On Monday night, in the commodious Wea- Padgate, a very instructive lecture on hospital work among ltaehl IYeda inel da Stuiecyhaot°sllonrPln ' Nigeria, West. Africa, was given by Dr. J. R. C. Stephens, who is the Wesley Guild medical missionary stationed at Igbora, Southern Nigeria. There was a very large at- tendance, many Warringtonians, as well as Pad- gate residents, being present. Dr. Bennett pre- sided. in his opening remarks, the Chairman pointed out that probably half the trade which was done in Lancashire had been pioneered by mission- ary work. Ile then gave a brief review of Dr. Stephens'. life, who, he stated, after being brought under the influence of Christianity, threw up a successful business in the South of England, went to London and studied for five years in medical science, qualified and passed his degrees as a doctor, in order to equip him- self • for the medical missionary nem. Dr. Stephens was then sent .out as a medical mis- sionary to West Africa to labour amongst the People there, and he was now over on "fur- lough. Dr. Stephens then gave an illustrated lantern leeture 'on his work among the "blacks," ex- hibiting on the screen many photographs which he had taken. He described the many surgical cases which' be had undertaken, and the great gratitude which had been evinced by those who had been successfully cured. 'flie demands made upon him by the natives for his services were very great, quite a common thing for him to have 40 patients waiting for him on a morning for treatment. As lie had only his house and the outside to " treat " the surgery cases, he as unable 'to do the work which was necessary to be done in a proper way, and so he was de- termined to erect a hospital, and was appeal- ing for funds for the purpose. :Some of the natives were helping, and tho king of that dis- storicte, having heard of his wonderful cures of m of his subjects, on being approached by Dr. Stephens for land on which to build the hospital, offered to give him all the land as far as the river, which was a mile away. Dr. Stephens replied he did not require so much as that. so at last the king gave him 16 acres for the purpose it is Dr. Stephens' intention to have a por- tion of the land cultivated for the benefit of the hospital. To equip and build the hospital, it will take <t2,504), and Dr. Stephens is spending his " furlough " or holiday in going up and down the country, lecturing to tho various Wes- leyan Guilds and other associations, appealing for funds for the purpose. ..t2 ss. will equip a bed in the Nigeria Hospital. So far, h,is appeal has been well responded to, as Ur. Stephens' work in Nigeria has been so prac- tically demonstrated to have been a success in every way, the health of the natives not only having been very much improved, but a higher civilisation has been attained, and a better feel- ing between " white and black" engendered. After a collection had been made, Mr. Duck- worth, in an appropriate speech, moved, and Jr. Bishop cordially seconded, a vote of thanks the lecturer, Mrs. Stephens, his wife in- cluded, also to Dr. Bennett for presiding, and to Messrs. Plinston and Appleton for their ser- vices at the lantern.

The funeral took place at the Grap- penhall Parish Church on Monday tiftern.iou. The Rev. H. V. Pigott officiated. The chief mourners were: 'Miss Lomas (daughbr), MeFsrs. Amongst the floral tri hates sent were tle following: From I,er worrownig children," "George and Annie," ' Elsie, Clarice, Mary and Mabel,"" Alf., Eva, and the boys," "Cousin Emma," "Emily," Mrs. Ireland, F. Holland, Mr. and Mrs. S. J. Woodcock, Miss. Ashton, Mr. Longshaw and family, W. and S. Fairhurst and J. Richards, C. Carter, Mrs. Ash- croft, Mr. and Mrs. J. Atkinson and Eleanor Williams.

parish Church Harvest Festival.—The har- vest services were held at the Parish Church on Sunday, when the preacher in the morning was the Rev. J. 11. G. Ilollingworth, vicar of St. Barnabas', Warrington. Preaching from Joel ii. xxiv., "And the fleors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil," the rev. genMman said scarcity and plenty • belonged to God. At times when the harvest was not so good, the floors were ,not full, ancl it should serve to remind us of our dependence upon God. In times of plenty, when we can get all we want, we were apt to forget God, and think it had all come by our own might and power. The preacher at the even- ing service was the Rev. E. E. Peters, .of St. Paul's. Warrington, who p'reached from the text, "There is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." The anthems were "The eyes of all wait on -Thee," and "Ye shall dwell in the land," the treble 0103 bping taken by Messrs. Phil Reece and 1. Sheplierrd, and the bass by Mr. J. Leigh, who sang splendidly. Mr. W. Asquith Wood was respon- able for the tuition of the choir. The church was tastefully 'decorated by the ladies of the congregation.

div.head: GENTLE ANGLER.
div.p: THE GENTLE ANGLER.

Every year the number of women who go in for sport grows greater; and among all sports none seem to hold more • attraction for the feminine sex than angling. There are many reasons to explain this. The piscatorial art is essentially a gentle one; which suits women who have not the heart to put an end* to the life of a glorious stag, or a splendid pheasant, and to whom the squeal of a stricken hare is absolutely painful. Then there is an /element of fair-play in one's struggle with a fish, great or small, which seems absent from shooting; the excitement of the hand to hand conflict, as it were, following the• delicate art of the lure, which in itself appeals to the feminine mind. Also fishing is not, as a rule, so fatig,tuing as either shooting or hunting; for there is muel delightful sport to be had that does not in- clude historic fights with salmon or gigantic tarpon, though many of these have beer. won by women. THE SPORT OF MANY CHARMS.

Perhaps the reason of the curious charm of angling lies in its combination of emotions. While it equals in excitement at given mo- ments almost any other sport, it surpasses all others in its sense of serenity and peace. There is none of the fret -and fever or bodily discomfort which form so large a part of deerstalking for instance Fishing is en- joyable. from the first moment one sets cut till one returns at even-tide with (we hope) a full creel, each silvery victim being the centre of a delightful experience differing in detail from every other, each prize gained by the use of personal intelligence, observation, and the cunning use of the lure. No wonder that 0, sport in which imagination plays so vivid a part should :lay the angler open to the temptation, as well as the reproach, of being too imaginative in his "fish-tales." No sport fills its adepts with greater enthu- siasm than does angling. What .of the rap- ture which rewards the Happy She who fills her creel with trout, or has come victorious out of a hand to hand battle with a sixteen or twenty pound salmon! The choosing cf tEe lure, the delicate sureness of the cas; the moment of suspense before the swirl cf the water and the sudden tug proclaim a bite; the quick turn of the wrist at the right mo- ment which strikes the hook home; and then the scream of the reel as the fish dashes off for liberty, followed by the angler down stream, up stream, reeling in only to let the line run again for a fresh flight; the person- kl element in the fights with the fish, an ele- ne-nt lacking in most other sports; and fin- ally the ever-growing FenDe of dominance and triumph owing to skill and endurance, until gaff or; landing-net come into play, and the prize so ha`rdly fought for lies on the bank. Such moments are incomparable; they are the salt of life; and to be able to enjoy them alone in such surroundings of exquisite oeau- ty as usually fall to the angler's share, place the sport on a plane apart.

div.head: PROPER "KIT."
div.p: A PROPER "KIT."

In fishing, as in other sport, one must be. properly " got up" if one intends to extract as much enjoyment as possible out of the pas- time. One should be so garbed that one can forget one's clothes entirely, and he able to &vote all one's attention to the sport in hand. For ordinary .fishing good stout slices, garnished with some nails to prevent slipping on treacherous banks and boulders, and warn with putties, are best. The ankle has thus free play and the putties preserve the lower legs from thorns and teazles. However, some people prefer boots, in which case it is well to choose those which are waterproofed by a film of rubber carried through the whole boot, the boot itself being made of specially prepared fine soft pliable leather. A well chosen boot of this kind (of which there are several excellent types) though expensive to start with, lasts for years. If wading is to be the portion of Piscatri, she should wear good thigh boots, as light and comfortable as pee- sible. As regards the rest of the outfit it should consist of knickerbockers, short skirt and coat, all of some woollen material, which is not only warm and light, but waterproof, though not air-proof. The latter is a mcst im- portant point, for a material that does not let the surplus heat of the body evaporate is not one fitted for any form of hard exercise. As regards the best kind of rode, no sort of rule can be laid down, for the personal equa- tion plays as great a part in the kit of an angler as it does in that of a golfer. Until experience has taught the lesson of prefer- ence, the -wisest thing for the novice is, in the •words of a wise man, "to go to a good rod-maker who also is an experienced angler, trust him, and do not grudge the initial ex- pense. Let him choose the rod best suited to your personal peculiarities." Beware of too heavy a red, for nothing will spoil a cast like a tired arm and wrist-. The improvement in rods of late years is immeme, and the modern split cane rods with steel centres are marvels of lightness, strength and balance.

div.head: FOR THE BEGINNER.
div.p: FOR THE BEGINNER.

Ono') you have acquired the proper outfit, let your thoughts turn wholly to casting. You can practise casting in a back garden with *a flower-pat as an objective and acquire aim and prgeision. It is in the perfect cast- ing and delivery of the fly that is found one of -the bareate.st jots of angling; and the more the difficult art of casting is practked the bet- ter hopes of success for the novice. Some are of opinion that a nov.ce should be encouraged to fish down stream at first, as, if the cast is not made correctly, the stlYzam willoome to the rezeue and float the line and flies out straight. This is to my mind a mistake, for it tancourages slovenly casting. It is much bet- ter to "begin as we Mean to \go on," and al- Ways remember to fish up and across stream, ;facing. the sun, and with the wind at one's bacK, If such things can be arranged. There are many reasons for always fishing up stream. The fish always lie with their heads up stream waiting for whdtever food the current brings down; thus they not only do not see the angler approaching from behind, but the carefully. thrown fries come down stream to them in a perfectly natural man- ner, and if taken the fish are muell more like- ly to be hooked from the relatrie position of their bodies to the rod behind them. 'Be care- ful not too strike too hard, a general fault with young anglers, or you will risk break- ing your tackle; a very slight motion of the wrist is all that is required to fix the sharp little hook in the mouth of the fish before he discovers his mistake and ejects the fraudu- lent morsel. Do not attempt to stop the fish when he first rushes off; humour him, but be ready to put on more pressure as soon as he falters, and if yqu can keep clear of the rocks, snags and' weed-beds it will not be long before you can slip the net under 17. m, and give him the coup de grace by a blow on the head. div.head: V'MD DESCRIPTION BY AU EVE-MTNESS.
div.p: V'MD DESCRIPTION BY AU EVE-MTNESS.

The stone bridge, which has for seventy-seven years been the most familiar of all Warrington structures, is in process Of speedy demolition. The central arch has been broken, the process having been begun from the east side, and it is expected that on Monday next the. keystone upon the west side will be removed. The ceremony of its removal will stand in marked contrast from the ornate ceremony with whiah it was inserted three days before the Christmas of 1836, and we feel sure that our readers will like to have the event recalled, and to have the best description that can be obtained of The events of a notable day.

_ _ That such an account is available we owe to a correspondent of the "Liverpool Journal " for, Warrington had then no newspaper of its own, and no separate account appears to have been published—whose keen interest in the event is manifest in the eloquent and very com- plete record he made. 1 In transcribing,the article it is only necessary to say that the ceremony was carried out by the Freemasons and with Masonic ritual and honours.

..--- - 'The reminder may also be given that the Town Hall of those days Was the building now known as the.old Music Hall, and that the space we know as the Fish Market- was the Market- place. The "Liverpool Journal" account. was as follows
Senior Provincial Grand Warden, with the level.
Steward.
Steward
--...,,._. Brother William Evans, bearing the volume -- -
of Sacred Writ. D.P.G.M., with (Tie square. Grand Sword Ilearer. Steward. Steward. Provincial Grand Standard I3earer.
- - .---____ _ _ • John lirinkwater, Esq., acting P.G.M. Steward. Steward.
Provincial Grand T37lers, with drawn swords.
DEPUTY CONSTABLES.
Menibers of the P. Confederation, two and two, with flags and scarfs. Inhabitants of the town, and others.

The procession having been duly formed and marshalled, under the actiVe superintendence of Brother Richard Brown, of Warrington—who officiated as Master of the Ceremonies—it pro- ceeded, in due order (the Royal Harmonic Band playing Masonic airs), to the bridge, by the fol- lowing route :—The Market-place, Mil-street, King-street, Sankey-street, and Bridgt-street. The early part of the procession passed to the Cheshire side of the Mersey', over the temporary bridge the Masonic brethren walked upon the new bridge on the Lancashire side, under the direction of Brother R. Brown, and the prin- cipal officers took their stand upon the centre arch. A great many ladies were in attendance, upon a platform, to view the fraying of the Key- stone. Among the ;gentlemen present we noticed J. I. Blackburn, -Esq., M.P.; J. W. Pat- ten, Esq., M.P., Thomas Parr. Esq., John Clare, Esq., John Greenall, Esa., G. Greenall, Esq., Joseph Wagstaffe, Esq., Edward Garvin, Esq., Joseph Lee, Esq.
The Memorial Box.

The Key-stone; weighing .• 12 cwt., was in readiness on the bridge, and oh arriving th&e, the .Deputy Provincial Grand Master was pre- sented with a silver trowel and a vessel con- taining sine cement. A space had been pre- pared, in the side of tile stone, for the reception of a glass box, containing gold, silver and cop- per coins of the present and last reign, and a Masonic medal. This box was deposited in the cavity, secured with cement, by the D.P.G.M., and a brass plate, placed over it, bearing the following inscription :

This key-stone of the centre arch of this bridge was laid by Le Gendre Nicholas Starkie, 'Esq., .P.G.NI.W.D.C.L., Dec. 22, 1836." The Bev. James - NVright, minister of -St. James's Church, Latchford, and Chaplain to the right honourable the Earl of Garr4ck, then pro. ceded to invoke the blessing of the Great Architect of the UniverSe to the work to which they were now about putting the Key-stone; tie prayed that the erection, which had been so far and so successfully advanced, might, by Divine Prov:dence, be completed, so as to be of advantage to the town and neighbourhood of Warrington. The P.G.S.W. responded "So mote it be."
Corn and Wine and Oil.
Oil, wine, and corn were then poured upon the stone out of the silver vessels.

The clergyman then prayed to the great Source of all plenty for the future prosperity of the town of Warrington, and fhett He would ,be pleased to' grant its inhabitants abundance of corn, Oil and wine, to the latest posterity. Tilt P.G.S.W. responded as. before: • - The stone was then raised by a pulley, and embedded in its destined place, by Brother Gan- non, an operatingonason. When the stone was laid, three times three shouts of applause Aere given, and the Royal Harmonic Band struck up "God save tile King."
Brother Bullough then advanced to the foot )of the Key-stone and there delivered an oration or locture upon the instruments of the craft. _

• The Deputy Provincial Grand Master then came forward, and spoke as follows :--"I m very much gratified to witness the -completion of an erection so well calculated to be of use, advantage, and ornament to the town of War- rington, and the two counties which it connects. I am not prepared to make a long speech upon this occasion, for I did not know, until a few minutes before the procession left the Town Flail, that I should have to officiate for the Pro- vincial Grand Master, whose absence has prob- ably been caused by some unforeseen circum- stance. He may, perhaps, be able to meet us at dinner." Three cheers were then given, after which the procession fell into line of march, as before. to the parish church, through Mersey- street and Church-street.
The Sermon.

Brother the Ilev. J. Wright read the evening service, and we have seldom heard a better reader. His voice is clear, his pronunciation devoid of any provincial burr, and hig manner In the pulpit simple and easy. Brother George Holden (of Liverpool) was ex- pected to preside at the organ, but did not at- tend. The organ was, therefore, played by Mr. tierfoot,' of Warrington, in a manner which could not and did not fail to give satisfaction to all his auditors. The vocal department-was effectively taken charge of by Mrs. Unsworth (of Warrington) and Messrs. Boothby and An- drews (of Liverpool). .

According to notice, the sermon wa4 preached by the fiev. T. V. Bayne, M.A.. Master of the Free School, Warrington. This gentleman is not a Mason, but we are confident that we speak the opinion of all our brethren when we say that if his discourse had been written by one of the craft, it could not have been more practically illustrative of the glorious and ancient art.

At the conclusion of the service, the proces- sion returned to the Market-place, through the Butter-market and the , Horse-market. The lodge was then closed with the usual formali- ties—a vote of thanks to Mr. Bayne for his ex- cellent sermon having first been moved and carried with unanimity. The Masons then proceeded to the Lion Inn, where an excellent and plentiful dinner was provided, to which amble justice was done. The D.P.G.M., John Drinkwater, Esq., filled the chair, and Brother Holt, G.S.W., was in one of the vice-chairs--the other being filled by Brother Richard Brown, of • Warrington. Stubbs's Royal Harmonic Band was in attend- ance, and played several admired and appro- priate airs after the toasts.

Reflections, Upon a Memorable Day. Nothing during he whole day occurred to cloud, even for a moment, the harmony and good brotherly love which prevailed. The assemblage consisted of men of different per- suasions of religion, and varied sentiments in politics; but, as Masonry meddles not with creeds or politics, nothing could spring from this diversity of opinion to check that kindly feeling of brotherly .love, which hinds the fol- lowers of the craft together by a chain, so ancient., that its origin derives from time 'imme- morial, qnd - its bonds are as permanent as. those, in the physical world, which bind the Conflicting elements of matter in an union which nothing can destroy. To . the members of the Warrington Locige, much of the pleasantness of the meeting is attributable. Their. arrangements were most. complete, and they had everything conductet: onia scale of the most extensive liberality. The ceremonial was indebted for much of its Continued in next column
HOW THE KEY-STONE WAS PLACED IN WARRINGTON BRIDGE.—Cont.

div.head: GRAND MASONIC FESTIVAL.
div.p: GRAND MASONIC FESTIVAL.
Ceremonial of Laying the Keystone of the New
Bridge at Warrington.

On Thursday, there was a Grand Masonic Festival at Warrington, 'upon the occasion of laying the keystone of the new bridge, at tdat town, over the Mersey, trills connecting the counties of Cheshire and Lancashire, at a point which must materially add to the convenience of the inhabitants of Warrington, in particular, and of the residents in the two counties pala- tine, generally.. Tile display, however, was not confined exclusively to that made by the Free- masons, as the leading gentry of the town and ,neighbourhood joined in it; the tradesmen also fell into the 'procession ; and (last, though not least) the assemblage of ladies in the windows of the various streets through •iVchich, the proces- sion passed, reflected a . grace and brilliancy upon the scene which harmonised admirably with the splendour of the general exhibition. Seldom has a more imposing sight been be- held in Warrington than that which made Thursday a memorable day in its annals. Sel- dom, indeed, in any part of the kingdom has there,. of 'recent years, been a more splendid spectacle, in Masonry, than that which dazzled and delighted the eyes ,and minds of the good people of Warrington. The inspiring and j. spiriting strains of music—the handsome ban- ners scattered at intervals through the long line of the procession—the magnificent jewels and insignia worn by the Masons—the brethren of the craft, with the appropriate and becoming apparelling of the order—the handsome decora- tions of the members of Confederation—the re- spectable and numerous •attendance of the gentry—the interesting exhibition of the chil- dren of the Blue Coat School, with their own band—the orderly accompaniment of the town's people, at each side of the procession—the well- dressed and well-looking ladies, who appeared to take such an interest in the, proceedings of the day—the decorum which was maintained, without the slightest interruption, during ,the whole proceedings—and 'the interesting occa- sion which had caused the assemblage . of so many thousands, formed a whole very rarely surpassed in the province's.
A Great Scene in the Market-place.

At 'half-past • eight o'clock, Stubbs's Royal Harmonic Band commenced the business of the day by playing on their way from the railway station to the Market-place. They were hand- somely attired in their new uniform—the same in make, substance,. and adornment as that worn by the King's Dragoon Guards. At half- past nine o'clock they took their station in the Market-place, near the Town Hall, and con- tinued playing lively and appropriate airs until the procession was marshalled .in order, at half- past eleven o'clock.

- At ten o'clock Erie Freemasons proceeded to the Ton Hall, where the lodge was opened on the first degree. On this occasion the chair was filed by John Drinkwater, Esq. (of Liver- pool), Deputy Provincial Grand Master; Brothers bit and Persin, as Senior and Junior p. Grand Wardens; Brother Penketh, Senior. P. Grand Deacon; Brother Staley, Junior P. Grand Deacon; Brother Woodward, Provincial Grand Secretary ; Brother Gatley, P. Senior Deacon, of Cheshire. The lodge was most numerously attended by deputations from WaFrington, Liverpool, Manchester, . wigan, Nantwich, Preston, Chester, and other neighbouring lodges. The Rev. James Wright (Royal Arch) officiated on -this occasion as Provincial G. Chaplain. The brethren were all handsomely attired in Niasonic costtime—black, with white gloves—and, of course, Wore the aprons, col- lars, and various insignia which at once marked the' degree of each Mason, and declare their offices in their respective lodges. We suppose that not less than 400 brethren were at this general meeting; the large room in the Town Hall was crowded, and the appearance was ex- tremely handsome. Almost every brother wore a jewel. Having thus stated the constitution of this general "chapter," the public must excuse us If we decline to inform them of the proceedings which took place. They may be assured that all was upon the square—straight as a rule— continuous as a line--corrective as a plumb line—accurately measured by the compasses of good feeling, morality, and Christian practice —and adjusted to the exact level of Masonic duty. There vas no occasion 'for the R.W,D.P.G.M. to chisel off any angles—the key- stone of brotherhood was fixed in by the corn- nron union of heart and act, for the good of the craft—and further than this, the public cannot know.
The Procession.

At eleven o'clock the Masonic brethren left the lodge in procession, as we shall presently describe. They fell in with the general caval- cade, and the procession proceeded -in the fol- lowing order:— The Boys belonging to the Blue Coat School. The Town Crier and, Bell flinger. Flags. . .
Constables, v#., Mr. L. C. Dutton, Mr. C. Leyland, Mr. W. H. Golden, and Mr. W. • Grice. Deputy-Constable, Mr. James Jones. The Churchwardens and Sidesmen.

Gentlemen of • the Town and Neignbourhood (four a-breast). The Magistrates and clergy. Brother StUpbs's Royal Harrhonic Band. MASONIC BRETHREN, In the following order;— Two Tylers; each with a drawn sword. Entered Apprentices (two and two). -Fellow Craft (two and two).
Master Masons, two and two (the members of the junior lodges first). Mr. Ginnon, the builder of the bridge, bearing the plan.
Junior Provincial Grand Warden, with the " plumb.
Steward with a wand. Steward with a wand

div.head: World's Tribute of Interesting
div.p: The World's Tribute of Interesting
Items of News.
QUAINT AND AMUSING.

Some women burn pastilles and ribbon of Bruges to scent their rooms. A delicate per- fume can be procured in Bond-street, which Lady Warwick uses at Warwick Castle. Some use scented handkerchiefs. A few pin their faith to incense, and put it in a red-hot spoon which they carry, about their apartments. Others use a scent syringe and waft white rose, violtt or heliotrope over themselves and their belongings.

div.head: NEW CHINESE ALPHABET.
div.p: NEW CHINESE ALPHABET.

An educational conference sitting in Pekin has devised a new alphabet for expressing the sounds of the Chinese language. This alphabet consists of parts of Chinese characters which represent fixed sounds, there being 24 initials and 15 finals, making an alphabet of 39 letters. It may be called a Chinese Roman alphabet, as the 'method of combination is similar to the Roman. One of the greatest difficulties en- c‘duntered was the fact that many of the Chinese sounds have different meanings for different in- tonations.

div.head: BRIEF CHEESE HISTORY.
div.p: A BRIEF CHEESE HISTORY.

The first cheese factory in Ontario was started in Oxford County! in 1864, and the man who had the honour of that important initial step was Mr. Harvey Farrington. Since then the growth of the cheese industry has been very great, something like the difference, figuratively speaking, between a common-sized cheese and the "mammoth clieese " exhibited by Ontario at the Chicago World's Fair. That cheese re- quired 202,2001 b. of milk, or equal to the milk of one day in .September of 10,000 cows. It weighed 22,00016. and was 6ft. in height and 28ft. in circumference. •

div.head: SPEED OF ANIMALS,
div.p: SPEED OF ANIMALS,

No animal is known to have exceeded the speed uned by tile horse (say ".Science Sift- ings ). Instimittneous photographs of die famous specimen snowed tne full length clone complete stride of about it. In tile stride of the fastest racers the hind quarters and limbs are raised considerably higher than the shoul- ders, and from this relatively great height are brought downward and forward widely separ- ated irom each other, to avoid striking the fore legs: The hare has not in reality the speed of the dog. The dog, on ate other hand, does not attain the speed of the horse. The 'giraffe is said to run at the rate of 15 yards per second under the most favourable conditions.

div.head: REMARKABLE FAMILY HISTORY
div.p: REMARKABLE FAMILY HISTORY

One of the most remarkable family histories on record is contained in a letter received by the United States Commissioner of Pensions, who has asked for data so that a readjust, ment in the writer's pension might be made. "My father," wrote the pensioner, "had 25 children by three wires, who were sisters, and of whom the first two wives were twins. The third wife also was one of twins. My mother haa triplets, three boys, of whom I am one. she had no other children. All the other wives' children were twins: In all, of the three wives, there were 13 boys, all of whom were soldiers. All of the 25 children are dead but myself."

div.head: FUTURE OF THE PIANOLA.
div.p: THE FUTURE OF THE PIANOLA.

Let the price of pianolas come down, like the price of bicycles a few years ago, and the " Timer " musical expert thinks that every one whose idea of music is bpunded by he long- ing to "do it too will do it on a pianola in- stead of spending years at a music school, fol- lowed by brief appearances on a-concert plat- form. The time is already well within sight when the pianola will have gathered to itself all the mere copyists on the piano, and people will only listen to those pianists who through the touch of their fingers -on the keys have something to give which is genuine and first- hand art, that something which can ncver be caught and reproduced by the most subtle con- trivance of levers and bellows.

div.head: ,MUNICIPAL RABBIT FARM.
div.p: A ,MUNICIPAL RABBIT FARM.

German agricultural papers report a unique enterprise which has been jointly undertaken by thirty rabbit-breeders representing various rabbit clubs in the municipality of Eisenbach and the Government of the Grand Duchy of Saxe-Weimar, says "The Smallholder." The Government has made a grant of £25, towards the establishment of a farm. The town council of Eisenbach undertakes to erect the, necessary building, which will be a stable three storeys high and 250 ft. long. It has placed at the dis- posal of the breeders a piece of land 30 acres In extent, and has undertaken to‘erecra rabbit fence Gft. deep below the ground and sft. above ground.

completeness to the activity and zeal of Brother H. Brown, who superintended every part of it. Personally, the writer of this report is indebted to his friendship for information and facilities which, he feels, confer upon what' he has written a considerable share of its value. The completeness of this narrative—which is fuller, he believes, than anything of We sort which has ever appeared in print--is owing, in some degree, to the 'extent and accuracy of the in- formation communicated by Brother Brown.

the B.W. Chairman remarked, by the perform- ancesharmony of Brother P. Stubbs's Royal iHarmonic Band—nearly one-half of whom are Masons. In order to do honour to the occasion, Brother S. took the old Masonic air, "Prosper the Art," as the theme for a beautiful quadrille, which he composed expressly for tfiis day, and which was played by the band when the procession was going to the bridge. It may be necessary to State that the bridge over the Mersqy, of which, on this day (Decem- ber 22, 1836) the key-stone was laid, was corn- vienced in 1835. The cost is defrayed by the counties of Chester 4ind Lancaster. There were, we calculate, from 10,000 to 12,000 persons present during the ceremonial we have described. The day was kept as a holiday in Warrington, every strop being shut from -nine o'clock a.m. until three p.m. We should not be impartial reporters of the proceedings if we omitted to declare that, in our opinion, there were two drawbacks upon the pleasure of the day, and the completeness of the ceremonial. These are, the absence of Le Gendre Nicholas Starkie, Esq., Provincial Grand Master of the Western Division of Lan- cashire, and the unexplained fact that, although there was a general invitation for all clubs in Warrington to join in the procession, the only body which did so join it was the Protestant Confederation, to the number of about one hun- dred and fifty. They were separated from the Masonic portion of the procession by the inter- vention of a body of constables. If the clubs of Warrington had joined in the procession it would have added much to its splendid appear- ance. As it was, it conveys the idea that while the gentry of the borough took great pains to render the exhibition as imposing as possible, the tradesmen were more indifferent to the in- terests of the town.—AS regards the absence of Mr. Starkie, we may state that, since our return from Warrington, we have heard that he reached that town some time after the proces- sion (which had whited an hour for his arrival) had proceeded to the bridge, and that, not wish- ing to interrupt the ceremonial by appearing at the bridge after it had commenced, he returned home. Wc are confident that he, as much as anyone, regrets his absence.

div.head: New Books.
div.p: New Books.
MacMillan's Shilling Theological Library. (Cloth, is. net per volume.)

It may be safely anticipated that the pub- lishers of the Shilling Theological Library have embarked upon an experiment which will prove completely successful. Much of the best litera- ture in many departments of knowledge has now for long been open to the public at a reasonable cost, and the arrival of a cheap pub- lication of serious theological works has been for some time overdue. Here and there, it is true, there have come reprints Of such produc- tions, many of them in the sixpenny paper- backed form, which have been within the com- pass of the average purchaser, but there is ample scope for such an ordered and definite plan of. publication as appears to be fore- shadowed by the volumes DOW issued under the above title. Unless the signs of the times are misread, there will be great numbers' of people who will avail themselves with avidity of the opportunity thus offered of forming acquaintance with religious thought of the first order, hi an age when the human mind feels, often, perhaps, only vaguely', and yet with con- cern, that religious questions have .moved to a new plane, and that very much of what was once held to be sure and authoritative is now called in question; when vast numbers of think- ing people have, become. uncertain as to the standing-ground of tile Christian faith, it is all to the ) good that there should be made, in its present form, this attempt to issue a Theolocrical- , e Library of ' definite value.

Not that all these books are new, nor indeed that any of them are new. in the sense of hav- ing.becn written specially for th,is series. It is indeed many years kince some bf them first saw the light, though in the case of 'others they are comparatively recent produCtions., Apart from that,' however, the very fact of the experiment is of considerable moment, ,and the- beginning having ben made, it is Possible to look hope- fully to the future for issues of increasing value. • •

The present series contains much of great -iriL terest. Of the older writers, whose work has been re-issued, many.:readers will welcome the inclusion of Bishop Phillips 'Brooks, bean Church and Charles Kingsley. Though much ground has been traversed since their work was done,. and though there are to-day aspects of thought with which they were more or less unfamiliar, it is still true that in the analysis of permanent human emotions, and in the genius with which they deal with the elemental passions of the human soul and hold tip the mirror to human life, there isilittle that anyone can teach them, and much that they are able to teach our own • time. It is of The greatest value that the two well-known works of Dr. Illingworth, "Personality, human and divine," and "Divine immanence," should have found a place in the selected series. Familiarity with mu9li that is destructive.'of past knowledge is not uncommon: Acquaintance with many new ideas is a comparatively universal possession. Too often lacking Is any power of re-construc- tio'n, or any synthesis bringing new concep- tions into ordered combination and relation- ship. It is this re-constructive • faculty which 'lds made We work of Dr. Illingworth a force to be reckoned- with in the realm of philosophy and theology, and it is open to question whether this first 'series c6ntains any other 'writing of equal weight.

In saying this there is no attempt to minimise the vivid interest attaching. to the persuasive statement made by the tßev. Bernard Lucas in "The Faith of a Christian," a little volume pub- lished first in 1904, and now in its third edition. It is a courageous and remarkably able effort ,to re-state the Christian faith in terms of modetm thought, and in the language of our own time, and whether agreement be felt or not with all the positions taken by the writer, nothing but admiration can be given to the evident honesty with which he endeavours to face every situation, and the lucidity with which ' the whole case is presented. Quite arresting, too, in certain aspects is another number of the series in which- much the same problem is dis- cussed by the Bev. William Temple under the title "The Faith and Modern Thought." ' The shortest review of this library would be incomplete without mention of the remarkable Imsigned production "Pro Christo et Ecclesia," an acute analysis of the conditions Of society in the days of Jesus, the main contention of which is that the Pharisees condemned in the Gospels were honest, God-fearing and conscientiou§ men. Out of this there *springs naturally a criticism of the typically religious mind of our own day, especially as identified with the Chris- tion Church, so that the whole work becomes, I in the author's own words, an attempt "to show that the Gospel story is the verdict of Eternal Truth upon defects to which all of us who fol- low an historic religion are naturally prone, and the more prone when We are intense and conscientious in our devotion to an unchang- ing religious ideal." This is aibook of unusual penetration. It will repay clos6' and careful study. Finally, amongst the older books; men- tion may be made of the re-publication- of a I lseries of addresses on the "Books of the Bible," Iby Professor Hort, treating very simply and from an elementary yet interesting standpoint, their story and message, and calculated to give, where it niay not already exist, some conception of the Bible as a whole literature.

Quite 'obviously there is,pot spac6 in such an article. as this to deal from the critical stand- point with any single volume of the series. No one will, of course, go through the variety of thought here offered without feeling that there are many points to be debated. Nor will any- one read some of these pages without having his own .thought challenged in certain directions. It is to be hoped that the publication of this first selection, will more than justify 'further attempts along the same line. Many thinking men and women will welcome this Theological Library. Many have been waiting for what has now been well begun. A wide field may be covered by, continued experiment.

List of the Series. The .Candle of the Lord and nine other Ser- mons (Bishop Phillips BrooRs). Sixteen Village Sermons (Dean Church). Discipline of the Christian Character (Dean Church). Sermoneon the Books of the Bible (Rev. Pro- fessor ion). , Personality, Human and Divine (Rev. Dr. Iftingworth). - Divine Immanence (Rev. Dr. Illingworth). Village Sermons (Charles Kingsley). • Good News of -God, Twenty Sermons (Charles Kingsley). • The Faith of a Christian (Rev. Bernard Lucas). The Faith and Modern Thought (Rev. William Temple).

div.head: EUGENICS IN THE STATES
div.p: EUGENICS IN THE STATES

The first eugenics law in the United States has been adopted in Pennsylvania, wherq in the future every prospective bride and Bridegroom must answer 48 questions before they can obtain a marriage licence. Applicants must state whether they are imbecile, epileptic, of unsound mind, or given to the excessive use of Intoxicants or narcotic drugs, and whether within the previous five years they have been inmates of either an asylum or a workhouse. Bridegrooms must also declare whether they are physically able to support a family. It is expected that sufficient statistics will be ob- tained to permit further legislative action pro- hibiting marriages amongst these who are un- desirable as parents.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
WHAT BOWLERS DO NOT LIKE.

The one thing a bowler dislikes more than , anything else is to be treated with scant cere- stony. It does not please him to behold his best balls met with bold assurance and played well, and he is apt to become almost visibly annoyed if a ball which he considers worth a wicket re- sults in a boundary instead. This may sound like unduly insisting on the obvious,. but it is so important that I have given it 'place of honour in my article. When a bowler finds himself treated with respect he will bowl his best all the time until beaten by sheer fatigue, and batsmen who do not wish to study a bow- ler's feelings would do well to 'ponder on this fact. • The batsman who simply will not be denied in his energetic quest for runs uses up his bowlers far more quickly than the man who is content to play over after over "for keeps," , and allow runs to come from their own initia- tive. Scoring strokes off good balls are the pet aversion of our friend the bowler, who, con- trary the popular idea, is by no means averse to that Slow batting of the safe type which does not make rapid runs of his average, and keeps him buoyed up with the constant hope of getting a wicket cheaply—even if he has to wait a long time for B. Hobbs, in the September "Strand Magazine."

div.head: POINTS FOR THE P.O.
div.p: POINTS FOR THE P.O.

It has been suggested that the postal author- ities should go in for a little attractive adver- tising_in order to bring their various schemes more prominently before the public. . The following hints for a postal poster are offered to the P.M.G. gratis : " Patro•nise the Good Old Post Office." (Estab- lished over a Century.) "A large number of stamps in all the latest art shades kept in stock. Have you tried the new raspberry flavoured one? They are lovely to lick."

"Postal orders in great variety. They make charming presents for friends and relations. Always appreciated. Send one to your dear old mother to-day." "Have the telephone laid on. Causes endless amusement."
"Are you getting on in years? Don't worry. We specialise in old age pensions."
THE CHARM OF ANGLING.

There is an indefinable charm in summer angling; on a hot day, when London seems so far away as New York, even the most ardent disciple of Walton is apt to forget the. fish in favour of his pipe. And, above all, there is a restfulness about a Thames fishing punt that is peculiar to the river. I have found it in no other fishing. craft throughout the length and breadth of the land. There is room enough in it for even the most lax of us to be tidy; there is a place for everything, and room for more than you could possibly bring with you. It is ideal for a summer day's angling, for there is also room to sleep. And, after the day I have just described, I unmOored the old punt and paddled along to the lock, and by that time I had come to the conclusion it might be easier to gather `I y tackle together and walk home along, the towing path. So I left the punt in charge of the lock keeper, promising to call for it the next day, and footed niy way to home— and dinner. In looking over what I, have written, I see that the whole day resulted in the capture of only two fish, an eel and a gudgeon. The latter/was returned, and the former, re- turned of its own accord. Disappointing ? never; the true angler is never disappointed. He thinks of the glories of to-morrow, knowing well in his heart that the morrow may be just the same. It is that which constitutes the whole charm of angling; its glorious uncertainty puts every good angler on the scratch mark, for even the professional has his blank days like the rest Of us. But does it matter very much? I think not; all the above only concerns one blank day, but if I put all my blank days together, I could easily make another volume for the Badminton Library. The only difficulty I can see is that no one would read it. But these few paragraphs will serve to bring all my friends around me in sympathy; we all have our blank days—too many of them?—and they do us good. They help to spur us on for the morrow.—" Fry's Magazine."

div.head: MOST REMARKABLE RAILWAY.
div.p: THE MOST REMARKABLE RAILWAY.

Unique among railways- is 'the Lima-Oroya line in Peru, South America. In just over 100 ,miles it rises from sea level to an altitude of 15,665 feet, or to about that of the summit of Mount Blanc, or a rise of three miles. In a few hours the traveller is transported from tropical surroundings to the eternal snows of the Andes. More wonderful still, from an engineering point of view, is the fact that the system adopted Is that known as the open-rail principle; that Is to say, the cog-wheel and rack system, in- variably resorteld to for climbing mountains, has not been taken advantage of. But in descending this railway from the mountains the train,is always preceded by a pilot car entirely controlled by hand. It means that the occu- pants of the car indulge in what is nothing more than a delightful coast for a distance of 100 miles, down the steep mountain sides, through innumerable tunnels cut out of the hills, past mining camps, over deep ravines and gorges, to the terminus station on the seashore.

Many no.table persons have purposely as- cended the mountains to taste the delights of coasting down this unique line. It is a thril- ling experience, as in some of the steeper por- tions of the track speeds of eighty and ninety miles are often attained by the cars. They are, of course, equipped with powerful brakes, so that, if necessary, the cars can be brought to a standstill, while here and there are sidings on to which they can run should anything be on the line in front of them.

In many respects the railway is the most daring of its kind in the world. Many were the difficulties and dangers which the engineers were called upon to surmount. The surveying party, particularly, met with many thrilling adventures. The work of locating the track among the mountains could often only be car- ried on from niches cut in the rock, to which the adventurous engineer and his instruments were swung in baskets. Indeed, we get an idea of the difficulties encountered in the build- ing of this three-mile railway into the air when It is stated that in its course it passes through 65 tunnels of varyini length, laborioushr cut out of the mountain des, and over 67 bridges, many of them perfect marvels of construction. The line is principally uSed for the conveyance of ore from the great copper mines situated among the mountains here..
