div.head: IOLLI"lIME AT SOUTHPORT.
div.p: A IOLLI"lIME AT SOUTHPORT.

The first fortnight of my holidays I Spent very quietly, only going , for 'walks with - my. friend and her mother, but I did not see nor do anything worth mdntioning. Then came the third week. This was the best of all. At half_ past six on a Monday morning I heard my mother calling " Vera," and up I jumped, because I knew this was the day I was going to Southport to stay till the following Saturday. By a quarter to eight J was ready, waiting for my friend and her mother, with whOm I was going. _ !__

- . At last they came, and off we started for the station. We were only just in time to get Our tickets and get into the train, when the porter on duty shouted "Right away," and then we commenced our journey. When the train was nearing Souhport, the first thing that caught my eye, as I'was looking through the carriage window, vas a, great Stretch of sand hills, reacliing as far as I could see. All of a sudden the train slowed down and into The station we went. The first thing I did was to Pick up my luggage, and out of the carriage .I stepped, and went straight to my lodgings.

The first place I visited after the lodgings Was the sands, where I played with my _friend ciiiite a long time. The sands stretched a very. long way, and they were dotted with happy chil- dren and gay holiday-makers. When I first looked at the sea it was very calm and blue, then by some way or other it became very rough. There 1 saw children piddling, so,, of course, I thought I would do the same. Off came my slippers and stockings, and into the water I went, and it was simply lovely meeting the _waves. 'After half an hour's paddling it was dinner time.

\ After dinner my friend and I visited the amusements. here we had great fun, first in the House of Nonsense, and then in the river eaves, and then at the Pierrot concert.--- I U.-link enjoyed that afternoon the best of all my holi- days.. Tea 'time came a lot too soon each day, but more so did bed time. Each morning I was up at eight o'clbck and out on the sands pad- dling in the water by half-past nine. Tuesday and Wednesday I spent something similar to Monday, on the sands and at the amusements, and at night in the Park in Lord-street.

On Thursday morning, when I was paddling in the water, a "Daily Mail " photographer came up to my friend and I and snap-shoted us. On Thursday afternoon,we visited Church Town, which is a lovely place, and had a very nice sail on the lake. At night we again visited Lord-Stet Park and listened to the band. Thn trees in the Park are all illuminated with small different coloured fairy lamps, and it was a lovely sight. We went home about nine o'clock. Friday passed a lot too quickly. During Saturday morning we went round to have a last look at the sands and amusements. My face was not so bright on Saturday morning as it ,was on the Monday morning I arrived, because I knew I had to leave all the good things behind me. At half-past three I was on my way home, only to think of the happy week I had had at Southport. The last week of my holidays were spent 'at home, like the first and second weeks,, but k am feeling a lot better and happier after a'feW days at the seaside.. VERA JONES, 12, St. Mary-street, Latchford.

A MERRY 1-01:NG HAY-MAKER. I would like to enter your competition, "What I did during my holidays." Our holi- days began on ,the 18th of July and extended to the 18th August. During part of that month I went to Mr. Alker's farm, just across the road. Mr. Alker and his fellow workers were 'cutting and carting the hay. The country was fresh, and refreshing lireezes came over the fields. The sun shone overhead, and we were supplied with .milk to quench our thirst.

We had. great fun jumping over and playing In the hay. When the hay was quite dry we had to Cart it \into another field to rriake two large Stacks. Ido not know when I spent such - a healthy holiday as I did in August. I went to the seaside, but did not enjoy it lialf so • much as the refreshing country. GILBERT COOKSON, • 29, Folly-lane, Warrington.
A HAPPY DAY BY THE SEA.

The happiest day of my holidays was when we went to Blackpool. We had buckets and spades and built castles on the sands. We were paddling also,- and had such fun, with a little dog, which ran into the sea when we threw our spades in, and it brought them back- to us. We' were in the 'great tower and went round the big wheel, and it made you dizzy to look down on the streets below.

We were in the circus and saw a lot of per- forming animals, and game of the tricks they did were very funny and °lever. I was glad to get to the lodgings, I was so tired, but still it was the happiest day.. , _
MAMIE BAYNE, 12, WaiturtoTstreet, Stociiton Heath.
HAPPY TIMES IN THE COUNTRY.

We'did not go to the seaside during our holi- days, because we have only livekt in."beauMul" Bucks since March. .So we have spent much time in the open air; looking around the nice country places,Jaking food with us for a picnic, just as we did at Stockton Heath, when we had picnics ,to the "Denna." We have seen some nice birds here, more plentiful than those at home, and they are beautifully coloured. We have also §een more molehills, new wild flowers and grasses. Then when school commences we are better ready far our nature lessons and di•awin gs. _
WILLIAM and DOROTHY E. REEVES, -6, Beaconsfield Place, Bucks. Newport P4gneii,

ON THE HELTER SKELTER. • • The bes day ih my Holidays wast when I went :to :Southport. When we arriv&l there we went Lou house for dinner. The first thing I went on was the helter-skelter. I WDS dizzy. I went in a snow called "Fairyland" where - some .little 'dwarfs were ,acting as blacksmiths. We Went for a sail in a'boat through the river eaves, sometimes the boat would run against the sides. There were twins with -us who kept crying ii"ecause it was dark. I brought some rock back with me. , LEONARD DICKINSON, 177 Stevenson-street, Warrington. Continued in preceding colurun. ,

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. C. E. Linaker presiding.
CLERK'S ESTIMATE.

The Clerk submitted the estimates for the ensuing half-year. The .general expenses he estimated to be £5,281 and contingencies £1,573, making a total of £6,854. Deducting £1,574, probable balance at the end of the current half- year, there would be a net expenditure of £.5,280 to be provided for. A rate of 6:1-cl. in the X produced £5,280. It was proposed to call for this amount from the various parishes. The estimates- were accepted.

Lazenby; coal, Richard Evans and Co., Hay- dock; coke, Runcorn Gas Company; milk, Mr. T. S. Wardle, Aston. div.head: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION.
N.A. CENTRE.
THE CHAMPIONS AT CHESTER.

Two hundred and sixty-four crack anglers, selected from different associations from all parts of the country, took part in the champion- ship contest, held on the Dee on Monday last. Several anglers travelled 200 miles to take part in the match. The eritry was a record one; the banks of the river were lined for six miles with the competitors. They were divided into .12 sections, and each section of 22 anglers were attended to by a superintendent, a measurer, and a weigher. The signal for starting was the waving of a flag on the iron bridge, and the superintendents ,passed the word along at 11.15 a.m.

Competitors were soon busy with their dif- ferent styles of angling, but the fish were dead off feed, and all the Wiles of 'cracks could not induce them to take the bait. As the contest proceeded, friends from all parts came along the banks with lunch for the anglers. It was to be plainly seen that the chartered steamers would be insufficient. to 'carry all back to Chester, and arrangements were made for them to make a double journey.

div.head: NORTIIERN ANGLERS WIN, BUT ARE DISQUALIFIED.
div.p: NORTIIERN ANGLERS WIN, BUT ARE DISQUALIFIED.

As time wore on it was apparent that no great weight would be registered, and word soon passed along when one angler landed a bream of 21b. 4oz. Then came word of an objection to the same angler for using two hooks.

When time was called at 3.30 the weighers had a somewhat easy task, and all weights were handed in by 4.30. Different opinions as to who Were winners kept the competitors at fever heat, until Mr. Miller read -out the result about five o'clock, as. follows Nottingham Association, 21b. 15oi. lldr. ; 2, Sheffield and District, 21b. 90z. 3dr. ; 3, Leeds Association, 21b. soz. sdr. ; 4, Bradford City, 21b. 4oz. ; 5, Sheffield Amalgamated, 11b. 13oz. 14dr. ; 6, .Hull Association, 11b. 7oz. 9dr. ; 7, Notting- ham Federation, 11b. 70z. 4dr. ; 'B, Boston, 11b. 50z. 14dr. ; 9, Newark Association, 11b. 30z. Bth-.; 10, Northern Anglers, 11b. loz. sth.. Mr. Miller gave out that the Northern Anglers had won easily, with the weight Of 31b. soz. 50., but for the disqualifying of one man, who used two hooks, the rule being one rod, one line, one hook.

div.head: DIFFERENT STYLES OF ANGLING.
div.p: THE DIFFERENT STYLES OF ANGLING.

The London team, with their 'famous roach poles, came in for quite a lot of criticism. The general opinion of Lancashire anglers was that they were not handy enough for our waters. When a fish is caught they need uncoupling, and again when a bait has to be put on, al- though, with tivir tight line, they are pretty smart at striking the fish. Some of the roach poles are 201 t. long, in. six lengths. One Lanca- shire angler remarked that he could walk up the rod and dive off the top length! The Sheffield anglers were the smartest up the river as regards getting in mid-stream. They could cast out from 30 to 40 feet with a single shot on their line, weighing -less than half a dram; but again our locals argue that fish cannot be struck with the same quickness as they can with only about 31t. of line, and they contend that if Sheffield anglers had to have fr6m 30 to 40 fish to win a two hours' match they would soon adopt different 'methods. Some remarked that they have a lot better waters than we have round this part' of the country, And their style may - suit the waters better' than ours. . •If these methods were adopted in the Weaver the fish caught during a twi) hours' contest would (to use an angler's phrase) have to Commit suicide.
The Boston team appeared to our men to be the smartest team. Their- methods are some- what. Similar to ours,. with the exception Of the.

div.head: ZULU WEDDING DANCE.
div.p: ZULU WEDDING DANCE.

A large green clearing in the bushveldt ;, the kraal a congeries of giant beehives in the midst of it; the Indian Ocean lying calm'and peaceful In the sunshine of the quiet murmurous evening of Southern Natal. Such was the scene and its setting.

The men of the bridegroom's party were massed for dancing, having replaced those of the bride's tribe, who had previously danced. They were drawn up in line In a wide semi- circle with shields and sticks, silent under the gaze of their old chief, who exhorted them to beat the other tribe in this that is in reality a rhythmical rendering of a battle scene. In the distance a group of girls, well-propor- tioned, with kilts of curious crepe-like material and bead anklets, giving them a strange simi- larity to a Highland regiment, marched—the bride's party. The bride carried a large knife with which, in sport, she makes the last attempt at her freedom. Suddenly, a quavering swelling into a very ocetin of sound issues from the bronze battalion. A thousand heels come down at once on the earth, which quivers at the sudden onslaught. A thousand sticks hit their respective shields. The haunting, searching melody ebbs and flows In a certain rhythm. The women fall in behind the warriors, clapping their hands in time, and uniting their voices with the men's. The excite- ment increases ;.the men's faces become fiercer; they keep marvellous time with their feet to the singing; perspiration pours from them, ,and their muscles stand out, avd one can imagine the warrior Zulus charging—tile light-boned but muscular and gracefully built Zulu, notwith- standing that he is degenerating.

An occasional shout of the Zulu war-cry, " Sesute," is heard. Anon a warrior springs forward, capers, and a very torrent of words pours from his lips. Is it the fame of bygone warriors he reCites? These emotional exalta- tions were not confined to the young warriors.

Here an old keshler (headman) springs to the front. He is extremely thin; his legs are mere lengths of bone with the skin of the knees thick like a rhino's. He might have been 'one of Chaka's men, the man of blood and maker of the Zulu nation. His ribs almost escape through his skin. In his eye there is the stark look of the visionary. He capers about with marvel- lous , agility for an old man—few Zulus live to be old, but those who do are tough indeed. He shouts and gesticulates. He may be • telling the young warrior of bygone prowess, of fights with the white conqueror some of them of but yesterday, and even remembered by the younger men. When the medicine men gave them charms to turn the bullets into water, they Oelieved,' and rushed straight through the bullets—to death.

Suddenly the old man slows down. The sun is setting. fie stops and goes back to his com- pany. The keshler has grown very old. A white man looking on is strangely touched by the show of barbaric fire, perhaps his own blood responds, being bred of a warlike race far in the .North. Love and war—in such are •all men 'alike. In all things else eaqh his own Individuality.

float. Many of them have their float shotted, as well as their line, with the idea to get down quick for the larger fish. Their rods also are similar td the Lancashire style? from 10ft. Gin. to 121 t., with a free reel. Their ,baits used were creed wheat, India meal, and, for the hoop, yellow, annatta, and white maggot.

div.head: NEXT YEAR.
div.p: NEXT YEAR.

The contest next year is to be fished at Hull, and the Northern Anglers say they have a good chance there. As one of our members re- marked,, he caught 281 b. of bream in two hours' fishing, and that alone speaks for the anglers of this district doing justice to themselves. One great thing is knowing the Water. Our team should be sent on the Saturday previOus to the contest on the Monday. The winning team this year was at Chester on the Monday pre- vious to the contest to get to know the water ,and any little item worth knowing from the natives along the river.

THE DISQUALIFICATION. The disqualified member of the Northern Anglers' Association—who, by the Way, was not a Warrington representative—when interviewed after the contest as to why he used two hooks, said that in the excitement he quite forgot what the rule was, he being used to the rule of one rod, one line, and not more than two hooks. He said: "If I had any intention to evade a rule I could easily have done so, as it•was fully 20 minutes, after I landed my bream that the steward drew my attention- to the fact that two hooks.was illegal; and if would be reported and probably disqualified. I could easily have taken the top hook off after landing My fish, and nobody would have known about it. But the one hook rule never struck me, although my captain, Mr. Jolley, told me. about it on the Sunday morning. I tool the fish on my bottom hook, with double maggot, and I think would have got it just the same if my top Nook .had been off. lam very sorry, this thing has happened, and. I wish to apologise to the remainder of my team for losing them the cup and medals, besides the English championship. How I will go on in St. Helens amongst my clubmates, I don't know, as it is all my own carelessness that our team are not the cham- pions.'! A. S. •

div.head: POLLUTION AND FISH DESTRUCTION
div.p: POLLUTION AND FISH DESTRUCTION

Mr. Peter Knight, of Warrington, read a paper on "The Pollution. of Rivers and Canals" at a meeting of the Fresh Water Preservation League, held at the Bear and Billet, Chester, on Saturday evening. He referred to the Bridge- water Canal at Warrington, and illustrated how the weeds, when allowed to grow, acted as a filter. He prodUced a sample of water taken from the Old . Quay Canal on September 4th. This canal is about three miles long, and Mr. Knight said that when the sample was taken there were over 100,000 fish, all a quarter of a pound and upwards in weight, which had died simply from Pollution of the water. The causes of pollution included. tar-spraying on roads and the laying of calcium chloride. The tatter. chemical was a chief cause, because it was more easily dissolved and: got into neigh- bouring w-atercourses. Fillan (Manchester) said that a short time ago he took out of the River Dee at Trevor two salmon, each weighing over •101 b. They . were both dead, but in good condition. The water bailiff of that district had said that they had taken a good quantity of dead fish out of the - water through pollution. .

Walker, of Sheffield, pointed out that the anglers there had. formed a Board, to protect rivers from pollution, 'but the movement had been smothered by the manufacturers. A vote of thanks having been accorded Mr. Knight, it -was decided that the members should try to collect evidence and take action in any specific case of pollution.

div.head: MOST VALUABLE FRUIT TREE.
div.p: MOST VALUABLE FRUIT TREE.

What is probably the most valuable tree in the'world is an alligator pear tree at Whittier, Cal., which netted its owner a profit of 3,206 dollars in one year. This tree,was plantCd in 1905, and began bearing in its fourth year. In 1912 it bore 3,000 pears which sold for 1,500 dollars, while the sale of buds during Che same year 'amounted to 1,706 dollars, making the total given above. The tree is a seedling, the seed having been planted with a quantity of other seed which had been imported, presum- ably from Mexico. Another tree which was planted at the same time, and Which stands close to this phenomenal bearer, has never borne more than 50 pears in a soason.
THE CYCLIST'S EOTE BOOK
Delights of Cycling in the
Winter-time.

div.head: BY "SILVER STREET."
div.p: BY "SILVER STREET."
TO A.M.C.

I do not see any reason to put your cycle up anywhere for the winter season. I presume it is not an "all black" model, as all cycles should be in this age, or you would not want to lay it on one side. Anywhere in a dry corner of a bedroom, especially against an inside wall, ought to do, with the bright parts covered with a thin rubbing of vaseline, renewed' Once a month, so my dealer tells me. I never had that experience. In any case, whether the tyres are off the ground or not, they will suffer, for rubber is like a good many human affairs, it is best preserved by being used. A small paint brush quite full of vaseline daubed thick on the hubs and other out-of-the-way bright parts'used to be my plan for the winter. - It gets covered with dust, and then in the spring, a paraffin rag takes it all off, and the brightness was undimmed.. But the delights of cycling are quite as great in winter as in Summer. A ride to Beeston Castle is a revelation of Che'shire in a new coat. The smell of the fallen leaves us you ride through Whitley, through Delamere and Beeston, is charming; the air on the top of the hill, with its pleasant nip, gives you an appetite for the tea you have ordered at the bottom, and the relish is all the more because you get that same tea by lamplight in the wooden hut. The sunsets you can enjoy from Appleton, from Beeston, from Alderley Edge, and especially from Peckforton Hills are alto- gether more beautiful than in 'the _misty even- ings of summer, and there is a new field open to the cyclist of the 'north of Warrington, for the contrast between the drab workmanship of Lancashire and the loveliness south of the river disappears, and Leigh, Wigan, Bolton, Pres- cot and even St. Helens do not look so bad in winter.

Widnes? Well, Widnes attacks ()tier organs that act as keenly in one season as another, so Widnes lies on a different plane. Do you know .the song of the redbreast? Well, he is practising now for the November concerts. I often wonder why Nature has left us one beautiful song for !Tie dull December (days, but it shows how good she has been to us in, Britain and France and Germany. Do you know the beautiful rosette of the thistle, as it crowds the grass and every 'other plant on one side, so as to spread itself for all the light it can get? That can only be seeri,on the bank-s in winter, and the beautiful fernlike leaves of the wayside umbellifers are ever so much pret- tier when they are small, than in the growing season, when they are as tall as a child. No, there is only one class of travellers that I pity in winter, and that is. the motor cyclists, who have to keep themselves warm as best they can, and the. chauffeurs, of course. So' that the roads are freer and safer to us, because the motors are met at rarer intervals, and there are no flies! The only time we are liable to
feel cold is on setting off after 'tea. A good plan is to put in your low gear, and the quick pedalling soon puts that right.,
PUNCTURES.

At night we are obliged, to keep to the main roads, and so escape these ,nuisances to some extent. But I will add two remarks to those of last week's ,notes. They are about putting patches inside the air • tube, as well as outside. No, we don't need to get inside the air tube to do that. Before putting solution over the prick, squeeze some through it. It soon dries inside and prevents the outside patch, blowing off. You can easily feel by the stickiness of the two inner surfaces whether you have managed the inside repair. When a rip or a burst occurs a patch ought always to be put inside. The white sulphur coating inside the tube, and/the outside coating, too, is most easily removed by a minute bit of rag soaked in paraffin. This bit of rag is easily prepared on setting out, and kept in a scrap of paper in the tool bag.

- To fix the inner patch a suitable piece is rolled up and inserted dry through the hole. It is then worked into its place and held there until the solution is squeezed and rubbed over it. Notice that no solution must touch either patch or tube until the inner patch is centrally fixed in .its place. , The outer patch is then easily placed.

'An amateur can easily splice a new length of tube into an old one, if he gets about 1.1 inches thoroughly cleaned inside and outside with petrol or paraffin.. Then the dry tubes must be fixed in their places before the,scilution is introduced. It must be rubbed over thor- oughly NVith the finger.

White Star kicked off and were defending the railway goal. From a scrummage Warren broke nicely -away and got his threequarters going, but offside tactics spoiled Griffiths of a splendid chance to get over at the corner. Warren was repeatedly very tricky. Bylands' pressed for ' some time, and the Star defence had all their work cut out to keep the " Wiremen " from scoring. White Star at length got their passing machinery into motion, and a fine run was made by the left threequarter, but Bramhall brought him down. , The Star were now giving the " Wiremen " a warm time of it and their for- wards rushed the ball over the line, but the point was not allowed by the referee. Bylands' were then penalised for obstruction, and Jolley was not successful with the kick. Rylands' once more had a turn on the attack, and a fine bout of passing between Gallop, Warren, Carter and A. Horrocks. was spoiled by the latter kick- ing too hard, the ball going dead. Some good forward work was now indulged in by both sides and play was very exciting. The White Star half-backs eventually got possession, and, beating their opponents, once more got their threequarters going. The ball travelled along to the right wing man—BrOwn—who showed a capital turn of speed, and managed to elude Griffiths and score a beautiful try-

A Faulty Kick at Goal.

The goal-kick, however, failed. Mid-field play was now indulged in for some time, and then Sid. Carter made a splendid kick and follow-up and tackled the Star full-back beTore he could make any return. White Star were now kept busy on the defence, and time after time 'Viands' were on the point of scoring, but faulty passing spoiled their chance. For a glaring case of obstruction the White Star were penalised in front of goal,.but Warren failed to add the goal points. Another forward pass again spoiled the " Wiremen," after which the Star got away • once more and were almost over, but Bramhall (who, by the way, was playing a fine game) again came to the rescue and saved splendidly. Shortly after this the whistle went for half-time, and the White Star led by one try (three points) to Rylands' nil. The play throughout this half had been very even, but White Star showed the better passing, the " Wiremen " failing to get into their stride properly.

div.head: RENWICK MAKES THE PEACE.
div.p: RENWICK MAKES THE PEACE.

The little difference of opinion, which in some quarters has been magnified into a matter of grave importance to the club, which has existed between Renwick and the committee has now been amicably settled. The player met the committee prior to the game on Saturday, ex- pressed his satisfaction with their terms, and signed on. It will not be long before we see this useful man in the team, and his advent will prove of service. This may mean a re-arrangement of some departments 'of the thirteen, and possibly Brookes will go into the front rank, where, I am certain, he would prove of much value. At the time of writing, it was not known whether Ren- wick would be fit enough to turn out to-day for the match at Swinton, but we shall see when the team is finally selected.

RENWICK AND TRANTER TO PLAY. Warrington are taking their strongest side to Swinton to-day, and 1 hope to see them re- turn with a victory. A great game may be anticipated, but with a greatly strengthened team, Warrington ought to be able to more' than hold their own against the home 'side. Renwick .will make a welcome re-appearance in the threequarter line. He will have for his companion in the centre, Tranter, who has now recovered from his illness, and with Bradshaw and Davis on the wings, this line nould prove a formidable one. Otherwise there is no change in the side, which will be :
WARRINGTON. Jolley. Bradshaw, Renwick, Tranter, Davis. Nicholas, Ruddick. Thomas, Chesters, Fearnley, Cox, Clare, Green.

div.head: WARRINGTON "A" STILL WINNING.
div.p: WARRINGTON "A" STILL WINNING.

The Warrington "A" men are still out for scalps, and they are getting them. Their latest victims were the 'Broughton Rangers, whom the Warringtonians defeated on their own pitch by 1 goal 3 tries (11 points) to 3 points. It was a good game from the Warrington point of view, and at half-time Warrington led by eight points to nil. The visitors added an additional try in the second half, and the Rangers also scored.

Baker was again conspicuous. Every game he plays seems to show an improvement. The way he outwitted the home back and dashed over with a pretty try, was one of the features of the game. A. Brown and Douglas played a smart game at half-back. The Warrington forwards all worked well, and J. Brown was most reliable at full-sack.
Warrington "A" Team Against Swinton.

- The meeting of Warrington "A" with the Swinton Reserves should produce a fine game at Wilderspool to-day, and there should be a good "gate." The home team will have Way- well, who did sp much useful work for the seniors on Saturday, back in his old position. Dickenson will figure in the threequarter line, and ought to make that department even stronger than it is. The teams will be : Warrington—J. Brown; Waywell, Dainteth, Dickenson and Baker; A. Brown and Douglas ; Harmer, Naylor, Boardman, Critchley, Blun- dell and Clark. Swinton—Flynn ; Grice, Whitehead, Kilgariff, and Holland; Brook and Heaton; Booth, Curd- den, Daley, Holden, Moss, Riley and Shedlock.

THREE COUNTY MEN. Jolley and Chester Selected. Three Warrington men figure in the inter- county match to be played at Manchester on Monday. Ruddick, as I stated last week, has been chosen to represent his native county Of Cumberland, and we will thus sec him in a team which is opposing that in which his club- mates, Jolley and Chester, are expected to play a great game. All three well deserve the honour conferred upon them. - The choice of Jolley and Chester to play for Lancashire is a honour to the club, as well as to the players.
Ben Jolley : The Smart "Little 'Un."

Ben Jolley .has been described as the " star " back. The county has now recognised the fact. He is a natkve of Runcorn, and first learned his ,art, now finally developed, with the White Star, and was mainly responsible' for the defeat of Bylands' in a Lancashire Junior Cup final.
Jack Chester: A USeful Heavy-weight.

Jack Chester has waited a long time, but the wefirmerited honour has come at last. He IS a native of Warrington and learned his football with Whitecross in a Works Competition. He joined the Warrington team in 1908, and for five years has played honestly for his club.
J. Ruddick, who plays for 'Cumberland.
Learned the game at Egremont, Cumberland, and played for Hunslet for two seasons. Came to Warrington last season and is already a most popular player. One of the smarteSt half-backs in the country.
RYLANDS' OVER THE FIRST STILE. They Win the Junior Cup Match.

Bylands' Recreation tiad Runcorn White Star as visitors to the Gorse Y-lane enclosure, in the first round of the Lancashire Junior Cup Com- petition, on Saturday. The "gate" was not a very large one, considering the great rivalry that exists between these two clubs, but there is no doubt that had Warrington been playing away instead of entertaining Broughton Rangers at

div.head: Lively Second Half.
div.p: A Lively Second Half.

The play was full of incident in the second half, and at times was rather rough. The tackling of the Star was very keen, with the result that the attendants were often called upon, Warren, Griffiths and Brandwood having to receive attention at their hands. The " Wiremen " did most of the pressing and played a much improved game than in the initial half, their combination being much better. From a breakaway A. Horrocks scored, and Bramhall landed the goal, thus giving Rylands' a lead of two points. This reverse put fresh life into the Star men and they tried hard to bring about a score, but could not penetrate the defence. Carter then got away for Rylands' and scored a fine try, but Bramhall failed with the kick. Result : Rylands' Recreation, one goal two tries (eight points) ; Runcorn White Star, one try (three points).
Dramhall Has a Day put.

For the " Wiremen " Bram- hall played a splendid game at full-back, his kicking and tackling being all that could be desired: Of the threvuarters, Carter and Griffiths were an effective left wing, and the former showed rare resource. A. and F. Horrocks did many smart things, but the centre would have done better if he had served the wing man more instead of kicking too hard and thus allowing the ball to go dead. Warren was a very tricky half-back and got away repeatedly, and he and his partner were much smarter than the White Star pair. ' It would be hard to individualise amongst the forwards, each man playing his best. For White Star, Brown played well on the right wino and his try was well deserved. The full- back, too, showed rare skill in fielding and kicking the ball, but seemed to fall away to- wards the end of the game. The forwards were well matched, though Rylands' got the ball away from the pack much more often than the White Star.

Backhouse ; G. Ogden, S. Cooper, H. Welsby, R. Bibby, Well- don and Myles. Reserves: Back, T. Scarfs- brick; forwards, Jackson and Myles.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

The club runs of Saturday were chiefly of the " blackberrying " sort, and beyond the Winning of the mile break of the Boundary Harriers by o: promising runner, H. Lonsdale, there was little deserving of special comment:
'Warrington Athletic Club.

The local people have fixed Tuesday next, 7.15 p.m., at their pavilion, as the time and place for the annual ,general meeting, and as their energetic honorary secretary, Mr. C. 'Berry, has intimated to the committee that pressure of business entirely precludes the'possibility of his taking any official position, likely to make calls on his time, it is of the utmost importance that all members should attend the meeting. Subject to approval of the meeting, the opening run will be fixed for Saturday next, so new members and intending members should keep in touch with some Of the old brigade, as it is essential to start properly if beginners are to obtain full enjoyment and benefits of the sport.

div.head: OLYMPIC APPEAL.
div.p: THE OLYMPIC APPEAL.
The Views of Lord Ilarris on Professionalism.

In acknowledging one of the subscriptions to the Olympic Fund, Lord Harris writes :—ln these days of keen competition, success can be secured only by drganisation, and organisation costs money. As a matter of fact, there is only a difference of degree between the wide-reaching and expensive organisation necessary to pre- pare a team of British athletes for this Olympic competition, and the organisation that is neces- sary even to put the best eleven of a small public school on to the cricket field with some prospect of success. Nor can I see that we . run any serious risk of ,introducing ariything novel in the 'shape of professionalism.. For :instance, some people suppose that it is a novelty for amateur cricketers to take their ex- penses. That is a delusion. I can prove that as long ago as sixty years some amateurs took quite as much expenses as the professional cricketers who were their comrades. The ama- teur does not make himself a professional by taking his expenses. He does not engage him- self, as does the professional, to do this, that, or the other for a term of weeks or months

I quite expected before ,I Fignecl the aPpeal that there would be some such opposition as has displayed itself, but opportunity having been given for that, the rest of us who agree that we must take part in the competition, and that organisation is essential, can now set to work to make the fund a success, and for your sup- port, and the broad view you take of what this country had better under the circumstances do, we are most grateful.
Has Ruddick been taking dancing lessons? His side-stepping is worthy of the ballroom. And when he side-steps he gets room for the ball. _ _

Some dancing masters would like to know how He manages to do this fascinating step. The Bangers did not like it at all. Waywell got away well several times. Although called in unexpectedly, he played nicely. Neither Bradshaw nor he got many chances. Had they got the ball more often there Would have been tries. Where was Jolley's goal-kicking boots? He was not up to usual at this work.

It was very good Warrington "A " to Win away. And that, too, with Waywell an absentee. Eleven points to three was good indeed. The Bangers did not like it, but- Warrington did not consult their dislikes. Had the goal-kicking been better The score would have been higher. Still, 11 points was something to be going on with. Baker and the Browns were lively members. What did Critchley think of the tackle? It was a bit hot, but he didn't mind it. Has the " A " team lost Waywell for good?

Have the " A " men fixed upon a definite score For all the matcheS during the season? It seems remarkable that out of three meetings They should have won two by 11 points-to 3, And the other by 10 points to three. Strange! Shall we now call them the " eleven " men
Instead of the rollicking "bhoys of thirteen "7 Swinton are to face our youngsters at Wil- derspool.
Will this result be 11 points to 3, or a trifle more?
Perhaps our lads may make a change And give us 22 points to 6, or 33 points to 9. If they keep on the multiple they will be all right.

Ilylands jumped into the second round of the Junior Cup. They won a stiff match by five clear points. It was a hot game all the way through. The spectators became more excited than the players. They should, however, try to be a " leetle " - less abusive.

There are a few youths who might be taught .a lesson. That kick was a bit too hard, A. Horrocks. Gently does the trick and the kick spoilt a try. The threequarters were much too fond of "forwards," But for this the Rylands' score would have been taller. Bramhall was in 'the pink of form, wasn't he? His kicking and tackling made the Star men "white."
Bravo, Brothers Horrocks, you did great things.

The crowd appreciatEd the work of the " twins." Warren is b. tricky man at half-back. He smartly dodged the men of the Star. The forwards were a spicy lot. They did well both in the tight and the loose. Are !Viands' to get all the way to the final? The prophets seem to think it will be so. • Who has made a five to one wager That the cup, as well as the shield, Will be found at Gorsey-lane this year? Perhaps it will happen so—and p'rh'ps not.

div.head: ORFORD ATHLETIC v. ORFORD JUNIORS.
div.p: ORFORD ATHLETIC v. ORFORD JUNIORS.

Owing to both the above teams originating from the same district, there was _a good deal of interest in the above fixture, and a keen match was anticipated. The Athletic won the toss and played with the hill in their favour. Jackson started the ball rolling, anct the Jtiniors at once made an attack on their opponents' goal, and O'Day drew the first. blood for the Juniors. This .reverse made both teams play more vigorously,-,but the Juniors continued to show the better form, and the Athletic backs defended their charge in great style. After even play in midfield, Jackson, the Juniors' centre, received the ball, beat the opposing backs and scored the second\ goal for the Juniors. This second reverse made the Athletic players more desperate, and altering their trio- tics, they broke through the Juniors' defence, and A. Woodhouse reduced the lead. The Ath- letic, by their, rushing attacks, equalised the scores, S. WoOdhouse doing the needful. At half-time the score was two goals each:

On resuming the Juniors again took up the attack, and after some smart passing, Riley added a third point. From now the Juniors appeared to have got the measure of their oppo- nents, and kept up a continual attack on their goal, *here Slater gave a good display of goal, keeping, and could not be blamed for the score put up against him: Jackson, Retford and Houghton added to the score, and the game ended: Orford Juniors, 7 goals; Orford Athletic, 2 goals. Mr. C. S. Essenhigh refereed the game much to the satisfaction of both teams.

div.head: PADGATE UNITED JUST BEATEN.
div.p: PADGATE UNITED JUST BEATEN.

_ The above club played Dapesbury Parish A.F.C. at home, and were just beaten by 4-3 in a pleasant and well-contested game, the issue being in doubt right up to the last minute, when a fine goal from the head of the visitors' outside right had the home custodian com- pletely beaten.

Padgatse were best served by their outside right, whose centres were not made full use of: Two fatal slips on the part of the home goal- keeper contributed chiefly to the defeat, although the visitors, who played the open game well, were full value for their win; as they recognised that after recent heavy rains, short passing was quite out of the question. This afternoon , Padgate travel to Preston Brook, and will be represented by the follow- ing: J. Warburton; W. Wadsworth (captain) and R. Hankinson ; \V. Cooper, W. Whitlow and P. Rigby; John Houghton, A. Derbyshire, James Houghton, T. Williams and S. Hardman. Train leaves Bank Quay at 2.55 p.m.

div.head: SHOTS AT THE GOAL.
div.p: SHOTS AT THE GOAL.
A good goal getter is Meachin, of Orford St John's.
in three matches played, he has put on 'ten goals to his own account.
Shuttleworth, of SL Barnabas', did the "hat ,rick "last Saturday.
Leah, of the sarne team, finds the net every week.
The Adult School were unfortunate with Weaver liefining Company.
They only shared the points, after having the best of the game. Lees, Challinor, Smith, Fogg and Webb were the corers in the Latchford V. Knutsford Mi. match.

Crosfield'S Bees. disappointed their supporters. by losing to Broadheath at home. Constable and Quinn scored fine goals for the visitors, and Foster rei)lied for the Bees. Crosfield's Bees. "A" team paid their first visit to Penketh Bee.
They found the Great Sankey boys in fine trim.
Booth, H. Ditchfield and Poulton were the scorers for the boys., .
Herbert Ditchfield is going to be the utility man at Penketh.
Supporters of the Latchford team say that the Knutsford M.T. team are no class. '
The Latchford ePub have the best forward line they have had for several seasons.
Dykes, of the Adult School, was the best for- \\-nrd, and scored two lovely goals.
Warham, of the Excelsiors, was a great stumbling block to the Emmanuel forwards. Orford st. John's have played three matches and won them.
They have scored 20 goals against none in the Warrington and District League (Second Division). •
The Bank Quay boks say they are 'going to get their first- whacking at Lovely-lane. The Soldiers from Orford Barracks are sure of a great reception at Weston Point.

div.head: Lively Games in the Warr:nat.-on and District. League contests.
div.p: Lively Games in the Warr:nat.-on and District. League contests.
LATCHFORD PRESENTS A WINNING SiDE.

In last Saturday's games both our senior clubs in the North Cheshire League were engaged on their own grounds. The Latchford Club had The Knutsford M.I. as visitors, but they were not 'equal to the home players, for after the first 20 minutes of the game Latchford had the best of it, and they easily annexed both points. The Latchford Committee are to be complimented on the abilities of the team they have now got together. They have the best forward line they haVe had for several seasons past, backed up with a capable half-back line. 'choir weakness lies in the rear division, which they are hoping to strengthen for the coining I cup-ties. I The Crosfleld's Recreation team did not sus- tain the form they displayed the previous week, and after 4 hard and even game they had to I acknowledge defeat again on their own ground. I The visitors proved themselves to be the ,better trained Players, while the home team Only finished their work very weakly. Constable and Quinn scored two capital goals for the visitors, and Foster scored for the home team. Birchall performed very creditably in the home , goal.
By 64 Linesman."

brought into the forward line and Gardiner in- troduced at centre-half. The home team won the toss and the game started in their favour. Some smart passing movements were seen amongst the Great Sankey forwards and at the end of ten minutes' play they opened the scor- ing. Houghton, on,the extreme left, made some fine centres, thus causing'the visiting defenders .a great amount of trouble. At the interval the home team were leading by two goals to nil. On resuming, it was soon evident that thii visitors could not do much with the home defence and they were confined chiefly in their 'own half. The Great Sankey forwards added three 'More goals. Crosfield's have to thank their goalkeeper for the way in which he did his duty between-_ the uprights, clearing his lines when he appeared to be well beaten, the spectators cheering him for his brilliant saves. The final score was: Great Sankey, five goals; Crosileld's, none. The goals were obtained by Booth (two), Ditchfleld (two) and Poulton (one).
Adult School v. Weaver Refining Company.

These clubs opened their League-engaeme-fits in Victoria Park, with the following players:— Adult School—Welsby ; Garnett and Spencer; Leigh, Ridyard and Clark; Scarisbrick, Hunter, Webb, Banner and Dykes. Weaver Refining Company—Bean; D. Woodward and Aspey ; Wilkinson, Brookes and Newton; Powell, Les- ter, Evans, A. Johnston and J. Johnston. Referee, Mr. T. Pittam. The game was very fast and evenly contested, both teams playing very, hard and attacking in turn, only to be driven back by the respective •lefen•krs. Ihe Adult School players had slightly the I€st of the exchanges, owing to the grand wing play of Dykes, the School leading at half-time by one goal to nil.

On turf-ling round the• Weaver boys livened up a bit, but the School lads were the first to score, Dykes again doing the needful. Nettled by these reverses, the visitors made a hot attack on the home goal, where Garnett had the Lis - fortune to breast the ball through his own coal, giving the visitors their first point. Encour- aged by their success, the visitors came again, and after several shots at goal they drew Welsby away from his charge and Powell scored the equaliser.

The game was now fought in ding-dong fashion by both teams, but Beans was not to be beaten again, and when the whistle blew the game ended with the score two goals each. Dykes, of Adult School, and Beans and Powell, of the Weaver, showed up most prominently for their respective sides.

div.head: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Latchford's Easy Win.
div.p: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Latchford's Easy Win.

- The Latchford Club opened their season's fixtures at Thelwall-lane with a match against Knutsford M.I. in the above competition. The home club was represented by: Kite; Robinson and Broadhurst; Downs,- Webb and Carter; Smith, Challinor, Lees, Fogg and Taylor. The visitors won the toss and Lees kicked off, the opening exchanges being equally divided. Dur- ing the first twenty minutes some good play was shown, after which the homesters got the measure of their opponents and Lees scored the first point for the home team. Challinor scored a second, and at half-time the home side were leading by two goals to nil. On resuming, the visitors made strenuous efforts to reduce the lead, but: their attempts were of no avail, the home defenders being too strong for their attack. On.one occasion Kite, the Latchford custodian, was penalised for carrying the ball, and from the ensuing free- kick the visitors sent the ball into the net. The point was disallowed, owing to the ball not having been played by a second player. The home team. continued to have the best of play, and further goals were scored by Fogg (two), Challinor, Smith and Webb (one each). 'Latch- ford •ran out easy winners by seven goals to none. The visitors were best served by their half-backs `and goalkeeper, who made •several good saves during the game.
Crostield's Recreation v. Broadheath.

The match was played at Folly-lane before a fair sprinkling of spectators. The game was very tame for the. first ten minutes. Then the visitors made an attack, and, from a good pass- ing movement, Constable scored. From the kick-off lroadheath continued to have the best of the game, and gained a couple of corners, but they could not improve upon them, and after the home goal had several narrow escapes from downfall play was carried on in mid-field.

The Recs. now showed some- improvement in their methods, and Foster, working for a posi- tion, scored a grand goal, thus equalising. Quinn, the visitors' centre-half, scored again. Half-time: Broadheath, two goals; Crosfield's Recreation, one goal..

On resuming, the play was very even, each goal in turn being attacked. Birchall did good work for the Recs. Each. team then indulged in a lot of big kicking and there was very little combination. Near the finish the home team made a confident appeal for "hands" in the penalty area, but the referee ignored it, and the game ended: Broadheath, two goals; Cros- field's Recreation, one goal.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE NOTES. The First Division.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE NOTES. The First Division.

The Adult School and the Weaver Refining Company opened their League engagements at Victoria Park, where a hard and even game was witnessed. The fact that each side scored twice was a fair indication of the run of the play. Thus the sharing of points was satisfactory to both clubs.

At the, Penketh Recreation' Ground, Great Sankey and Crosfield's " A " teams were opposed to each other, and, owing to the rivalry which has already arisen between the clubs, their supporter § turned Up in large numbers to wit- ness the game, but they were somewhat dis- appointed in the display shown. The score of five goals to none in favour of the home team clearly indicates the one-sided nature of the game. The visiters were outplayed, except in goals where Jones gave a very good display, and it was owing to his abilities that CroStiold's , got off so well.
Second Division.

14 the* Second Division the Orford st. John's team had a comfortable win over their near neighbours, Fairfield, whom they defeated by seven goals to mine. \ Thus far their forwards have shown their 'ability to get goals, as in three matches they 'have' placed the ball in the net 20 times, against none by their opponents.

Fairfield United were at home to St. Barna- bas', but they had to retire defeated by four goals' to nil. The visitors were always able to hold the • home team well in hand, and were never really extended in their attempts at de- fending their goal. • The game between Excelsior and Emmanuel at Bewsey-road was very keenly contested, and although the score of 3-1 was in favour of the home teain, the visitors played ,up to them closely. The home' team excelled hi: -their shooting abilities and owe their victory to that alone. -
Padgate United. received a visit from Dares- bury Parish F.C. and got a surprise with ,the exhibition of the visitors; who won the match by -four goals to three.
._, Stockton Heath 'paid a visit to LYmm played a friendly game with the Your Men's Institute F.C., and returned with, q vieUrY bY 10 goals to nil.
SOME OF THE FIRST LEAGUE GAMES.
Great Sankey V. Crosfield Recreation "A."

The above match was the opening game of the home team's fixtures on the Penketh Recrea- tion Ground, and owing, to the keen rivalry which has sprung an between the clubs there was, a crowd of 300 spectators when the game started. The following players turned out:— Great Sankey--COughoon ; Glover and Caldwell; Ireland,- Gardiner and Payne ;• Darlington, Ditchileld, Booth, Poulton and Houghton. Crosfield"s—Jones ; Hoyle and Calagan ; Scott, Pagett .and Jackson ;- Howard, Rowlands, Walsh, Farrell and piddall. Referee, Mr. B. Gough, Widnes.
Owing to Midge being dropped, Ditelitield was

div.head: GAMES IN THE SECOND DIVISION. Fairfield v. St. Barnabas'.
div.p: GAMES IN THE SECOND DIVISION. Fairfield v. St. Barnabas'.

The above match was•played at Orford-road before a fair number- of supporters. Challinor kicked off for the home team and even play ensued; both defenders playing well for a while. Then the home defenders made several weak returns, and the visiting forwards took possession of their chances and swarmed round the .home goal. There Bibby played a very cool game and proved himself equal to " the emergency. After end-to-end play, Vernon, on the extreme left, made a grand run and finished with a capital centre to Brown, who made a judicious pass to Shuttleworth, which enabled the latter to open the score for the visitors. From the centre kick St. Barnabas' made an- other attack on the home goal. Shelmardine handled the ball in the penalty area, and from the ensuing kick Shuttleworth made no mis- take, Bibby having no chance with the shot. Half-time arrived with the visitors leading by two goals to nil. On chahging ends play was very keen, the home team doing their utmost to reduce the lead against them, but the visitors were not to be denied, and after 14 minutes' play Wareham, with a long shot from neat the half-way line, hit the upright ,and the ball went slowly into the net. Bibby, being taken by surprise, made no effort to save. This reverse upset the home players, and some wild kicking was indulged in. A very bad mistake by Dolphin let in Shuttleworth, who scored with a fine drive. The game ended in favour of the visitors by four goals to nil.

Teams :=Fairfleld--Bibby ; Rowlands and Shelmardine,;Bebbington,Appleton and Dolphin; Gleave, Downes, Challinor, Burns and Simcock. St. Barnabas'—Bevan ; Forster and Spruce; Buttery, Shuttleworth and Wareham; Ryan, Maddock, Brown; Holt and Vernon. Referee, Mr. G. Rushton.
Excelsior v. Emmanuel.

This match was played at Bewsey, on the ground of the former. The following players lined out :—Excelsior—J. Rigby; Holcroft and Warham ; O'Neil, Spencer and Hunt; Walker, Leah, G. FI. Cox, Holmes and E. Hughes. Emmanuel—T. Knight.; Harrison and Harding; Wainwright, Hatton and Eyres ; Lawless, New- ton, A. Hughes, Isherwood and E. Green. Referee, Mr. H. L. Clayton. The opening exchanges .of this match were very even, and play was chiefly in mid-field, each team fighting hard for the upper hand, and this resulted in Emmanuel losing several splendid openings, through too -eager shooting. The Excelsior men played a cool \game, and Leah opened the score for them; while in an- other, attack on the visitors' goal, Harrison kicked into his own net. Half-time: Excelsior, two goals; Emmanuel, nil. The second half was resumed in determined fashion,, both sides attacking in turn, with the Excelsior's having rather the best of the ex- changes. T. Knight, the visitors' custodian, was the stumbling block to the home forwards. He made some daring saves, several times tak- ing thO ball from' the feet of his opponents. W. Leah and A. Hughes scored for their respective sides, and the visitors failed from a penalty, which Rigby was successful in clearing. TIN final whistle blew with the scores: Excelsior, three goals; Emmanuel, one goal.
Orford St. John's v. Fairfield.

This match was played on the St. John's ground, before. a good concourse of spectators. The following players lined out.:—Orford. St. John's—J. Forbes; Smith and W. Millward ; J. Denny, L. .Atherton and E. Mathews.; J. Smith, T. Tickle, A. Meachin, S. Hankinson and T. Sudell. Dainteth ; B. Byrani and S. Jackson; G. Webb, F. DO and J. Hal- lowes ; F. Taylor, P. Titley, C. Taylor, F. Osborne and 11. Bates. ,Beferee, Mr. George Baraber.

The game started very evenly and a fast pace was set up, the defence on both Sides clearing their slines with good kicking, and the half- backs keeping the respective forwards well in check. Close on half-time the Orford forwards broke through and scored 'their only point in the first 45 minutes' play. On changing ends, the home team played strongly* and scored again. The visitors' defence, owing to the stron attack against them, began • to waver, and they allowed St.

John's to score two simple goals. After these reverses, the visitors, on two or three occa- sions, were unfortunate in not scoring, but they fell away -again towards the finish, and when the final whistle blew they retired defeated by seven goal's to none. The scoters were: Nfeachin (three), Millward, J. Smith, Hankin- son and Sudell (one each).

ST. HELENS SUNDAY SCHOOL LEAGUE. Burtonwood Wesleyans V. Ilaydock Independents. This match, in the above competition, took place at Newton Common, the ground of the Wesley-tins, when, owing to a delay in the train service, the game was twenty minutes late in starting. Players Burtonwood : Welsby ; Morris )Ind Griffiths; Eaton, Eaton and Taylor; Collins, Connor,. Collins, Bothwell and Griffiths. Independents: Lloyd; Burrows and Mayer. ; Cunliffe, Livesley and Mercer; Barnett, 3. Stevens, Roberts, Swift and Mason. Referee, J. Smith. Owing to the visitors having been suc- cessful in their previous games, a good crowd lined the playing area, when the visitors, win- 'fling the toss, defended the Common goal. It was early seen that both teams were out to do their best, and the ball travelled from end to end at a quick rate, the players contesting every inch. Livesley and S. Collins, midway in the first half, got at loggerheads with .each other, and were sent off for fighting. The action had its effect on the players, and the game pkoceeded more satisfactorily. When half-time was called the score sheet was blank.

On. resuming, the game was keenly fought. The defences of both, teams -cleared their lines in fine style, and the opposing forwards made strenuous efforts'. to score, but fhey could not break through. Lloyd, the visitors' goalkeeper, gave away two free kicks in his own area for carrying the ball, but the home team failed to improve on them. The game ended without either side being able to score. The Independ- ents thus kept their record sheet clean. Morris., Taylor, Welsby, Eaton and Collins, for the home team, and Lloyd, Burrows, Mayer, Lives- ley, Stevens and Mason played very well for their respective sides.

div.head: Mr. J. Kelp Hardie Criticises the Attitude of the
div.p: Mr. J. Kelp Hardie Criticises the Attitude of the
Syndicalist Supporters.
THE QUESTION OF LABOUR CANDIDATES.

The great attraction at the Labour demonstra- tion held in the Parr Hall, Warrington, on Thursday evening, was Mr. J. Keir Hardie, M.P., the chairman of the Independent Labour Party. Still there was not a large crowd to welcome the " star "of the Labour world. The hall at the start was scarcely half tilled, the wet night evidently militating against a better attendance.. WAIIDMAN, who prOSided, said the meeting was to celebrate the 21st anniversary of the organisation of the Independent Labour party, which had created an intelligent interest in politics that no organisation ever created in the history of their times. - We, he continued, in Warrington, might not, from a Socialist and Labour point of view, have made the strides Accomplished in sonic centres. We might be described as the "black spot of the Mersey," but this I want to soy, knowhig the men, the conditions end the public opinion of Our town, that as 'things are to-day, as ours men are organising indusliialty,- and even politically, that whether the General Election comes. next year or the year after, the Labour party will be able to give Such an account of itself that the other political forces will have to seriously reckon with it. (Applause.) Mr. J. H. HUDSON,. prospective Labour candi- date for the Eccles Division of Lancashire, said their object was to get at the workers, and now. it was for Warrington folk to say whether they 1. would have a candidate who would. be able to advocate the principles put before them. There was, a growing support Of Socialism, and one wopdered if the jury at Aisgill chsaster had not been touched with Socialism when. they sought to get behind the legal rulings of the Coroner, and not place the blame on the man on the footplate, but on those really responsible. (Applause.)

State sends out an army to assist the railway directors to defeat the men, and in _ smaller strikes the police are sent out. Both state- ments are true, but it is not the fault of the State as a State. So long as the workers con- tinue to send their masters to make the laws and govern the State the powers of the State will be used on the side of the masters, but the workers acquire the wisdom to forget about Liberalism and Toryism, and combine to send their own party tO control the State, then the baton of the policeman and the rifle of the soldier will no longer be used to protect employers when men are fighting, for .better conditions. The I.L.P. means to organise in- dustrially, and to organise politically.

. • I suppose that in Warrington there are some people who cannot see the need for a third party. They say we have had Liberals and Tories ever shice the State commenced in its modern form, and why cannot you be content to work through this .one or other of these parties? If the Tories or Liberals are desirous of redressing your wrong, why have they not done it during the past 100 years of our indus- trial system?
Making a "Second Part."

girtere esxt is of Why do conditions like they are to-day in the industrial vr Everybody m labour is concerned there is not a pin difference between officipl Liberalism and offi- point of O.NNI,s o r Id where f the NV avrirtianl cial Toryism. But we are not trying to create a third party. .Liberalism and Toryism are two sections .of one party. We are trying to create a second party to represent the interests ; of the Worker. - . We meet as the I.L.P. . with criticisms, from the Syndicalists and other Socialist sections, who said, Why then do you go to Parliament and ask for reforms? They say—arid they say very truly—that reforms will never solve the industrial problem. They said if the workers have the power to do things for themselves why do you, as the I.L.P. do, go to the State and ask the State to do it for you? Why not do it by direct action? Well, I say Labour representa- tion is as much direct action by the workers as is the Syndicalist strike. What we do is to-hwite you to help us to become the mastdrs of ,the State, to compel it to do our (the workers') bidding. (Applause.)
What is the Good-?

The object of the Independent Labour party is to educate the community in the principles of Socialism. It is to bring the working classes party politics and to give them a plat- their own, from which to fight their What is the good of ruling the State if you cannot rule the brewery and the soap works; where you are employed? Why call youi selves democrats if your masters can turn you out to starve, and they can do that without lily test pro- upon your part. It is not democra--ty if it does not.control the food supplies. Whoever controls the cupboard is master of the situa- tion- and So long as the landowners and great formbol latt t f:. f caPitaliSts are able to dictate to you the terms upon Which. you *all be allowed to live end labOU, you are -not free in any sns cf the word- (Applause.}
Completing Radicalism.
Socialism thus comes to complete the work of 'Radicalism. Our fathers fought for the vote to control the State. We are lighting for Socialism to control the rhole production c,f the world.

There are other Socialist societies beside ours, but they have not yet' learned the problems that we are attacking. Then why, you might ask, does not our Socialism make greater headway? is not because of the Liberal party, the Tory It parfy, the Church, or the Press, or the Capital- ist system, but because of the. apathy and ignorant indifference of our own class. Before we can make one step towards Socialism we have got to organise the working class into a impossible, and to achieve it we self-tonscious, self-respecting party of their Until this has been done progress is tpracticallYo make the basis of our movement own. so simple that an elementary school child can understand it. shall haNr

when‘ith cany you one outcome of this meeting will be a large ophaeceession to the Independent Labour party in Warrington. I want you to build up your labour forces so that you can get Labour men and women into your Town COuncil, for you want to administer the laws, as well as a majority of Labour members, and then you . make them. I hope to see your Town Council /1 see about the House of Commons, and fill the House of Commons with Labour members Socialism at once comes within your reach. When that time comes the organised Labour movement of he world will say to its rulers: "If you want war, go and do the fighting your- self. We have no quarrels and we shall use. all our power even to the extent of an Inter- national, universal, revolutionary strike to pre- vent war occurring between any two countries." (Applause.),•

div.head: SOCIALISTS AND REFORM
div.p: SOCIALISTS AND REFORM

• • He , argued that the Socialist party were re- sponsible for forcing on reforms. The Liberal Party passed the Old Age Pensions Bill, but it was forced from them by the Socialists. The Liberals Nirould have' done nothing at all until, after 20 or 30 years of promises, were they not rushed on by the Socialists. If they in War- rington were keen on britiging the time when warfare shall be no more, it could only be got. through a Socialist movement of International scope.

The Tories were now promising to relieve,the workers from the tyranny of trade unionism. The Tories had no need to talk about liberty. They saw their liberty by the descending ,of Smith, Carson and Company on the. filthy plains of Ulster, asking the officers not to fight against the Ulster men in the Ulster field, and telling Tommy Atkins to turn their rifles on the people fighting in the industrial field of the country.

div.head: MR. KEIR HARDIE'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. KEIR HARDIE'S SPEECH.

Mr. KEIR HARDIE reviewed the history of the Independent Labour party, and said that meet- ing was not political in )he usual sense. If it were a gathering in suport of a Labour candi- date in Warrington, as he hoped to have the ple sure of attending in Warrington before lon I, that could be a different 'matter. He pr ceeded to review what had happened in the 21 years. Greater solidarity characterised the working-class movement than 21 years ago. They now realised that they were up against not so much trade as ,labour questions. They recognised that the interests of the wOrkers, Whether they be scavengers, artis,ans, or school teachers, were one and identical, and if one section suffered all must suffer.

They saw that illustrated in the Dublin strike. At that moment a ship was about to sail from Manchester acrosS to Dublin laden with provi- sions, as proof that the workers of England, Scotland and Wales were going to stand by their Irish comrades. That was a typical illustra- tion of the solidarity in the ranks of labour.
A Question of Syndicalism.

We have got to the stage, said Mr. Hardie, when the trade union movement is solidly show- ing Vigour and 'encouraging strikes, disputes, agitations and organisations, but inside the trade union movement a small section has grown 'up, which calls itself Syndicalist, and which seeks to cast aside the asset of political Power in seeking to achieve the emancipation of labour.

I have said from the beginning, and I knew Syndicalism years ago, before it was so named in this country, that there is much that is good in the Syndicalist movement, in so far as it teaches the workers to rely upon themselves and their own power to achieve their own emancipation. But the Syndicalists go beyond that, and say to the working classes that the State is their enemy, that it is a Capitalist State, organised to crush the worker. It is then the Syndicalists become a bit confused. What is the State? It is anything the citizens care to make it. At the present moment the British State is a combination of the old feudal element and the modern capitalist system, and it exists primarily for •the purpose of main- taining the existing oyder of society anq pro- tect the rights- of property.
To Defeat the Men.
The Syndicalists say—and they say truly— that when the railwaymen come on strike the

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" CLAUDIAN."

" Claudian," the late Wilson Barrett's Roman drama, occupies the boards at the Royal Court Theatre this week./ The play is too well known to require any word of commendation, as a play, from us. But we may be allowed a word of praise for those who, under Mr. Wm. Maclaren's leadership, are interpreting the con- ceptions of the late author-actor. Mr. Maclaren himself as Claudian, and Miss Lily C. Boardman as Almida, sustain their respec- tive parts" with power and dignity, and a well- balanced cOmpany give them every support.

NEXT WEEK. \'‘ Proof,", which will be resented next week by Mr. and Mrs. William Maelar,en's company, is a standing denial of ale oft-repeateid state- ment that the public,_as a whole, cannot appre- ciate a work of art. The public can, and does, appreciate works of art, which base their claim to the title upon a sincere and sympathetic pre- sentment of,human interests and human emo- tions. Romantic without extravagance, pathe- tic without a trace of maudlin sentiment, humorous but never coarse, this play makes the majority of more recently-written dramas look as tawdry as the spangles of the circus set side by side with robes of State. The com- pany chosen to present the play has everywhere met With unqualified success, mad lids— been commented upon by Press and public alike, as one of tile very best now touring.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

A host of good things are to been at the hippodrome this week. Undoubtedly the palm must be-given to Aldrich, who is most accur- ately described as the man of many ,parts. He is one ,of the cleverest quick-change artists on the stage. 11e causes much mirth with his humorous sayings. Jean Schweller and Co. give an excellent musical turn, in which splen-

did tastd and refinement play a prominent part. Schwiner is an expert 'cellist, and gives a de- lightful entertainment. "The Vision of the Wandering 'Musician" i thoroughly appreci- ated, the special scenery and, effects being(' ar- tistically carried out. In his • latest success, The Village Bazaar," Randolph King executes some smart and humorous quick changes, and Is a refined entertainer. "A Daughter of Pleasure " is the title of a sketch depicting an episode of Parisian life, admirably presented by ,Miss Zerlina Harrington and Mr. J. G. Gra- hame. Layton and Douglas are instrumental soloists, with an extensive repertoire, and manipulates handbells and concertinas in an appreciable manner. The Sisters Allen are dainty duettists and dancers, who sing a popu- lar song in a catchy manner. They also dance well. Jewel St. Leger is a songstress with an excellent voice, and a. concertinist of some ability., Her items have been greatly enjoyed. The pictures on the biosCope are of the usual high standard.

NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. E. Frederick Hawley, Frances Haight and Co., present " The Bandit" next week at the Hippodrome. It is an immensely dramatic playlet, and should prove a big attraction. Other items will be Haley'sdluvehiles, 20 highly trained children dancers and vocalists; Vic- toria Campbell, the Scottish Nightingale; Chas. Heyn and Co., cornet and xylophone quartette; Farrow and Fiske, in harmony, wit and humour; R9wland Hill, popular "dame" come- dian; Tom E. Hood, original comedian; and Olga Du Barrie, in song and artistic mono- logues.

THEATRE ROYAL. The pictures during The woe]: have been of the usual high standard, and large audiences have been delighted, and entertained nightly. A capital programme has been arranged for to-night and for next week. The principal pic- tures will be "The Wager (Monday and Tues- day), "Wonderful Rays" (Wednesday and Thursday), and "Return of Thundercloud's Spirit" (Friday and Saturday).

div.head: WEEK OF-SWIMS
div.p: A WEEK OF-SWIMS
The Warrington Club and Other Interesting Galas.
WELL-CONTESTED EVENTS.

A full and varied programme, and a large and enthusiastic attendance, despite the rain, characterised the 30th annual gala of the War- rington Swimming Club, which was held on Thursday evening in the Caporation Baths. One of the most interesting- events .was pro- vided by Miss Louise Wilkinson, a Preston lady, whose exhibition of life-saving was much admired. This young lady early in the present month distinguished herself by swimming from her native town to Lytham, a distance of nine miles--:--a feat which she accomplished in the re- markably good time of 1 hour 57 mindes,.espe- eialiy considering that after she had covered seven miles she was seized with cramp, and finished the remainder of the course .with the use of only one leg and one arm.- Alderman W. Bolton presided over the gala. Details The 50 yards scratch race fOr boYs drew 11 competitors. Thirteen season tickets had been offered as prizes, so that each ot the swimmers was rewarded. Prize-winners: S. Makin, F. Simpson, C. Graham, K. Ward, W. Bennett, F`; Simcock, S. Mounfield, B. Oxley, S. Spittle, W. Crawley, Smith. The 50 yards schoolboys' championship of Warrington was keenly contested, and resulted in a win for W. Brady, J. Nolan coming second, and N. Roberts third. The winner holds. for the next 12 months the," Henry Thornton" Per- petual Challenge Bowl. Time, 54 2-ssec. The 150 Yards Ciampionship.

Great interest centred in the 150 yards cham- pionship of Warrington and district. There were only four compe,titors, and it proved an, interesting affair, althdugh with the commence- ment of the third length the race resolved itself into a struggle between S. Roberts and H. Sisson. This state- of affairs contipued until •near the end of the penultimate sttige, when Iloberts took the lead, and showing his superi- ority, won the championship for the third time in succession by a quarter of a length. H. Sis- son finished second and E. Miller third. Time, 2min.

The 50 yards ladies' handicap took five heats to decide the finalists. Heat winners: Amy Fair, Amy Grounds, Ruth Balmford, Florrie Malkin, and Cissy Houghton. Result: 1, A. Grounds.; 2, Cissy Houghton; 3, FlOrrie Mal- kin; 4; Ruth Balmford. Close finish. ; The 50 yards club' handicap was rQsPonsiisle for the largest number of entries, and each of the five heats Were contested with the great- est interest.' Heat winners: H. Horrabin, T. Chantler, P. Higham, L. Graham and J. Peers. The result was close, there being very little between the contestants. L. Graham was the first to finish, but he was disqualified for start- ing before his handicapped tithe. Result: 1, Horrabin ; 2, Chantler ; 3, Higham. A Clever •Lady Performer.

Miss Wilkinson's performance was watched with interest. She executed. with marvellous ease what Would wear to be , very difficult ,evolutions, and which were exceedingly pic- turesque.. Her contributions consisted of such items as "revolving star," " ship wreck," and "water ,wheel," and it seemed, no matter how she lay on the water, that she could not pos- sibly sink. Later on her exhibition of life-sav- ing was warmly applauded.. In, the diving competition, eight entries were received,- and the result was declared: 1," W. O'Neil ; 2, A. T. Farrar. '. The police handicap of one length - caused much merriment on account of full uniform being a condition and an obstacle... Heat winners: P.C.'s Corbett, Grubb, Adcock, Brom- wich, and Keating. Result: 1, Grubb; 2, Cor- bett; 3, Keating; 4, Adcdck ;'5, Bromwich.

Warrington Win The Polo Match. During the evening Warrington and Wigan were engaged in a friendly water polo game. Defending the -shallow end, in the first half, Warrington-put up a good fight, and, imme- diately. following a good passing .movement, Turner put Warrington, in front with a _throw horn half-way„before play had been progress- ing a couple of minutes. Bennett equalised for the collierg, but at, half-time the local men were three up, to the one ify Wigan, Turner and Sisson adding the extra: goals.
Warrington took charge of -affairs after the interval, and Turner added his third goal, Pepper and Peers bringing the total to six. Result: Warrington, six goals; Wigan, one goal.
A humorous situation arose by a " hoax " newspaper boy refusing to quit the baths, ,and ended by his being knocked into the water and his " res Cue " by a " spectator."
The Prize Presentation.

At the conclusion :Alderman Bolton said he was pleased to see such a large gathering and such. a Success. He thought the prograinme had been appreciated by the ladies. They were going to .make the new • baths second to none.

Mrs. W. Bolton presented the prizes to the winners. As an incentive- to the ladies, all who did not obtain one of the advertised prizes was presented with a souvenir of the occasion. The arrangements were admirably carried out by Mr. S. Ince, the hon. secretary, with Mr. B. A. Pepper as his assistant, and Mr. J. Wilkinson, the hon. tredsurer. The officials were: Judges, Messrs. A. Ashton, W. Furnival, n. T. Harding and A. 1305c0w ; starters, Messrs. j. A. Barlow and J. Critchley ; timekeeper, Mr. T. S. Pemberton. competitors' stewards, Messrs. A. Beddard, J. Newton and F. Garside ; stewards, Messrd. li. Furnival, P. Higham, P. Grall4m, P. Marsh and A. Ashton. SECONDARY SCHOOL ANNUAL GALA. Increasing Number of Entries. The annual swimming gala for the students connected with the Warrington Secondary School was held in the Corporation baths on Thursday afternoon. A large amount of. in- terest is taken in the event by parents of the seholars, ,and a capital programme of races was gone through, before a large number of spectators:

The coinpetitorS .were more numerous than last year, and this gave Mr. E. S. A. Robson, the headmaster, a great deal of satisfaction, as also did the capital swimming by some of the scholars. In the one length girls' handicap, Muriel Critchley, who went at "go," was suc- cessful out of nine swimmers, and she was also announced later as the girl champion. Ruth Balmford was second. Young Bell, who started at "six," won the boys' two lengths handicap, away from nine other boys, and Grant was second. The race for girl beginners one width of the bath was won by 'Miss D. Darbyshire, with Doris Parker second, whilst a promising boy swimmer named Newall, won the length race for boy beginners, the second prize being won hy young Pugh. Miss Ethel Roberts won the girls' two lengths handicap, Miss R. Balniford being second. In the boys' neatest dive competition, A. Farrar was suc- cessful, with Bailey second, whilst ,Ethel Roberts and Ada 'Leigh were first and selond in the neat diving competition for girls. A four lengths handicap for boys was won by D. Cooper, with Grant second. Cooper was also awarded Mr. Robson prize for the champion boy swimmer. A girls' squadron race Was Won by 'Ethel Roberts' team', and a boys' squadron race was won by D. Cooper's team, Mrs. Baxter, wife of one of the masters, gracefully presented thg, prizes and congratu- lated the successful cdffipetitors. Miss Muriel Critchley presented Mrs. Baxter with a beautiful bouquet. Mr. Robson, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Baxter, referred to the increasing, inter- est taken in the event by parents. The entries were rather more than last year, and the begin- ners were coming forward better. He hoped they would have an even larger number of entries next year. They had seen an interest- ing exhibition, and their thanks were due to Mrs. Baxter, who had so kindly presented the prizes. (Hear, hear.) He had also great pleas- ure in handing his prize to,the boys' champion. Mr. Baxter briefly replied on behalf of his wife.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S SCHOOLS' GALA.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S SCHOOLS' GALA.

The sixth afinual swimming gala for childreo attending the Elementary Schools was held last night. .The winners were :—One-bread for boys under 14: 1, J. Crozier (St. Mary's); 2' B. "HULLO RAGTIME." Lancaslike folk have been delighted with tho presentatio'n of the famous revue ",Hullo, Bag:, time," at the New Theatre, Manchester, UT week, and Warringtonians have figured pro 9: nently in the audiences. Those .whci went e-si pecting solemn drama were disappointed, btli the huge majority who went unbiased, foul, themselves swept 'away with a breezy flood 0` music, mirth, colour and whirlwind dancing; The "Wedding Glide" is the crowning poia: in a masterpiece of stage setting, acting an“ effect. The artistes are first class. 'Mr. Lo Hearn makes many a side ache with his 1001; ter-provoking business. Mr. George Gregor. !, was equally as humoroy, and the chief lam parts were charmingly 'filled by Miss TeddY Gerrard, Miss Maud Tiffany, the belle of We. rag-time vocalists, and ,Miss 4Maud Ward, all- other capable singer.

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. ELECTRICITY DEPARTMENT. The Electricity ,and Tramways Committee of the county Borough of Warrington are prepared to receive TENPERS for the following:- 1. LOW TENSION CABLE. 2. LOW TENSION FEEDER PANEL. Specifications and Form of Tender can be obtained from the undersigned on payment of One Guinea for each specification, which will be returned on receipt of a bona-fide Tender. Five shillings each will be charged for extra copies- of either specification. Tenders, addressed to the "Chairman of the Electricity and Tramways Committee, Town Hall, Warrington," must be sealed with wax, and endorsed Tender for Cable," or "Feeder Panel," as the case may be, and delivered not later than 12 o'clock noon on Tuesday, October 14th, 1913. The lowest or any, Tender will not necessarily be accepted. F. V. L. MATHIAS, Borough Electrical & Tramways Engineer. Howley. Warrington.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES. CHILD FATALLY SCALDED. The death occurred at the Runcorn Cottage Hospital of Phyllis Darbyshire, aged two years, daughter of Samuel Darbyshire, chemical works labourer, who lived at 2, Ivy-street, Runcorn. On the 16th inst., the child, in her play, acci- dentally pulled over a saucepan containing boil- ing pea soup. She was severely scalded. FARM FIRES CAUSED BY TRAMPS. Supt. Owen told the magistrates at Runcorn on Monday that they were repeatedly having complaints from the farmers concerning per- sons sleeping in their farm buildings. It was a serious thing, and many of those people were responsible for farm fires. Thomas Johnson, a Frodsham man, was discovered asleep in an out- building on Prospect Farm, Halton. When searched he was found to have in his possession three boxes of matches, two pipes, and other things, but no money. Fourteen days' hard labour was the penalty imposed. NEW FACTORY FOR WIDNES. It is announced that an important Manchester firm of blousemakers are to open a factory at Widnes. The intimation that several hundred girls will be required has been welcomed in a town entirely devoid of outlets for female labour. It is stated that Widnes furnishes more domes- tic servants for the surrounding residential towns than any industrial centre in Lancashire, and no difficulty has been experienced in en- gaging the number of girls required by the firm in question. EXPRESS HAS A NARROW ESCAPE. An alarming mishap befell the Leeds to Liver- pool express (L. and N.-W.) at Widnes on Mon- day morning. The train was passing through Widnes Station, when it dashed into a porter's truck, which was being wheeled across the line by Richard Woods. The truck, which was of a large and heavy make, was hauled about twenty yards, and hampers of fruit and vegetables with which it was laden were strewn all over the line. Fortunately, the engine kept the metals, and the dismantled truck fell clear of the line upon which the train was travelling. The por- ter Woods had a very narrow escape.
